Office of Personnel Management
5 CFR Parts 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, and 10
[Docket ID: OPM-2026-0562]
RIN 3206-AP19
(
printed page 75161)
AGENCY:
Office of Personnel Management.
ACTION:
Direct final rule; confirmation of effective date.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is confirming the effective date of the direct final rule updating and amending obsolete and outdated provisions of the Civil Service Rules. OPM received no significant adverse comments and therefore confirms that the direct final rule became effective as scheduled.
DATES:
The effective date of October 13, 2026, for the direct final rule published on August 14, 2026 (
91 FR 52475
) is confirmed.
ADDRESSES:
Please refer to the direct final rule published at
91 FR 52475
(August 14, 2026) for address information.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Aaron Gottesman, Office of Personnel Management, Office of the Director, (202) 606-1300.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
On August 14, 2026, OPM published a direct final rule at
91 FR 52475
removing or updating obsolete and outdated provisions of the Civil Service Rules, codified at
5 CFR parts 2
,
3
,
5
,
6
,
9
, and
10
. The direct final rule implements Section 2(g) of Executive Order (E.O.) 14410,
Implementing Schedule Policy/Career in the Excepted Service,
91 FR 34893
(June 10, 2026), which directed the Director of OPM to “take steps to prepare and issue revisions that remove or update, as applicable, obsolete provisions of the Civil Service Rules that do not substantively affect agency operations.”
The direct final rule stated that it would become effective on October 13, 2026, unless OPM received a significant adverse comment by September 14, 2026. It defined a significant adverse comment as one that explains: (1) why the rule is inappropriate, including challenges to the rule's underlying premise or approach; or (2) why the direct final rule will be ineffective or unacceptable without a change. A comment recommending an addition to the rule was not to be considered significant and adverse unless it explained how the direct final rule would be ineffective without the addition. 91 FR at 52477.
II. Comment Analysis
OPM received four comments during the comment period. A reference to a comment provides the location of the item in the public record (
i.e.,
the two-digit number associated with the location in the docket.) Comments filed in response to the direct final rule are available at
https://www.regulations.gov/​comment/​OPM-2026-0562-00nn
,
where “nn” is the comment number. None of the four comments is a significant adverse comment. Two commenters support the rule and recommend additions to the administrative record. Two commenters oppose the rule on grounds that rest on misreadings of the rule and of the existing Civil Service Rules and that concern actions this rule does not take. OPM addresses each comment below.
A. Comment 02
Comment:
The commenter supports the rule's objectives and recommends five safeguards: (1) an express confirmation that no amendment, deletion, redesignation, or terminology change may be read to modify competitive-service status, veterans' preference, appointment or reinstatement eligibility, due-process protections, or administrative, grievance, or appeal rights; (2) controls to ensure that variations under
5 CFR 5.1
are consistently evaluated and documented, with a public record identifying the provision involved, the supporting circumstances, the variation's scope and duration, and information sufficient to assess consistency across agencies; (3) a centralized, permanent, searchable, and archived repository on OPM's website for variations, with publication within a defined period; (4) an express confirmation that the disability-terminology revisions to
5 CFR 3.1(b)
are terminology-only; and (5) preservation in the rulemaking record of the analysis supporting OPM's determination that no current positions, incumbents, appointments, or agency operations depend on
5 CFR 6.8(a)
through
(c)
.
Response:
The comment does not challenge the rule's premise or approach and does not contend that the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without the recommended additions. It is not a significant adverse comment. OPM responds to the recommendations as follows.
First, OPM confirms that the direct final rule makes no change to any substantive right, obligation, or protection. No amendment, removal, redesignation, or terminology change in the rule modifies competitive status, veterans' preference, appointment or reinstatement eligibility, or any adverse action, grievance, or appeal right.
Second and third, the reorganization of
5 CFR 5.1
retains, without substantive change, the four elements the Director must note in the official record whenever a variation is granted. Those provisions are the operative controls on the variation authority, and the rule leaves them intact. The commenter's further recommendations concerning the design, retention practices, and posting timelines of OPM's website concern the administration of the website rather than the text of Civil Service Rule V and are outside the scope of this rule.
Fourth, OPM confirms that the revisions to
5 CFR 3.1(b)
are terminology-only. Revised § 3.1(b) retains the same three classes of employees, the same requirement of at least two years of satisfactory service in a position excepted from the competitive service, and the same predicate of an employing-agency recommendation subject to requirements OPM may prescribe. It does not narrow eligibility, alter any substantive standard, or reduce any opportunity to acquire competitive status.
(
printed page 75162)
Fifth, the basis for OPM's determination regarding
5 CFR 6.8(a)
through
(c)
is set out in the preamble to the direct final rule, which traces each paragraph to the Executive order from which it derives and explains why each is obsolete. The preamble is part of the rulemaking record. Prospective removal of these paragraphs does not affect the interpretation of personnel actions taken while they were in effect; those actions remain governed by the law in effect when they were taken, and the text of prior editions of the Code of Federal Regulations remains publicly available.
B. Comment 03
Comment:
The commenter supports the rule, states expressly that its comment is not a significant adverse comment, and suggests that OPM add to the record a confirmation, parallel to the one the direct final rule provides for
5 CFR 6.8(a)
through
(c)
, that no current positions, incumbents, appointments, or agency operations depend on the provisions removed at
5 CFR 2.1(c)
,
2.2(a)(4)
, and
2.3
.
Response:
The comment recommends an addition and does not contend that the rule would be ineffective without it. It is not a significant adverse comment. OPM adopts the suggestion. For the reasons stated in the direct final rule with respect to Civil Service Rule II, 91 FR at 52475-76, OPM confirms that no current positions, incumbents, appointments, or agency operations depend on the provisions removed at
5 CFR 2.1(c)
,
2.2(a)(4)
, and
2.3
. Since the Postal Reorganization Act of 1970, appointments in the Postal Service have been made under procedures established by the Postal Service rather than through OPM-administered competitive examination,
39 U.S.C. 1001(b)
, and the apportionment requirement formerly codified at
5 U.S.C. 3306
was repealed in 1978. Public Law 95-228, 92 Stat. 25.
C. Comments 04 and 05
Comments:
Both commenters characterize their comments as significant adverse comments and ask OPM to withdraw the direct final rule and reissue it as a proposed rule. Both raise two objections. First, they object that the rule revises the authority citations for
5 CFR parts 2
,
3
,
5
,
6
,
9
, and
10
to cite
E.O. 14410
, which they contend embeds Schedule Policy/Career in the Code of Federal Regulations, legitimizes it, and effects a substantive change to civil service tenure, merit principles, and appeal rights without notice and comment. Comment 05 adds that amending Civil Service Rule VI under the authority of
E.O. 14410
normalizes Schedule Policy/Career alongside the other excepted service schedules. Second, they object that the amendments to
5 CFR 3.2
,
5.1
, and
6.1
remove mandatory
Federal Register
publication requirements and replace them with publication on OPM's website, which they contend reduces transparency and lacks retention and indexing safeguards; comment 04 adds that this conflicts with
5 U.S.C. 552(a)(1)
and prevents effective judicial review under
5 U.S.C. 706
. Comment 04 further contends that the rule exceeds OPM's authority under the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 and the major questions doctrine by diminishing tenure protections without clear congressional authorization.
Response:
Having considered both comments in full, OPM has determined that neither is a significant adverse comment. Both rest on a misreading of what the rule does, and both direct their objections at Presidential and regulatory actions taken in other proceedings that this rule neither effects nor alters.
1. Authority citations.
An authority citation is not an enforceable regulatory provision. Under the regulations of the Administrative Committee of the Federal Register, each section of a document subject to codification must be covered by a citation of the authority under which it is issued, and an agency that amends a part must set out the complete authority citation for that part and revise it when the authority for the amendment differs from the authority previously cited.
1 CFR 21.40
,
21.41
,
21.43
. The authority citation identifies the source of authority for the regulatory text; it confers no authority, imposes no obligation, and has no operative effect of its own.
The Civil Service Rules are prescribed by the President under
5 U.S.C. 3301
and
3302
and are amended by Executive order.
E.O. 14410
is such an order: Section 2 of
E.O. 14410
directly amended Civil Service Rules I, III, VI, and XI, and Section 2(g) directed the Director of OPM to prepare and issue the revisions made by this rule. Citing
E.O. 14410
in the authority citation for each part amended by this rule therefore accurately identifies the directive under which the amendments were issued. OPM's regulations implementing Schedule Policy/Career in
5 CFR part 213
were issued through notice-and-comment rulemaking at
91 FR 5653-54
(Feb. 6, 2026). This rule does not amend § 6.2 or part 213. Apart from revising the authority citation for part 6 and redesignating current § 6.8(d) and (e) as § 6.8(a) and (b) without change to their text, the only amendments this rule makes to Civil Service Rule VI are the replacement of an obsolete annual-report reference in § 6.1(a) and the removal of three obsolete grandfathering provisions in § 6.8(a) through (c), none of which concerns Schedule Policy/Career or any other excepted service schedule. Objections to Schedule Policy/Career are objections to
E.O. 14410
and to the part 213 rulemaking, not to this rule, and are outside its scope.
2. Publication provisions.
The premise of the second objection is mistaken. None of the three provisions at issue required publication in the
Federal Register
. Before this rule, § 3.2 required that statements of reasons for noncompetitive appointments be published “in OPM's annual reports”; § 5.1 required that variation decisions be published “in a Federal Personnel Manual Letter or Bulletin and in the Director's next annual report”; and § 6.1(a) required that excepted positions be listed “in OPM's annual report for the fiscal year in which the exceptions are made.” The general annual report was eliminated by the Congressional Reports Elimination Act of 1980 and the Federal Personnel Manual was abolished in 1994. Congressional Reports Elimination Act of 1980, Public Law 96-470,  121, 94 Stat. 2237, 2241;
5 U.S.C. 1308 note
(1994). The rule therefore removes no
Federal Register
publication requirement. To the contrary, revised § 5.1(c) and revised § 6.1(a) add the
Federal Register
as an authorized publication where the prior text did not mention it, and the rule leaves undisturbed current § 6.1(c), which independently requires that notice of OPM's decisions granting authority to make appointments to excepted positions be published in the
Federal Register
, as well as
5 CFR 213.103
, which requires
Federal Register
publication of Schedule A, B, C, D, and Policy/Career appointing authorities.
Nor does the rule alter any obligation under
5 U.S.C. 552(a)(1)
. That provision applies by its own force; the Civil Service Rules neither implement nor displace it, and nothing in the revised text authorizes OPM to withhold from the
Federal Register
any matter that statute requires be published there. The assertion that website publication prevents judicial review under
5 U.S.C. 706
identifies no agency action whose reviewability depends on the medium in which it is published.
3. Statutory authority.
Comment 04 identifies no provision of this rule that alters any tenure protection, adverse action procedure, or appeal right. The rule removes obsolete provisions and updates obsolete references, and the
(
printed page 75163)
direct final rule identified the basis for each change and explained why each has no current substantive effect. 91 FR at 52475-77. An argument that OPM lacks authority to diminish tenure protections is not an argument against a rule that does not diminish them.
Because comments 04 and 05 misdescribe the rule's provisions and direct their objections to actions this rule does not take, they do not explain why the rule is inappropriate or why it would be ineffective or unacceptable without change. They are not significant adverse comments within the meaning of the direct final rule.
III. Confirmation of Effective Date
OPM did not receive a significant adverse comment on the direct final rule. Accordingly, OPM confirms that the amendments published at
91 FR 52475
on August 14, 2026, became effective on October 13, 2026.

Office of Personnel Management
5 CFR Part 178
[Docket ID: OPM-2026-0364]
RIN 3206-AP10
AGENCY:
Office of Personnel Management.
ACTION:
Direct final rule; confirmation of effective date.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) confirms that the direct final rule updating the procedures for submitting certain administrative claims to OPM became effective as scheduled.
DATES:
The effective date of September 29, 2026, for the direct final rule published on July 31, 2026 (
91 FR 48231
), is confirmed.
ADDRESSES:
Please refer to the direct final rule published at
91 FR 48231
(July 31, 2026) for address information.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Joe Knouff, by email at
adjudications@opm.gov
or by telephone at (202) 606-7948.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
On July 31, 2026, OPM published in the
Federal Register
a direct final rule titled “Procedures for Settling Claims” (
91 FR 48231
) (the direct final rule or DFR), amending
5 CFR part 178, subpart A
. The DFR removed outdated office and contact information from § 178.102, required claimants and their representatives to submit claims through OPM's electronic filing (eFile) system absent an OPM-authorized exemption, and required claimants to provide additional information to support OPM's review of claims for compensation and leave under
31 U.S.C. 3702(a)(2)
, money due deceased employees under
5 U.S.C. 5583
, and proceeds of canceled checks payable to the beneficiaries of deceased veterans under
38 U.S.C. 5121
and
5122
.
OPM issued the DFR under the exception for rules of “agency organization, procedure, or practice” in
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
, and, in the alternative, under the good cause exception in
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
. OPM stated that, absent significant adverse comment submitted by August 31, 2026, the DFR would take effect on September 29, 2026.
As the DFR explained, a significant adverse comment is a comment that explains why the rule is inappropriate, including by challenging its underlying premise or approach, or why the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without a change. In applying that standard, OPM treats a comment as significant and adverse if:
1. The comment opposes the rule and provides a reason sufficient to require a substantive response in a notice-and-comment process—for example, because the comment causes OPM to reevaluate its position or conduct additional analysis, raises an issue serious enough to warrant a substantive response to clarify or complete the record, or raises a relevant issue not previously addressed by OPM;
2. The comment proposes a change or addition to the rule, and it is apparent that the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without incorporating it; or
3. The comment causes OPM to make a substantive change to the rule.
As discussed in Section II, OPM evaluated each comment received against these criteria. For the reasons explained below, OPM determined that no comment, standing alone or in combination with other comments, rises to the level of a significant adverse comment. Accordingly, OPM confirms that the amendments to
5 CFR part 178, subpart A
, published at
91 FR 48231
(July 31, 2026), became effective on September 29, 2026.
II. Public Comment Analysis
OPM received five timely comments in response to the DFR. A reference to a comment provides the location of the item in the public record (
i.e.,
the two-digit number associated with the location in the docket). Comments filed in response to the direct final rule are available at
https://www.regulations.gov/​comment/​OPM-2026-0364-00nn
where “nn” is the comment number.
One commenter submitted a detailed legal analysis organized in nine sections (Comment 02). Two commenters submitted identical form-letter text opposing the rule (Comments 03 and 05). One commenter submitted an individually written comment (Comment 04). One commenter submitted an extensive formal comment styled as a legal demand, raising a series of statutory and constitutional arguments together with a list of document requests (Comment 06).
OPM has reviewed and carefully considered all five comments. Because several comments raise overlapping points, they are addressed together by subject below.
Use of the Direct Final Rule Procedure
Comments 02, 03, 05, and 06 argue that OPM improperly proceeded by direct final rule. Comments 03 and 05 contend that a rule that “substantially affect[s]” the rights of regulated parties cannot qualify for the procedural-rule exception in
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
merely because of its form, citing
American Hospital Ass'n
v.
Bowen,
834 F.2d 1037, 1045 (D.C. Cir. 1987), and
JEM Broadcasting Co.
v.
FCC,
22 F.3d 320, 326-27 (D.C. Cir. 1994). Comment 06 similarly argues that the rule is “substantively arbitrary” and cites
Batterton
v.
Marshall,
648 F.2d 694 (D.C. Cir. 1980), for the proposition that a rule “extinguish[ing] statutory property claims” cannot be procedural.
An “oft-cited formulation,” drawn from
Batterton
itself, is that the “critical
(
printed page 75164)
feature” of the procedural exception “is that it covers agency actions that do not themselves alter the rights or interests of parties, although it may alter the manner in which the parties present themselves or their viewpoints to the agency.”
JEM Broadcasting,
22 F.3d at 326 (quoting
Batterton,
648 F.2d at 707).
Batterton
also observed that the exception does not reach agency action that “trenches on substantial private rights and interests,” 648 F.2d at 708, but the D.C. Circuit has since “gradually shifted focus from asking whether a given procedure has a `substantial impact' on parties” to asking whether the action “encodes a substantive value judgment or puts a stamp of approval or disapproval on a given type of behavior.”
American Hospital Ass'n,
834 F.2d at 1047. Under either formulation, a rule prescribing the method through which a claim is submitted is procedural. The D.C. Circuit has sustained application-processing rules as procedural “even though `failure to observe [them] might cause the loss of substantive rights,' ”
JEM Broadcasting,
22 F.3d at 327 (quoting
Ranger
v.
FCC,
294 F.2d 240, 244 (D.C. Cir. 1961)), where, as here, the rule “did not change the substantive standards” by which the agency evaluates the merits.
JEM Broadcasting,
22 F.3d at 327. That is the character of this rule: it prescribes the manner in which a claim is submitted without altering who may file a claim, the substantive standard OPM applies in deciding it, the evidence required to support it, or the duration of any codified time limit. Where a filing requirement bears on timeliness, the D.C. Circuit asks whether the requirement is “so short as to foreclose effective opportunity to make one's case on the merits.”
Lamoille Valley R.R. Co.
v.
ICC,
711 F.2d 295, 328 (D.C. Cir. 1983), quoted in
JEM Broadcasting,
22 F.3d at 328. The exemption process in § 178.102(e)(2), which may be invoked by telephone or in writing as described below, and the agency-submission option in § 178.102(b) preserve that opportunity. The procedural exception therefore applies.
The reliance of Comments 03 and 05 on
JEM Broadcasting
is unpersuasive for the proposition asserted.
JEM Broadcasting,
as an alternative holding, sustained the FCC's rule dismissing incomplete license applications without opportunity to amend against the identical argument, reasoning that “procedure impacts on outcomes and thus can virtually always be described as affecting substance, but to pursue that line of analysis results in the obliteration of the distinction that Congress demanded.” 22 F.3d at 326-27 (quoting
Air Transport Ass'n of America
v.
Department of Transportation,
900 F.2d 369, 383 (D.C. Cir. 1990) (Silberman, J., dissenting), remanded, 498 U.S. 1077 (1991), vacated as moot, 933 F.2d 1043 (D.C. Cir. 1991)). Applying the same reasoning here, just because a filing method
may
affect the outcome of a particular claim does not convert a procedural rule into a substantive one.
Additionally, because the rule qualifies for the procedural-rule exception in
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
on the basis just described, the alternative good-cause finding under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
is not necessary to sustain the rule. OPM nonetheless notes, in response to the citation in Comments 03 and 05 to
Mack Trucks, Inc.
v.
EPA,
682 F.3d 87, 93 (D.C. Cir. 2012), that the DFR's good-cause statement was offered as an independent and alternative basis, and its sufficiency (or lack thereof) does not affect the validity of the rule under the separate and independently adequate
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
exception.
Effective Date
Comment 02 correctly identifies an inconsistency in the DFR's preamble. The
DATES
caption stated that the rule “is effective September 29, 2026 unless significant adverse comment is submitted by August 31, 2026.” 91 FR at 48231. Later in the same document, the preamble indicated that “this direct final rule will become effective 45 days after the comment period expires.”
Id.
at 48232. The reference to “45 days” was a drafting error. The
DATES
caption—which under Office of the Federal Register drafting convention states the document's operative dates—consistently identified September 29, 2026, as did the transition provision in the same document (“Claims filed before September 29, 2026 will be processed under the requirements in effect on the date of submission or postmark.” 91 FR at 48231). Comments 03, 04, 05 and 06, which addressed the effective date, correctly identified September 29, 2026, as the operative deadline, with Comment 04 urging OPM to act “before the September 29, 2026 deadline.” Comment 02, which identified the inconsistency, likewise recognized September 29, 2026, as the date stated in the
DATES
caption and in the transition provision, and asked OPM to confirm the operative effective date. OPM confirms that September 29, 2026, was the effective date of the amendments to
5 CFR part 178, subpart A
. A drafting error in the preamble discussion, which did not appear in the
DATES
caption, the transition provision, or the regulatory text, does not constitute a significant adverse comment.
Paperwork Reduction Act Status of the eFile Information Collection
Comments 02, 03, 05, and 06 ask OPM to confirm the status of Office of Management and Budget (OMB) review of the information collection associated with the eFile system (OMB Control Number 3206-NEW) and to address the relationship between that review and the rule's effective date. OMB approved this collection under OMB Control Number 3206-0282. Comment 02 also asks whether the burden estimate has been revised to reflect the addition of other appeal types to the eFile system. The 30-day notice (
91 FR 46802
(July 24, 2026)) reflects a revised estimate of 1,286 respondents and 13,039 annual burden hours, which reflects the full scope of appeals available through the eFile system.
As to the interaction between Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) clearance and the rule's effective date: consistent with
44 U.S.C. 3512(a)
, OPM confirms that it did not decline to accept, or delay action on, a claim submitted through the eFile system, nor deny a request for an exemption under § 178.102(e)(2), on the basis of the collection's control-number status. The assigned control number is displayed on the eFile system's public-facing pages.
The Discretionary Exemption From Electronic Filing
All five comments raise, in varying terms, concerns about § 178.102(e)(2), which allows OPM to exempt “a party or representative” from the eFiling requirement in its “sole and exclusive discretion,” and which provides that OPM “will not find good cause for failing to file a claim timely if the party or representative fails to contact OPM to request an exemption before any deadline to file.” Commenters describe this combination as lacking defined criteria, a response timeline, or a means of reconsideration, and Comments 02, 04, and 06 describe the requirement that an exemption request be made “as instructed on OPM's website” as placing an online-only contact method between offline filers and the accommodation meant to serve them.
OPM confirms that the standard governing exemption requests is the one described in the DFR's preamble: an exemption is available to “a party or representative who cannot reasonably file electronically.” 91 FR at 48232. Current contact information is available on OPM's website. Nonetheless, a party
(
printed page 75165)
or representative may request an exemption under § 178.102(e)(2) by contacting OPM using the telephone number or email address listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
caption of the DFR or of any successor document—both of which OPM publishes independently of, and without requiring access to, its website. OPM will treat a timely telephone or written exemption request the same as one submitted through OPM's website. OPM will likewise treat a documented, agency-side outage of the eFile system, and a claimant's literacy, disability, or other barrier to independently using the eFile system, as circumstances bearing on whether good cause exists for a late filing or a late exemption request under § 178.102(e)(2).
OPM has not adopted the requests to codify a fixed, non-discretionary tolling period for system outages (Comment 06) or a fixed response deadline for exemption requests (Comments 03 and 05). In OPM's experience administering this part for decades, claims-processing circumstances vary too widely to be usefully reduced to a single numerical rule, and a rigid rule risks producing arbitrary results in both directions. OPM likewise has not adopted Comment 02's alternative proposals that a timely exemption request toll the filing deadline, or that a non-electronic submission be deemed filed as of its original date once an exemption later issues, because such a provision would change how § 178.104 fixes the date on which a claim is received, a result the DFR did not propose and OPM does not adopt here. OPM will, however, treat a claimant's timely, good-faith attempt to contact OPM—whether by telephone, email, or a non-electronic filing—as bearing directly on whether good cause exists under § 178.102(e)(2). OPM's settlement of a claim remains subject to judicial review under § 178.107(b), which is unaffected by this rule.
Contact Information for the Denying Agency Official
Comments 03, 04, 05, and 06 note that § 178.102(a)(2), which asks a claimant to provide the name, address, telephone number, and email address of the agency official who denied the claim, may be difficult for some claimants to satisfy where the denial was issued by an office or an automated shared-service system rather than by a named individual, or where the claimant never received an individual staff member's contact information in the first place.
Section 178.102(a) already provides that a claim “should” include this information, together with “any other information which the claimant believes OPM should consider.” Consistent with OPM's existing practice under this part, a claim will not be rejected or delayed solely because a claimant cannot supply contact details for an individual agency official that were never provided to the claimant.
Cross-Reference to an Outdated Office Name
Comment 02 observes that the DFR removes the reference to the “Office of Merit Systems Oversight and Effectiveness” from § 178.102(e) as outdated, while § 178.207(b) and (c)—provisions the DFR did not amend—continue to direct disputed claims for money due deceased employees to that same office.
OPM limited its changes to sections that directly affect where or how a claim is filed or reviewed. OPM intends to conform the cross-references in § 178.207(b) and (c) to the office's current name, Merit System Accountability and Compliance, in a future rulemaking. The retained reference does not render this rule ineffective or unacceptable in the interim as the language in § 178.207(b) and (c) has no impact on claimants' ability to file a claim.
Electronic Service and the Written Record
Comment 02 asks whether a claimant's failure to observe an electronic posting in the eFile system will be treated as receipt for purposes that run a deadline or close the written record under § 178.105, given that eFile registration under § 178.102(e)(1)(ii) constitutes consent to electronic service and § 178.102(e)(1)(v) places responsibility on eFilers to monitor case activity.
Registration as an eFiler constitutes consent to electronic service. The responsibility to monitor case activity under § 178.102(e)(1)(v) is no different in kind from the obligation of a party who receives paper correspondence to review their mail. Where a claimant demonstrates that a technical failure of the eFile system, rather than the claimant's own inattention, prevented them from receiving or responding to a posting, that is a circumstance OPM will weigh in the same case-by-case manner it weighs any other question of good cause or excusable delay under this part. This rule does not foreclose that inquiry, and judicial review under § 178.107(b) remains available in any case where a claimant contends the written record was closed against them unfairly.
Requests To Withdraw the Rule and Retain Dual-Track Filing
Comments 03, 04, 05, and 06 ask OPM to withdraw the DFR and proceed by standard notice-and-comment rulemaking, and Comment 06 additionally proposes a specific severable alternative that would make eFile use voluntary for active civilian employees while permanently preserving mail and email intake for survivors, veterans' beneficiaries, retirees, and pro se claimants.
OPM has considered these requests together with the more specific points addressed above. The premise common to all of them—that the rule leaves claimants who cannot reasonably use the eFile system without a means of filing—is addressed by the exemption process in § 178.102(e)(2) and by the agency-assisted filing option in § 178.102(b). Because that accommodation already exists in the rule, OPM does not agree that permanent, parallel paper and email intake methods for entire categories of claimants are necessary.
III. Determination Regarding Significant Adverse Comment
OPM has evaluated each of the five comments received, individually and collectively, against the standard described in Section I. None opposes the rule on a ground that requires a substantive change to the regulatory text adopted in the DFR. The sentence in the preamble discussion regarding the rule's effective date was a drafting error; however, the same document provided notice of the effective date in the
DATES
caption, which is the date that is controlling for the Office of the Federal Register. No commenter disputed that the
DATES
caption identified September 29, 2026, as the effective date, and the one commenter that identified the inconsistency asked OPM to confirm the operative date, which this document does. The error does not bear on the substance of § 178.102 as adopted. The remaining points are either addressed on the merits above or, to the extent not separately discussed, were considered and do not alter this determination. None causes OPM to reevaluate the rule's underlying approach, none identifies a respect in which the rule as adopted would be ineffective or unacceptable absent a change to its text, and none has caused OPM to make a substantive change to the rule.
Accordingly, OPM confirms that the amendments to
5 CFR part 178, subpart A
, published at
91 FR 48231
(July 31, 2026), became effective on September 29, 2026.

5 CFR Part 551
[Docket ID: OPM-2026-0467]
RIN 3206-AO74
AGENCY:
Office of Personnel Management.
ACTION:
Direct final rule; confirmation of effective date.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) confirms that the direct final rule updating provisions concerning Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) claims submissions to OPM became effective as scheduled.
DATES:
The effective date of September 29, 2026, for the direct final rule published on July 31, 2026 (
91 FR 48236
), is confirmed.
ADDRESSES:
Please refer to the direct final rule published at
91 FR 48236
(July 31, 2026) for address information.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Joe Knouff, by email at
adjudications@opm.gov
or by telephone at (202) 606-7948.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
On July 31, 2026, OPM published in the
Federal Register
a direct final rule titled “FLSA Claims and Compliance” (
91 FR 48236
) (the direct final rule or DFR), amending
5 CFR part 551, subpart G
. The DFR removed outdated office and contact information, required claimants and their representatives to submit FLSA claims and supporting documents through OPM's electronic filing (eFile) system absent an OPM-authorized exemption, and required claims to include a verifiable signature, the employing agency's name, and the claimant's email address.
OPM issued the DFR under the exception for rules of “agency organization, procedure, or practice” in
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
, and, in the alternative, under the good cause exception in
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
. OPM stated that, absent significant adverse comment submitted by August 31, 2026, the DFR would take effect on September 29, 2026.
As the DFR explained, a significant adverse comment is a comment that explains why the rule is inappropriate, including by challenging its underlying premise or approach, or why the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without a change. In applying that standard, OPM treats a comment as significant and adverse if:
1. The comment opposes the rule and provides a reason sufficient to require a substantive response in a notice-and-comment process—for example, because the comment causes OPM to reevaluate its position or conduct additional analysis, raises an issue serious enough to warrant a substantive response to clarify or complete the record, or raises a relevant issue not previously addressed by OPM;
2. The comment proposes a change or addition to the rule, and it is apparent that the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without incorporating it; or
3. The comment causes OPM to make a substantive change to the rule.
As discussed in Section II, OPM evaluated each comment received against these criteria. For the reasons explained below, OPM determined that no comment, standing alone or in combination with other comments, rises to the level of a significant adverse comment. Accordingly, OPM confirms that the amendments to
5 CFR part 551, subpart G
, became effective on September 29, 2026.
II. Public Comment Analysis
OPM received eight timely comments in response to the DFR. A reference to a comment provides the location of the item in the public record (
i.e.,
the two-digit number associated with the location in the docket). Comments filed in response to the direct final rule are available at
https://www.regulations.gov/​comment/​OPM-2026-0467-00nn
where “nn” is the comment number.
One commenter submitted a detailed legal analysis organized in seven sections (Comment 03). Two commenters submitted identical letters addressed to OPM's point of contact, raising Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and back-pay arguments (Comments 05 and 06). One commenter submitted an anonymous individual comment describing accessibility and technology barriers (Comment 04). One commenter submitted an extensive formal comment styled as a legal demand, raising a series of statutory and constitutional arguments together with a list of document requests (Comment 07). Three commenters submitted comments that, while referencing this docket, did not address the subject matter of this rulemaking (Comments 02, 08, and 09).
OPM has reviewed and carefully considered all eight comments. Because several comments raise overlapping points, they are addressed together by subject below, with the originating comment or comments identified.
Use of the Direct Final Rule Procedure
Comments 05 and 06 argue that a rule that “substantially affect[s]” the rights of regulated parties cannot qualify for the procedural-rule exception in
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
merely because of its form, citing
American Hospital Ass'n
v.
Bowen,
834 F.2d 1037, 1045 (D.C. Cir. 1987), and
JEM Broadcasting Co.
v.
FCC,
22 F.3d 320, 326-27 (D.C. Cir. 1994). Comment 07 similarly argues that the rule is procedurally invalid because OPM did not establish good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
for a substantive rule.
An “oft-cited formulation,” drawn from
Batterton
itself, is that the “critical feature” of the procedural exception “is that it covers agency actions that do not themselves alter the rights or interests of parties, although it may alter the manner in which the parties present themselves or their viewpoints to the agency.”
JEM Broadcasting,
22 F.3d at 326 (quoting
Batterton
v.
Marshall,
648 F.2d 694, 707 (D.C. Cir. 1980)).
Batterton
also observed that the exemption does not reach agency action that “trenches on substantial private rights and interests,” 648 F.2d at 708, but the D.C. Circuit has since “gradually shifted focus from asking whether a given procedure has a `substantial impact' on parties” to asking whether the action “encodes a substantive value judgment or puts a stamp of approval or disapproval on a given type of behavior.”
American Hospital Ass'n,
834 F.2d at 1047. Under either formulation, a rule prescribing the method through which a claim is submitted is procedural. The D.C. Circuit has sustained application-processing rules as procedural “even though `failure to observe [them] might cause the loss of substantive rights,'”
JEM Broadcasting,
22 F.3d at 327 (quoting
Ranger
v.
FCC,
294 F.2d 240, 244 (D.C. Cir. 1961)), where, as here, the rule “did not change the substantive standards” by which the agency
(
printed page 75167)
evaluates the merits.
JEM Broadcasting,
22 F.3d at 327. That is the character of this rule: it prescribes the manner in which an FLSA claim is submitted without altering who may file a claim, the substantive standard OPM applies in deciding it, the evidence required to support it, or the duration of any codified time limit. Where a filing requirement bears on timeliness, the D.C. Circuit asks whether the requirement is “so short as to foreclose effective opportunity to make one's case on the merits.”
Lamoille Valley R.R. Co.
v.
ICC,
711 F.2d 295, 328 (D.C. Cir. 1983), quoted in
JEM Broadcasting,
22 F.3d at 328. The exemption process in § 551.710(b)(7), which may be invoked by telephone or in writing as described below, and the agency-assisted filing option in § 551.705(b) preserve that opportunity. The procedural exception therefore applies.
Comments 05 and 06's reliance on
JEM Broadcasting
is unpersuasive for the proposition asserted.
JEM Broadcasting,
as an alternative holding, sustained the FCC's rule dismissing incomplete license applications without opportunity to amend against the identical argument, reasoning that “procedure impacts on outcomes and thus can virtually always be described as affecting substance, but to pursue that line of analysis results in the obliteration of the distinction that Congress demanded.” 22 F.3d at 326-27 (quoting
Air Transport Ass'n of America
v.
Department of Transportation,
900 F.2d 369, 383 (D.C. Cir. 1990) (Silberman, J., dissenting), remanded, 498 U.S. 1077 (1991), vacated as moot, 933 F.2d 1043 (D.C. Cir. 1991)). Applying the same reasoning here, just because a filing method may affect the outcome of a particular claim does not convert a procedural rule into a substantive one.
Additionally, because the rule qualifies for the procedural-rule exception under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
, the alternative good-cause finding under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
is not necessary to sustain the rule. OPM nonetheless notes, in response to Comment 07's argument that OPM failed to establish good cause and to the citation in Comments 05 and 06 to
Mack Trucks, Inc.
v.
EPA,
682 F.3d 87, 93 (D.C. Cir. 2012), that the DFR's good-cause statement was offered as an independent and alternative basis, and its sufficiency (or lack thereof) does not affect the validity of the rule under the separate and independently adequate
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
exception.
Comment 07 also invokes
Loper Bright Enterprises
v.
Raimondo,
603 U.S. 369 (2024), asserting that courts owe no deference to OPM's interpretation of statutory filing requirements and that OPM lacks authority under
29 U.S.C. 204(f)
to affect the preservation of FLSA back-pay limitation periods.
Loper Bright
does not alter the analysis here, because the procedural-rule exemption does not turn on deference to an agency's statutory interpretation. The rule exercises OPM's authority under
29 U.S.C. 204(f)
to administer the Act's claims process, including the manner in which claims are submitted. A claim submitted through the eFile system, or through a method OPM authorizes under an approved exemption, is received in the ordinary course; the limitations periods in
5 CFR 551.702(b)
and
29 U.S.C. 255
are untouched by this rule.
Filing-Method Changes and the FLSA Limitations Period
Comments 03, 05, and 06 argue that, because
5 CFR 551.702(c)
ties a claimant's back-pay recovery to the date OPM or the employing agency receives the claim and because the exemption from mandatory eFiling in § 551.710(b)(7) is committed to OPM's “sole and exclusive discretion” with no stated response time, a claimant who cannot reasonably file electronically and who is awaiting action on an exemption request risks losing recoverable back pay for reasons unrelated to the merits of the claim. Comment 03 further observes that, under § 551.703(c), filing an administrative claim with an agency or OPM does not toll the separate limitations period governing an FLSA action filed in court, so such a claimant, in Comment 03's description, is consuming the administrative limitations period and the judicial limitations period at the same time and cannot preserve one by pursuing the other. Comments 03, 05, and 06 argue this shows the rule is not the kind of internal housekeeping matter the
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)
exception is meant to cover, notwithstanding the DFR's statement that it “does not change . . . the applicable time limits for filing.”
The interaction Comment 03 describes between the administrative and judicial limitations periods is not new to this rule. Section 551.703(c) has provided, since the current subpart G was adopted in 2007, that filing a claim with an agency or OPM does not satisfy the statute of limitations governing an FLSA claim filed in court, and nothing in the DFR amends § 551.703(c). A claimant who mailed a paper claim under the prior rule faced the identical structural feature. To the extent Comments 03, 05, and 06 challenge that pre-existing feature of subpart G, the challenge is directed at a provision this rulemaking does not touch and is outside its scope.
This rule simply changes the method used for submission and does not substantively affect a claimant's rights. OPM's statement that the rule “does not change . . . the applicable time limits for filing” refers to the duration of the codified limitations periods themselves—none of which this rule shortens, lengthens, or otherwise alters. The possibility that a change in filing method
could,
in an individual case, affect the date on which a claim is received does not convert a rule about filing methods into a rule about the length of a limitations period.
The rule also does not leave a claimant who cannot reasonably use eFile without recourse. Section 551.710(b)(7) permits OPM to exempt such a claimant from the eFiling requirement, and OPM will treat a claimant's timely, good-faith attempt to contact OPM—whether by telephone, email, or a non-electronic filing—as bearing directly on whether “circumstances beyond the claimant's control” support reconsideration of a cancelled claim under § 551.707(b) or a waiver of the 45-day period under § 551.708(a), both of which are unaffected by this rule and remain available, within their respective terms, on a case-by-case basis regardless of whether an exemption request was granted, denied, or still pending when a deadline passed. OPM therefore declines to adopt Comment 03's proposed regulatory text automatically tolling a deadline during the pendency of an exemption request, or deeming a non-electronic submission filed as of its original date once an exemption later issues, because such a provision would change how § 551.702(c) sets the date on which the claim period is preserved, a result the DFR did not propose and OPM does not adopt here. Finally, § 551.703(c) preserves a claimant's independent right to bring an FLSA action in a United States court regardless of the outcome of the administrative claim.
Claimants Subject to a Negotiated Grievance Procedure
Comment 03 correctly notes, as a limitation on the scope of its own comment, that under § 551.703(a) a claimant who at any time during the claim period was covered by a collective bargaining agreement that did not exclude FLSA matters must use the negotiated grievance procedure as the exclusive administrative remedy, and that §§ 551.704 through 551.710—
(
printed page 75168)
including the filing and eFiling provisions this rule amends—do not apply to such claimants. OPM confirms this is correct. The filing-method changes addressed in this notice accordingly have no bearing on claimants who are subject to a negotiated grievance procedure that does not exclude FLSA matters.
The Discretionary Exemption From Electronic Filing
Comments 03, 04, 05, 06, and 07 raise concerns, in varying terms, about § 551.710(b)(7), which allows OPM to exempt a party or representative from the eFiling requirement in its “sole and exclusive discretion” and provides that OPM “will not find good cause for failing to file a claim timely” if the party fails to contact OPM to request an exemption before the applicable deadline. Commenters describe this combination as lacking defined criteria, a response timeline, or a means of reconsideration; Comment 03 and Comment 04 note that the codified text directs an exemption request to be made “as instructed on OPM's website” with no non-electronic method specified in the regulatory text itself and Comment 04 offers twelve specific requested changes addressing technology access, literacy and disability barriers, temporary loss of access, and related concerns, while Comment 07 proposes a mandatory, permanently preserved dual-track paper-and-email intake method for field and wage-grade personnel (its “Component B”) together with a fixed, non-discretionary tolling period for system outages.
The standard governing exemption requests is the one described in the DFR's preamble: an exemption is available to a party or representative “who cannot reasonably file electronically.” 91 FR at 48237. Current contact information is available on OPM's website. Nonetheless, a party or representative may request an exemption under § 551.710(b)(7) by contacting OPM using the telephone number or email address listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
caption of the DFR or of any successor document—both of which OPM publishes independently of, and without requiring access to, its website. Similarly, OPM will treat a timely telephone or written exemption request the same as one submitted through OPM's website. OPM will likewise treat a documented, agency-side outage of the eFile system, and a claimant's literacy, disability, or other barrier to independently using the eFile system, as circumstances bearing on whether reconsideration of a cancelled claim is warranted under § 551.707(b) or whether the 45-day period in § 551.708(a) should be waived. This is all consistent with OPM's longstanding case-by-case approach to discretionary relief under this subpart and is unaffected by this rulemaking.
OPM has not adopted Comment 04's twelve requested textual additions or Comment 07's proposed fixed, non-discretionary dual-track and outage-tolling provisions or a fixed response deadline for exemption requests. Claims-processing circumstances vary too widely to be usefully reduced to a single set of numerical rules, and a rigid rule risks producing arbitrary results in both directions. In addition, § 551.705(b) already provides that, at the claimant's request, the employing agency may forward the claim to OPM using the eFile system on the claimant's behalf. Finally, § 551.703(c) preserves a claimant's independent right to bring an FLSA action in a United States court.
Electronic Service and Administrative Deadlines
Comment 03 asks whether a claimant's failure to observe an electronic posting in the eFile system will be treated as receipt for purposes that cancel a claim under § 551.706(a)(1) or run the 45-day reconsideration period under § 551.708(a), given that eFile registration under § 551.710(b)(2) constitutes consent to electronic service and § 551.710(b)(5) places responsibility on eFilers to monitor case activity.
Registration as an eFiler constitutes consent to electronic service. The responsibility to monitor case activity under § 551.710(b)(5) is no different in kind from the obligation of a party who receives paper correspondence to review their mail. Where a claimant demonstrates that a technical failure of the eFile system, rather than the claimant's own inattention, prevented them from receiving or responding to a posting, that is a circumstance OPM will weigh in the same case-by-case manner it weighs any other question of good cause or excusable delay under this subpart, through the existing discretion in §§ 551.707(b) and 551.708(a). This rule does not foreclose that inquiry, and a claimant's independent right to bring an action in court under § 551.703(c) remains available.
Effective Date
Comment 03 correctly identifies an inconsistency in the DFR's preamble. The
DATES
caption stated that the rule “is effective September 29, 2026 unless significant adverse comment is submitted by August 31, 2026.” 91 FR at 48236. Later in the same document, the preamble indicated that “this direct final rule will become effective 45 days after the comment period expires.”
Id.
at 48237. The reference to “45 days” was a drafting error. The
DATES
caption—which under Office of the Federal Register drafting convention states the document's operative dates—consistently identified September 29, 2026, throughout the comment period, as did the rule's transition provision (“Claims filed before September 29, 2026 will be processed under the requirements in effect on the date of submission or postmark. Any submissions on or after September 29, 2026 must comply with the requirements of this part as amended by this rule.” 91 FR at 48237). Comments 05, 06, and 07, which addressed the effective date, identified September 29, 2026, as the operative date, with Comment 07 demanding withdrawal “prior to September 29, 2026.” Comment 03, which identified the inconsistency, likewise recognized September 29, 2026, as the date stated in the
DATES
caption and in the transition provision, and asked OPM to confirm the operative effective date. OPM confirms that September 29, 2026, was the effective date of the amendments to
5 CFR part 551, subpart G
. A drafting error in the preamble discussion, which did not appear in the
DATES
caption, the transition provision, or the regulatory text, does not constitute a significant adverse comment.
Paperwork Reduction Act Status of the eFile Information Collection
Comments 03, 05, 06, and 07 ask OPM to confirm the status of Office of Management and Budget (OMB) review of the information collection associated with the eFile system (OMB Control Number 3206-NEW) and its relationship to the rule's effective date. OMB approved this collection under OMB Control Number 3206-0282. Comment 03 also asks whether the burden estimate has been revised to reflect the addition of other appeal types to the eFile system. The 30-day notice (
91 FR 46802
(July 24, 2026)) reflects a revised estimate of 1,286 respondents and 13,039 annual burden hours, which reflects the full scope of appeals available through the eFile system.
As to the interaction between Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) clearance and the rule's effective date: consistent with
44 U.S.C. 3512(a)
, OPM confirms that it did not decline to accept, or delay action on, a claim submitted through the eFile system, nor deny a request for an exemption under § 551.710(b)(7), on the basis of the
(
printed page 75169)
collection's control-number status. The assigned control number is displayed on the eFile system's public-facing pages.
Alleged Regulations.gov Comment-Submission Difficulty
Comment 07 asserts that OPM's docket was displayed on
regulations.gov
as belonging to a “Non-Participating Agency” that does not accept electronic comments, and that this display “effectively nullif[ied] the public's ability to submit electronic comments until the final hours of August 31, 2026,” which Comment 07 characterizes as an independent violation of the meaningful-comment-opportunity requirement in
5 U.S.C. 553(c)
warranting withdrawal and a fresh 30-day comment period.
The docket record does not support this characterization. OPM's docket reflects that timely comments were submitted and received through
regulations.gov
well before the close of the comment period, including comments received July 31 and on August 19, 2026—more than a month and more than a week, respectively, before the August 31, 2026, deadline—in addition to several comments received on the final day, which is a common feature of rulemaking dockets generally and is not itself evidence that earlier submission was unavailable. Whatever display irregularity, if any, an individual commenter may have encountered, the requirement that an agency provide the public a meaningful opportunity to comment is satisfied by a genuine opportunity to submit comments, and the actual receipt of substantive comments across nearly the full length of the comment period demonstrates that such an opportunity existed here. OPM does not find a basis in this record to withdraw the rule or reopen the comment period on this ground.
Section 508, the Privacy Act, FISMA, and Collective Bargaining Obligations
Comment 07 raises a series of additional compliance questions concerning the eFile system: accessibility under Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act (
29 U.S.C. 794d
), System of Records Notice coverage under the Privacy Act (
5 U.S.C. 552a
), security authorization under the Federal Information Security Modernization Act (FISMA) (
44 U.S.C. 3551
et seq.
), and bargaining obligations under
5 U.S.C. 7114(b)(4)
.
These are each freestanding statutory obligations that apply to OPM's operation of the eFile system on their own terms, through their own enforcement mechanisms, independent of whether this procedural rule was properly issued as a direct final rule under the APA; a deficiency in compliance with any of them, if one exists, would not retroactively convert this filing-procedure rule into a substantive rule requiring notice and comment. As to the Privacy Act specifically, the DFR already identified the System of Records Notices OPM has determined apply to information collected through the eFile system and described the routine uses under which that information may be disclosed. 91 FR at 48238. As to FISMA and the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP), OPM's July 24, 2026, 30-day notice for the eFile information collection confirmed that the cloud products and services supporting the system are FedRAMP-certified and that applicable FISMA requirements have been met and committed to publishing a Privacy Impact Assessment. 91 FR at 46802-03.
As to bargaining obligations under
5 U.S.C. 7114(b)(4)
, that provision requires an agency, as an employer, to furnish data to the exclusive representative of its employees upon request, to the extent not prohibited by law, in connection with collective bargaining over conditions of employment; it does not impose a duty to bargain over the content of governmentwide procedural regulations that OPM issues under
29 U.S.C. 204(f)
in its capacity as administrator of the Act's claims process, rather than as the employing agency of the claimants who file FLSA claims. To the extent Comment 07 invokes a broader duty to bargain over changes to conditions of employment, that duty runs under
5 U.S.C. 7114(a)(4)
and
(b)
between an executive agency and the exclusive representative of its own employees; it does not run to OPM when OPM acts as claims adjudicator rather than employer, and, under
5 U.S.C. 7117(a)(1)
, the duty to bargain does not extend to matters that are the subject of a Government-wide rule or regulation, such as the regulations in
5 CFR part 551
that OPM issues under
29 U.S.C. 204(f)
.
Requests To Withdraw the Rule and Retain Dual-Track Filing
Comment 04 asks OPM to withdraw the rule and restore permanent, unconditional postal-mail and email filing options; Comments 05 and 06 ask OPM to withdraw the rule and proceed by standard notice-and-comment rulemaking; and Comment 07 similarly demands withdrawal and proposes a specific severable alternative that would make eFile use voluntary for desk-based personnel while permanently preserving mail and email intake for non-desk, field, and wage-grade personnel and unrepresented claimants.
OPM has considered these requests together with the more specific points addressed above. The premise common to all of them—that the rule leaves claimants who cannot reasonably use the eFile system without a means of filing—is addressed by the exemption process in § 551.710(b)(7) and by the agency-assisted filing option in § 551.705(b). Because these accommodations already exist in the rule, OPM does not agree that permanent, parallel paper and email intake methods for entire categories of claimants are necessary.
III. Determination Regarding Significant Adverse Comment
OPM has evaluated each of the eight comments received, individually and collectively, against the standard described in Section I. None opposes the rule on a ground that requires a substantive change to the regulatory text adopted in the DFR. The sentence in the preamble discussion regarding the rule's effective date was a drafting error; however, the same document provided notice of the effective date in the
DATES
caption, which is the date that is controlling for the Office of the Federal Register. No commenter disputed that the
DATES
caption identified September 29, 2026, as the effective date, and the one commenter that identified the inconsistency asked OPM to confirm the operative date, which this document does. The error does not bear on the substance of
5 CFR part 551, subpart G
, as adopted. The remaining points are either addressed on the merits above or, to the extent not separately discussed, were considered and do not alter this determination. None causes OPM to reevaluate the rule's underlying approach, none identifies a respect in which the rule as adopted would be ineffective or unacceptable absent a change to its text, and none has caused OPM to make a substantive change to the rule.

5 CFR Part 551
Government employees
Wages
Accordingly, OPM confirms that the amendments to
5 CFR part 551, subpart G
, published at
91 FR 48236
(July 31, 2026), became effective on September 29, 2026.

abstract: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is confirming the effective date of its direct final rule revising the table of reduction factors for early commencing dates of survivor annuities paid to spouses of separated employees who die before the date on which they would be eligible for unreduced deferred annuities. OPM received no significant adverse comments during the comment period and confirms the rule was effective August 24, 2026.

5 CFR Part 843
[Docket ID: OPM-2026-0367]
RIN 3206-AP12
AGENCY:
Office of Personnel Management.
ACTION:
Direct final rule; confirmation of effective date.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is confirming the effective date of its direct final rule revising the table of reduction factors for early commencing dates of survivor annuities paid to spouses of separated employees who die before the date on which they would be eligible for unreduced deferred annuities. OPM received no significant adverse comments during the comment period and confirms the rule was effective August 24, 2026.
DATES:
The effective date of August 24, 2026, for the direct final rule published on June 23, 2026 (
91 FR 37307
) is confirmed.
ADDRESSES:
Please refer to the direct final rule published at
91 FR 37307
(June 23, 2026) for address information.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Kristopher Rogers, Office of Personnel Management, Retirement Services, (202) 606-0299,
RetirementPolicy@opm.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
On June 23, 2026, OPM published in the
Federal Register
a direct final rule titled “Federal Employees' Retirement System; Present Value Conversion Factors for Spouses of Deceased Separated Employees” (
91 FR 37307
), amending appendix A to subpart C of
5 CFR part 843
, to revise the table of reduction factors for early commencing dates of survivor annuities paid to spouses of separated employees who die before the date on which they would be eligible for unreduced deferred annuities. Within the rule, OPM stated that, if no significant adverse comments were received by July 23, 2026, the direct final rule would become effective on August 24, 2026.
A significant adverse comment is a comment where the commenter explains why the rule would be inappropriate, challenges its underlying premise or approach, or shows why it would be ineffective or unacceptable without a change. A comment is adverse and significant if:
1. The comment opposes the rule and provides a reason sufficient to require a substantive response in a notice-and-comment process. For example, a substantive response is required when: (a) The comment causes OPM to reevaluate (or reconsider) its position or conduct additional analysis; (b) The comment raises an issue serious enough to warrant a substantive response to clarify or complete the record; or (c) The comment raises a relevant issue that was not previously addressed or considered by OPM;
2. The comment proposes a change or an addition to the rule, and it is apparent that the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without incorporation of the change or addition; or
3. The comment causes OPM to make a substantive change to the rule.
As discussed in more detail in Section II, “Public Comment Analysis,” OPM evaluated the comments received against the criteria described above and determined that none of the comments rose to the level of a significant adverse comment.
II. Public Comment Analysis
OPM received 7 timely comments related to the direct final rule. Commenters included Federal employees, private citizens and one labor organization representing nurses. Two commenters supported the direct final rule, stating the revision of the table of reduction factors would help prevent unfunded liabilities, safeguarding the Civil Service Retirement and Disability Fund. Commenters also stated that removal of the obsolete table section improved clarity of the regulation. OPM agrees with these comments.
OPM received two comments that were unrelated to the direct final rule. Therefore, those comments are not addressed.
Three commenters raised concerns regarding the revision of the table of reduction factors. The following discussion summarizes and addresses their concerns. As discussed in those responses, the comments did not require OPM to reconsider the rule, conduct new analysis, supplement the factual basis necessary to support the rule, or make a substantive change to the rule.
Two commenters asserted that OPM did not provide sufficient information about the actuarial assumptions underlying the revised factors. OPM disagrees. The direct final rule identified the revised assumptions of the Board of Actuaries (Board) as the basis for the changes and referred readers to the revised Federal Employees' Retirement System (FERS) normal costs notice (
91 FR 37433
) published in the same issue of the
Federal Register
. The publicly available FY 2025 Civil Service Retirement and Disability Fund Annual Report (
https://www.opm.gov/​about-us/​reports-publications/​agency-reports/​fy-2025-csrdf-annual-report.pdf
) provides additional detail. The Board retained its long-term economic assumptions, including the 4.00 percent interest assumption, but revised certain demographic assumptions, including its assumptions concerning future mortality improvement. The revised early-commencement factors reflect those revised demographic assumptions.
Neither commenter identified an error in the Board's assumptions, an error in OPM's calculation of the factors, or an alternative calculation that would satisfy the statutory requirement for actuarial equivalence. The comments therefore did not cause OPM to reconsider its position, conduct additional actuarial analysis, or make a substantive change to the rule. OPM therefore concludes that these comments are not significant adverse comments.
One commenter questioned why the early commencing of survivor annuities factors changed but the Basic Employee Death Benefit (BEDB) factors did not. OPM did not revise the BEDB factors because the economic assumption relevant to that benefit did not change. The BEDB is a lump sum benefit that survivors can elect to receive in 36 equal monthly payments. The BEDB factors are used to convert the lump sum benefit into 36 equal monthly payments. They are not used to discount the lump sum benefit based on how long the surviving spouse is expected to live. If a surviving spouse elects the installment option and dies before receiving all 36 payments, the remaining portion is paid to the spouse's estate (see
5 CFR 843.309(c)(2)
). As a result, mortality assumptions do not affect the BEDB installment factor in the same way they affect a life-contingent survivor annuity because OPM remains obligated to pay the remaining BEDB amount even if the
(
printed page 75171)
spouse dies during the 36-month payment period.
The factors for early commencement of survivor annuities serve a different actuarial function. Those factors convert a survivor annuity that ordinarily would begin later into an actuarially equivalent annuity beginning immediately after the separated employee's death. Unlike the BEDB's 36-month installment option, a survivor annuity is a recurring life contingent benefit whose present value depends in part on the survivor's life expectancy. When the survivor dies, the annuity ends. Because the Board revised its demographic assumptions, including mortality assumptions applicable to survivors, OPM revised the early-commencement factors to reflect those changes.
One commenter opposed the revision of the factors because the updated factors would lower the annuity rates of spouses or former spouses of deceased separated Federal employees who elect to receive earlier benefits. Further, the commenter argued that their comment constituted a significant adverse comment and that the rule was inherently controversial. Compared to the previous factors, OPM agrees that the updated factors result in lower benefit amounts for those who elect to receive an earlier survivor annuity. However, when a survivor elects the earlier commencing date, OPM is required to pay a monthly benefit that is actuarially equivalent to the present value of the benefit that would be paid at the later commencing date option (see
5 U.S.C. 8442(c)
). OPM uses economic and demographic assumptions as set by the Board to determine actuarial equivalence. Although the economic assumptions remained unchanged, the Board changed several demographic assumptions at the 2025 Board Meeting, and this resulted in an update to the factors OPM uses to create actuarial equivalent benefits for spouses or former spouses of deceased separated Federal employees who elect to receive earlier benefits. Finally, in response to the commenter's assertion that this rulemaking is inherently controversial—OPM disagrees. Section 8461(i) requires OPM to make corresponding changes to factors used to produce actuarially equivalent benefits when the applicable actuarial assumptions change. Accordingly, OPM does not have discretion to retain factors that no longer produce the required actuarial equivalence. Additionally, the commenter does not identify an error in the revised factors, identify an error in the actuarial assumptions used to calculate them, or identify a legally permissible alternative that would preserve the prior factors while maintaining actuarial equivalence. Considering this, OPM has determined that this comment does not constitute a significant adverse comment.
One commenter argued that the removal of “1950 through 1966” column from the table titled “With at least 30 years of creditable service” was not fully explained. The commenter questioned whether the table's removal could affect pending claims and whether the column would later be available for reference. OPM appreciates the comment. The “1950 through 1966” column only applies when a separated employee dies before reaching their minimum retirement age (MRA). The youngest individuals in the 1950 through 1966 birth range were born in 1966. Those born in 1966 reached their MRA during 2023. Accordingly, after 2023 no employee within the 1950-1966 birth range could die before reaching their MRA, which is the circumstance in which this column would be used. The commenter also asked if the previous table is available for reference. The previous version of the table is available in the
Federal Register
(
88 FR 66679
) and prior editions of the U.S. Code of Federal Regulations. OPM would apply the appropriate version in older claims, if needed.
One commenter noted that the rule does not provide examples of how the updated factors affect survivor annuities. Because the amount of an early-commencing survivor annuity depends on several individual circumstances, including the deceased employee's age, years of creditable service, and base annuity amount, no single example would represent all affected survivors. OPM nevertheless agrees that individualized information is important and notes that survivors receive personalized information detailing annuity options, including amounts, during the claims process.
After evaluating all the comments received against the criteria for significant adverse comments described in Section I of this notice, OPM has determined that none of the comments caused OPM to reconsider the rule, conduct additional actuarial analysis, or make a substantive change. The comments also did not identify an error in the revised factors or their underlying assumptions or show that the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without a change.
Accordingly, OPM is issuing this notice to confirm that the amendments to appendix A to subpart C of
5 CFR part 843
published at
91 FR 37307
(June 23, 2026), became effective on August 24, 2026.
