AGENCY:
Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Interim final rule; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
This rule provides implementation by the Department of Homeland Security (“the Department” or “DHS”) of the HAVANA Act of 2021. The HAVANA Act provides authority for agency heads to provide payments to certain individuals who have incurred qualifying injuries to the brain. This rule covers current and former Department of Homeland Security employees and their dependents.
DATES:
Effective date:
This interim final rule is effective on December 21, 2026.
Comments:
Comments must be submitted on or before January 19, 2027. Commenters should be aware that the electronic Federal Docket Management System will not accept comments after 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on the last day of the comment period.
ADDRESSES:
If you wish to provide comments regarding this interim final rule, you must submit comments to DHS Docket No. DHS-2024-0010 through the Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the website instructions for submitting comments.
(
printed page 75172)
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Latousha Leslie, Senior Advisor, Office of Health Security; 202-617-5077 and
AHI_Compensation@hq.dhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background and Authority
This rule implements the HAVANA Act of 2021,
Public Law 117-46
, 135 Stat. 391 (2021) (codified as amended at
22 U.S.C. 2680b(i)
).
On December 20, 2019, Congress authorized the Department of State to pay benefits to employees and their dependents for injuries suffered in Cuba or China after January 1, 2016, in connection with certain hostile or other incidents designated by the Secretary of State. These benefits were limited to Department of State employees, their dependents, and other individuals affiliated with the Department of State.
Public Law 116-94
, Division J, Title IX, section 901, 133 Stat. 2875, 3079 (codified at
22 U.S.C. 2680b
).
On January 1, 2021, Congress amended this law to authorize other federal government agencies to provide benefits to their own employees under Department of State Chief of Mission (COM) authority who suffered similar injuries.
Public Law 116-283
, Div. A, title XI, section 1110, 134 Stat. 3892 (codified at
22 U.S.C. 2680b
).
On October 8, 2021, Congress further amended these laws in the “Helping American Victims Affected by Neurological Attacks” (HAVANA) Act of 2021.
Public Law 117-46
(codified at
22 U.S.C. 2651 note
&
50 U.S.C. 3519b note
), 135 Stat. 391. In the HAVANA Act, Congress authorized federal government agencies to compensate affected current employees, former employees, and their dependents for qualifying injuries to the brain. The HAVANA Act also removed the previous law's requirement that the qualifying injury must occur in “the Republic of Cuba, People's Republic of China, or other foreign country designated by the Secretary of State.”
Public Law 117-46
, 135 Stat 391, 394 (amending
Pub. L. 116-94
, Division J, Title IX, section 901, 133 Stat. 2875, 3080-81). The scope of coverage now includes a qualifying injury that occurs in any foreign or domestic location.
Public Law 117-46
, 135 Stat. 391, 394. The HAVANA Act requires federal agencies that make payments under the HAVANA Act to prescribe implementing regulations not later than 180 days after the effective date of the Act.
Public Law 117-46
, 135 Stat. 391, 396.
On March 15, 2022, Congress added a provision stating that payments made under
22 U.S.C. 2680b(i)(2)

II. Section-by-Section Discussion
A. Background and Authority—§ 61.1
The rule references
22 U.S.C. 2680b
and notes that the rule applies to covered employees (current and former employees) and their covered dependents.
B. Definitions—§ 61.2
The rule defines those who are eligible to receive payments: covered employees (including current and former employees) and covered dependents who on or after September 11, 2001, become injured by reason of a qualifying injury to the brain.
A covered employee includes Department employees who have been appointed in the civil service in accordance with
5 U.S.C. 2105
, employees on Limited Non-Career Appointments, employees on Temporary Appointments, personnel hired on Personal Services Contracts, citizens or nationals of the United States paid from non-appropriated funds under
32 CFR 756.2
, and students providing volunteer services under
5 CFR part 362
. Covered employees do not include employees paid from non-appropriated funds of an instrumentality of the United States under the jurisdiction of the armed forces who are not citizens or nationals of the United States, individuals receiving compensation under
50 U.S.C. 3519b
, or employees or retired employees of other agencies.
[
2
]
(
printed page 75173)
A covered dependent is a family member of a current or former employee of the Department who, on or after September 11, 2001, becomes injured by reason of a qualifying injury to the brain while the dependent's sponsor was an employee of the Department. For the purposes of determining whether someone is a covered dependent, the term “family member” includes unmarried children under 21 years of age at the time of the qualifying injury (or certain other children); parents; sisters and brothers; and spouse. Step-parents and step-siblings are included in the definition.
For the purposes of this rule, DHS adopts the Department of State's definition of qualifying injury to the brain codified at
22 CFR 135.2
. DHS has determined that this definition is reasonable and well considered. The Department of State consulted with the chief medical officers at other federal agencies and experts at civilian medical centers of excellence in determining this definition. There is no diagnostic code or criteria for anomalous health incidents (AHI) in the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification (ICD-10-CM). Because of the varied symptoms and still-nascent understanding of how to test or otherwise screen for AHI impacts, the standard adopted is broadly inclusive of the types of injuries that have been reported to date.
The definition of qualifying injury to the brain is based on current medical practices related to brain injuries. The individual must have been assessed and diagnosed in person by a physician who is currently certified by the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN), the American Osteopathic Board of Neurology and Psychiatry (AOBNP), the American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR), or the American Osteopathic Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (AOBPMR) as having:
(1) an acute injury to the brain such as, but not limited to, a concussion, penetrating injury, or an injury as the consequence of an event that leads to permanent alterations in brain function, as demonstrated by confirming correlative findings on imaging studies (to include computed tomography scan (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging scan (MRI) or electroencephalogram (EEG)); or
(2) a medical diagnosis of a traumatic brain injury (TBI) that required active medical treatment for 12 months or more; or
(3) the acute onset of new persistent, disabling neurologic symptoms as demonstrated by confirming correlative findings on imaging studies (to include CT or MRI) or EEG, or physical exam, or other appropriate testing, and that required active medical treatment for 12 months or more.
The definition of qualifying injury to the brain set forth in section 61.2 accounts for a variety of observable impacts to an individual, including a concussion or a penetrating injury, or absent either of those, the ability of a physician who is currently certified by the ABPN, the AOBPN, the ABPMR, or the AOBPMR to review one of a variety of forms of medical imaging evidence indicating permanent alterations in brain function. The goal with this standard is to ensure there is some documented evidence of impact to the brain, while minimally circumscribing what that impact entails. The second component of the definition (paragraphs (2)(i)-(iii) of the definition) is intended to provide alternative avenues for demonstrating sustained, long-term impact to the individual. This benefit is intended for individuals who experience long-term consequences, potentially to include their inability to gainfully work, as a result of their report of a suspected AHI.
The standard is consistent with that employed by other agencies, including the Department of State. Establishing a 12-month threshold of active medical treatment is indicative of a long-term injury. For example, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) broadly defines chronic diseases “as conditions that last 1 year or more and require ongoing medical attention or limit activities of daily living or both.” The Department notes that applicants who have suffered kinetic or external, physically caused injuries to the brain such as the head striking an object, the brain undergoing an acceleration or deceleration movement, or brain injuries from events such as a blast or explosion, including penetrating injuries, may be eligible if the injuries satisfy the other requirements of this rule.
Under the HAVANA Act, the injury must “have occurred in connection with war, insurgency, hostile act, terrorist activity, or other incidents designated by the Secretary of State [or head of any Federal agency under specified circumstances in accordance with
22 U.S.C. 2680b(j)
], and that was not the result of the willful misconduct of the covered individual.”
22 U.S.C. 2680b(e)(4)(A)(ii)-(iii)
& (B)(ii)-(iii). The Department will work with an applicant upon their submission of the DS-4316, “Eligibility Questionnaire for HAVANA Act Payments” to determine whether their alleged incident qualifies.
The definition of “other incident” is a new onset of physical manifestations that cannot otherwise be explained and that is designated under
22 U.S.C. 2680b
. The Department will review available information on the reported incident. If the treating physician does not indicate that there is a credible alternate explanation for the individual's symptoms, and if the information the Department has regarding the incident does not provide a credible alternate explanation for the incident, that incident will be recommended for designation. Incidents for which an explanation has been identified will not be recommended for designation.
C. Eligibility for Payments—§ 61.3
The Department will make available to its workforce information on the regulations and the process to apply for HAVANA Act payments. Current employees, former employees, and dependents (as defined herein) can apply for consideration. Applicants will be required to provide the necessary documentation so the Department may determine whether they qualify for payment. The DS-4316 “Eligibility Questionnaire for HAVANA Act Payments,” is the form associated with developing the necessary evidence to submit a claim, and it will be available upon request with instructions on how to apply for a HAVANA Act payment. A portion of the form must be filled out by a qualified physician; the rule specifies certain board certification requirements for physicians who can evaluate a qualifying injury to the brain.
The Department has determined that the payment scheme set forth in the Department of State's HAVANA Act regulations (
22 CFR 135.3
) is well reasoned and provides an effective means of compensating covered employees. Accordingly, the Department has adopted it for purposes of this rulemaking. Pursuant to this interim final rule, the Department, in its discretion, may authorize a one-time, non-taxable, lump sum payment based on Level III of the Executive Schedule (see
5 U.S.C. 5311
et seq.
). The payment is non-taxable pursuant to
22 U.S.C. 2680b(g)
. As indicated in section 61.3 of the regulatory text, payment eligibility and the amount of the payment will be at the Department's discretion. The maximum should only be awarded where a condition has a consistent, sustained, and exceptionally severe impact on a victim's quality of life or prevents current employees from successfully performing their work-
(
printed page 75174)
related duties. The purpose is to only compensate qualifying brain injuries that meet the criteria set forth in this regulation. The following factors will be taken into account to determine the amount of the payment to be authorized: (1) The applicant's responses on the eligibility form and (2) whether the Department of Labor Office of Workers' Compensation Programs has determined that the applicant has no wage-earning capacity or reemployment potential for an indefinite future, or the Social Security Administration has approved the applicant for Social Security Disability Insurance or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits, or the applicant's board-certified physician has certified that the individual requires a full-time caregiver for activities of daily living, as defined by the Katz Index of Independence of Daily Living.
The award thresholds are based on Level III of the Executive Schedule. A Base payment will be 75 percent of Level III pay, and a Base plus payment will be 100 percent of Level III pay. The specific use of Level III of the Executive Schedule sets the compensation at the maximum annual salary potentially available to most of the federal workforce. The Department believes this amount is the most it can reasonably compensate each requestor while ensuring funds for the total amount of requestors it believes will likely receive payments. If the applicant meets any of the criteria for severe impacts, the applicant will be eligible to receive a Base plus payment. Applicants whose board-certified physician confirms that the definition of qualifying injury to the brain has been met, but who have not met any of the criteria for severe impacts, will be eligible to receive a Base payment.
The criteria established for severe impacts are reflective of the Department's objective of ensuring that the individuals most severely affected by AHIs (as indicated by a lack of reemployment potential, an inability to engage in substantial gainful activity, or the need for a full-time caregiver) receive additional payment. The use of the Department of Labor or the Social Security Administration's (SSA) determination is to ensure that both federal employees as well as their dependents have access to a mechanism for this determination. The Department recognizes that the criteria the Department of Labor and SSA use in their determinations are distinct, as well as the fact that the procedural timelines for seeking and receiving approval may be different between these agencies. The third option, that a board-certified physician certify that the individual requires a full-time caregiver for activities of daily living, provides an alternative mechanism for all individuals. Finally, the Department notes that if an applicant who received a Base payment later meets any of the criteria listed for severe impacts, the applicant may apply for an additional payment that will be the difference between the Base and Base plus payment. As of 2026, a Base payment will be $157,200.
[
3
]
A Base plus payment will be $209,600 pursuant to Level III of the Executive Schedule. As the payments are tied to the Executive Schedule payment levels, the amounts will change over time based on changes to the federal salary schedule. Payments will be based on the Executive Schedule in effect at the time the payment was approved.
The use of Level III of the Executive Schedule sets the compensation at the maximum annual salary potentially available to most of the federal workforce. While payments under the HAVANA Act may be in addition to other leave benefits, disability, or workers' compensation payments that the applicant may be receiving or may be entitled to receive that also help augment any loss of income, this is an appropriate additional payment. This payment scheme is also consistent with what is being offered by other federal agencies and will ensure consistency of benefits among affected individuals.
The Department notes that payments may only be made using amounts appropriated in advance specifically for this purpose in the relevant fiscal year unless Congress specifies otherwise. Therefore, payments are contingent on appropriated funds, and all payments will be paid out on a first-come, first-served basis.
D. Consultation With Other Agencies—§ 61.4
The Department will adopt appropriate procedures for determining whether an incident has been designated under the HAVANA Act, including, where appropriate, consultation with the Secretary of State.
See
22 U.S.C. 2680b(i)(1)(D)

E. Procedures—§ 61.5
Each Federal agency is responsible for (1) processing applications for the HAVANA Act payment; (2) determining whether the incident causing the qualifying injury to the brain may be deemed a designated incident under the statute and consulting the Secretary of State if appropriate.
See
22 U.S.C. 2680b(i)(1)(D)
and
(i)(2)
(cross-referencing subparagraph 2680b(e)(4), and section (j)); (3) determining eligibility for the benefit, the amount of the benefit, and process payment of the benefit; and (4) notifying applicants upon receipt of their applications and when a decision has been made whether to authorize payment.
The Office of the Chief Financial Officer is authorized to approve any HAVANA Act payments to covered employees or their dependents. If payment is denied, the applicant may direct an appeal to the Office of Health Security within 60 days. Decisions on the amount of payment are not subject to appeal.
F. Severability
The Department intends that the provisions of this rule be considered severable. The definitions, eligibility criteria, payment criteria, application procedures, review procedures, and appeal procedures in this part operate independently to the extent permitted by law. If any provision of this part, or the application of any provision to any person or circumstance, is held invalid, the Department intends that the remaining provisions continue to apply to the fullest extent permitted by law.

§ 61.1
Background and authority.
(a) Under section 3 of the HAVANA Act of 2021 (
Public Law 117-46
), codified as amended at
22 U.S.C. 2680b
, the Secretary of Homeland Security (Secretary) or other agency heads may provide a payment to a covered employee or covered dependent who experiences a qualifying injury to the brain on or after September 11, 2001. The authority to provide such payments is at the sole discretion of the Secretary or their designee.
(b) This part is issued in accordance with
22 U.S.C. 2680b(i)(4)
and applies to covered employees (current and former employees) and their covered dependents.
§ 61.2
Definitions.
For purposes of this part, the following definitions apply:
Covered dependent.
A family member, as defined in this section, of a covered employee who, on or after September 11, 2001, became injured by reason of a qualifying injury to the brain while the dependent's sponsor was an employee of the Department of Homeland Security (Department).
Covered employee.
(1) A current or former employee of the Department who, on or after September 11, 2001, became injured by reason of a qualifying injury while they were employed by the Department.
(2) A current or former employee under paragraph (1) of this definition includes an “employee” appointed in the civil service in accordance with
5 U.S.C. 2105
, an employee on a Limited Non-Career Appointment, an employee on a Temporary Appointment, personnel hired on a Personal Services Contract, a citizen or national of the United States paid from non-appropriated funds under
32 CFR 756.2
, and a student providing volunteer services under
5 CFR part 362
. The term “current or former employee” does not include an employee paid from non-appropriated funds of an instrumentality of the United States under the jurisdiction of the armed forces who is not a citizen or national of the United States, an individual receiving compensation under
50 U.S.C. 3519b
, or an employee or retired employee of other agencies.
Family member.
For purposes of determining “covered dependent,” a family member is defined as follows:
(1) Children who are unmarried and under 21 years of age at the time of the qualifying injury or, regardless of age, are unmarried and due to mental or physical limitations are incapable of self-support. The term “children” must include natural offspring, step-children, adopted children, and those under permanent legal guardianship (at least until age 18), or comparable permanent custody arrangement, of the employee or spouse or domestic partner as defined in
5 CFR 875.101
when dependent upon and normally residing with the guardian or custodial party, and U.S. citizen children placed for adoption if a U.S. court grants temporary guardianship of the child to the employee and specifically authorizes the child to reside with the employee in the country of assignment before the adoption is finalized;
(2) Parents (including step-parents and legally adoptive parents) of the employee or of the spouse or of the domestic partner as defined in
5 CFR 875.101
, when normally residing with the employee at the time of the injury;
(3) Sisters and brothers (including step-sisters or step-brothers, or adoptive sisters or brothers) of the employee, or of the spouse when such sisters and brothers are at least 51 percent dependent on the employee for support, unmarried and under 21 years of age, or regardless of age, are physically or mentally incapable of self-support; and
(4) Spouse or domestic partner at the time of the injury.
Other incident.
A new onset of physical manifestations that cannot otherwise be readily explained and that is designated under
22 U.S.C. 2680b
.
Qualifying injury to the brain.
(1) The injury must have occurred in connection with war, insurgency, hostile act, terrorist activity, or other incidents designated by the Secretary of State when occurring under Department of State Chief of Mission (COM) authority or the Secretary of Homeland Security when not occurring under COM authority, as permitted by law, and that was not the result of the willful misconduct of the covered employee or covered dependent; and
(2) The individual must have:
(i) An acute injury to the brain such as, but not limited to, a concussion, penetrating injury, or as the consequence of an event that leads to permanent alterations in brain function, as demonstrated by confirming correlative findings on imaging studies (to include computed tomography scan (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging scan (MRI)), or electroencephalogram (EEG);
(ii) A medical diagnosis of a traumatic brain injury (TBI) that required active medical treatment for 12 months or more; or
(iii) Acute onset of new persistent, disabling neurologic symptoms as demonstrated by confirming correlative findings on imaging studies (to include CT or MRI), or EEG, or physical exam, or other appropriate testing, and that required active medical treatment for 12 months or more.
§ 61.3
Eligibility for payments.
(a) The Department may, in its discretion, provide a payment to a covered employee or covered dependent if the qualifying injury to the brain was assessed and diagnosed in person by a physician who is currently certified by the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN), the American Osteopathic Board of Neurology and Psychiatry (AOBNP), the American Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (ABPMR), or the American Osteopathic Board of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (AOBPMR); occurred on or after September 11, 2001, and occurred while the employee was a covered employee of the Department or, for a covered dependent, while the dependent's sponsor was employed by the Department.
(
printed page 75177)
(b) Payment for a qualifying injury to the brain will be a non-taxable, one-time lump sum payment, unless a second payment is authorized under paragraph (d) of this section.
(c) The amount of the payment is at the Department's discretion. The Department will determine the amount paid to each eligible person based on the following factors:
(1) The responses on the “Eligibility Questionnaire for HAVANA Act Payments” form; and
(2) Whether the Department of Labor Office of Workers' Compensation Programs has determined that the applicant has no wage earning capacity or reemployment potential for an indefinite future, or the Social Security Administration has approved the applicant for Social Security Disability Insurance or Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits, or the applicant's ABPN-certified neurologist or an AOBNP, ABPMR, or AOBPMR-board certified physician has certified that the applicant requires a full-time caregiver for activities of daily living, as defined by the Katz Index of Independence of Daily Living.
(d) The award thresholds are based on Level III of the Executive Schedule: Base will be 75 percent of Level III pay, and Base plus will be 100 percent of Level III pay. If the applicant meets any of the criteria listed in paragraph (c)(2) of this section, the applicant will be eligible to receive a Base plus payment. Applicants whose board-certified physician (as described in paragraph (a) of this section) confirms that the definition of “qualifying injury to the brain” has been met, but who have not met any of the criteria listed in paragraph (c)(2) of this section, will be eligible to receive a Base payment. If an applicant who received a Base payment meets any of the criteria listed in paragraph (c)(2), the applicant may apply for an additional payment that will be the difference between the Base and Base plus payment.
§ 61.4
Consultation with other agencies.
To ensure the appropriate Federal agency is processing a HAVANA Act request, the Department may consult with the appropriate officials in other Federal agencies to coordinate as appropriate regarding their current and former employees, and dependents of current or former employees who report an anomalous health incident. The Department will not process payment for qualifying injuries to the brain sustained by an employee, or dependent of an employee while the employee was employed by another Federal agency.
§ 61.5
Procedures.
(a)
Application.
A covered employee or covered dependent may apply for the HAVANA Act payment if he or she believes that he or she has sustained a qualifying injury to the brain on or after September 11, 2001. To apply for the benefit, the applicant must submit the “Eligibility Questionnaire for HAVANA Act Payments” form and additional documentation upon request to
AHI_Compensation@hq.dhs.gov
.
(b)
Review.
For covered employees and dependents, the Office of the Chief Financial Officer is responsible for reviewing the applications for completeness and eligibility.
(c)
Initial decisions.
The Office of the Chief Financial Officer may approve payments under the HAVANA Act and will notify the applicant of the decision in writing.
(d)
Appeals.
In the event of a decision to deny an application for payment under the HAVANA Act, applicants may direct an appeal to the Chief Medical Officer, Office of Health Security in writing within 60 days of the date of the notification of the denial. The Chief Medical Officer, Office of Health Security, is the final appeal authority and will notify the applicant of the appeal decision in writing. In the event that the Chief Medical Officer is unavailable, or the position is vacant, the Secretary of Homeland Security or Deputy Secretary of Homeland Security may act as final appeal authority.

Department of Defense
Office of the Secretary
AGENCY:
Personnel Readiness Management Agency (PRMA), Department of Defense (DoD).
ACTION:
Notice of revised per diem rates in non-foreign areas outside the continental United States (U.S.).
SUMMARY:
PRMA publishes this Civilian Personnel Per Diem Bulletin Number 333. Bulletin Number 333 lists current per diem rates prescribed for reimbursement of subsistence expenses while on official Government travel to Alaska, Hawaii, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, and the possessions of the U.S. The Calendar Year (CY) 2026 lodging and meal rate review for U.S. Virgin Islands resulted in rate changes for multiple locations.
DATES:
The updated rates take effect December 1, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ashley Aguilar, 571-372-1968,
ashley.aguilar5.civ@mail.mil
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This document notifies the public of revisions in per diem rates prescribed by the Per Diem, Travel, and Transportation Allowance Committee for travel to non-foreign areas outside the continental U.S. The CY 2026 lodging and meal rate review for U.S. Virgin Islands resulted in lodging and meal rate increases for multiple locations. Bulletin Number 333 is published in the
Federal Register
to ensure that Government travelers outside the Department of War are notified of revisions to the current reimbursement rates.
If you believe the lodging, meal or incidental allowance rate for a locality listed in the following table is insufficient, you may request a rate review for that location. For more information about how to request a review, please see the Defense Travel Management Office's Per Diem Rate Review Frequently Asked Questions page at
https://www.travel.dod.mil/​Travel-Transportation-Rates/​Per-Diem/​
.
Dated: November 18, 2026.
Aaron T. Siegel,
Alternate OSD Federal Register Liaison Officer, Department of Defense.

AGENCY:
Fish and Wildlife Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service), propose to list the White Sands pupfish (
Cyprinodon tularosa
), a fish species from southcentral New Mexico, as a threatened species with protective regulations under section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (Act). This determination also serves as our 12-month finding on a petition to list the White Sands pupfish. After a review of the best scientific and commercial data available, we find that listing the species is warranted. If we finalize this rule as proposed, it would add this species to the List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and extend the Act's protections to the species. All areas meeting the definition of critical habitat for the White Sands pupfish occur on Department of War (DoW) owned facilities and are exempt from designation as critical habitat in accordance with section 4(a)(3)(B) of the Act. Therefore, we are not proposing any areas as critical habitat for the White Sands pupfish.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Executive Summary
Why we need to publish a rule.
Under the Act (
16 U.S.C. 1531
et seq.
), a species warrants listing if it meets the definition of an endangered species (in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range) or a threatened species (likely to become an endangered species within the foreseeable future throughout all or a significant portion of its range). If we determine that a species warrants listing, we must list the species promptly and designate the species' critical habitat to the maximum extent prudent and determinable. We have determined that the White Sands pupfish meets the Act's definition of a threatened species; therefore, we are proposing to list it as such. While we found areas that meet the definition of critical habitat, we are not proposing to designate any critical habitat because all areas are exempt from such designation. Listing a species as an endangered or threatened species can be completed only by issuing a rule through the Administrative Procedure Act rulemaking process (
5 U.S.C. 551
et seq.
).
What this document does.
We propose to list the White Sands pupfish as a threatened species with a species-specific rule establishing protective regulations under section 4(d) of the Act.
The basis for our action.
Under the Act, we may determine that a species is an endangered or threatened species because of any of five factors: (A) the present or threatened destruction, modification, or curtailment of its habitat or range; (B) overutilization for commercial, recreational, scientific, or educational purposes; (C) disease or predation; (D) the inadequacy of existing regulatory mechanisms; or (E) other natural or manmade factors affecting its continued existence. We have determined that the White Sands pupfish meets the Act's definition of a threatened species due to the following threats: extreme flooding events (Factors A and E), increased drying (Factors A and E), and increased temperatures (Factors A and E); and the impacts of saltcedar and aquatic emergent vegetation on White Sands pupfish and its habitat (Factor A).
Section 4(a)(3) of the Act requires that the Secretary of the Interior (Secretary), to the maximum extent prudent and determinable, concurrently with listing designate critical habitat for the species. Section 3(5)(A) of the Act defines critical habitat as (i) the specific areas within the geographical area occupied by the species, at the time it is listed, on which are found those physical or biological features (I) essential to the conservation of the species and (II) which may require special management considerations or protections; and (ii) specific areas outside the geographical area occupied by the species at the time it is listed, upon a determination by the Secretary that such areas are essential for the conservation of the species. Section 4(b)(2) of the Act states that the Secretary must make the designation on the basis of the best scientific data available and after taking into consideration the economic impact, the impact on national security, and any other relevant impacts of specifying any particular area as critical habitat.
Information Requested
We intend that any final action resulting from this proposed rule will be based on the best scientific and commercial data available and be as accurate and as effective as possible. Therefore, we request comments or information from other governmental agencies, Native American Tribes, the scientific community, industry, or any other interested parties concerning this proposed rule. We particularly seek comments concerning:
(1) The species' biology, range, and population trends, including:
(a) Biological or ecological requirements of the species, including habitat requirements for feeding, breeding, and sheltering;
(b) Genetics and taxonomy;
(c) Historical and current range, including distribution patterns and the locations of any additional populations of this species;
(d) Historical and current population levels, and current and projected trends; and
(e) Past and ongoing conservation measures for the species, its habitat, or both.
(2) Threats and conservation actions affecting the species, including:
(a) Factors that may be affecting the continued existence of the species, which may include habitat modification or destruction, overutilization, disease, predation, the inadequacy of existing regulatory mechanisms, or other natural or manmade factors;
(b) Biological, commercial trade, or other relevant data concerning any threats (or lack thereof) to this species; and
(c) Existing regulations or conservation actions that may be addressing threats to this species.
(3) Additional information concerning the historical and current status of this species.
(4) Information to assist us with issuing protective regulations under section 4(d) of the Act (“4(d) rule”) that may be necessary and advisable to provide for the conservation of the White Sands pupfish. In particular, we seek information concerning:
(
printed page 75259)
(a) The extent to which we should include any of the Act's section 9 prohibitions in the 4(d) rule;
(b) Whether we should consider any additional or different exceptions from the prohibitions in the 4(d) rule;
(c) Impacts (conservation and economic) associated with implementing the 4(d) rule;
(d) How frequently and in what geographical areas are activities that we propose to regulate under the 4(d) rule (
e.g.,
sale, “take”) currently occurring;
(e) Whether there are other laws currently in place beyond what we describe in the economic considerations document that regulate the activities or “take” prohibited in the proposed 4(d) rule;
(f) Any entities likely to request section 10(a)(1)(A) permits for conducting activities that would involve “take” such as capture or handling of the White Sands pupfish;
(g) Data available on the time and economic costs of obtaining section 10(a)(1)(A) permits in accordance with
50 CFR 17.32
;
(h) Any entities likely to develop habitat conservation plans and request section 10(a)(1)(B) permits for conducting activities that would involve incidental “take” of the White Sands pupfish that we propose to prohibit;
(i) Data available on the time and economic costs of obtaining section 10(a)(1)(B) permits in accordance with
50 CFR 17.32
;
(j) Any other entities not addressed in this proposed rule that may be affected by the 4(d) rule; and
(k) Comments and suggestions regarding additional guidance and methods that we could provide or use, respectively, to streamline the implementation of this proposed 4(d) rule.
(5) Specific information related to critical habitat, such as:
(a) The amount and distribution of White Sands pupfish habitat;
(b) Any areas occurring within the range of the species (including areas not covered by the existing integrated natural resources management plans (INRMPs)), in Sierra, Lincoln, and Otero Counties of New Mexico, that should be included in a designation because they (i) are occupied at the time of listing and contain the physical or biological features that are essential to the conservation of the species and that may require special management considerations or protection, or (ii) are unoccupied at the time of listing and are essential for the conservation of the species;
(6) Whether we could improve or modify our approach to identifying critical habitat in any way to provide for greater public participation and understanding, or to better accommodate public concerns and comments.
Please include sufficient information with your submission (such as scientific journal articles or other publications) to allow us to verify any scientific or commercial information you include.
Please note that submissions merely stating support for, or opposition to, the action under consideration without providing supporting information, although noted, do not provide substantial information necessary to support a determination, as section 4(b)(1)(A) of the Act directs that determinations as to whether any species is an endangered or a threatened species must be made solely on the basis of the best scientific and commercial data available, and section 4(b)(2) of the Act directs that the Secretary shall designate critical habitat on the basis of the best scientific data available.
You must submit your comments and materials concerning this proposed rule by one of the methods listed in
ADDRESSES
.
If you submit information via
https://www.regulations.gov
,
your entire submission—including any personal identifying information—will be posted on the website. If your submission is made via a hardcopy that includes personal identifying information, you may request at the top of your document that we withhold this information from public review. However, we cannot guarantee that we will be able to do so. We will post all hardcopy submissions on
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Comments and materials we receive, as well as supporting documentation we used in preparing this proposed rule, will be available for public inspection on
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Our final determination may differ from this proposal because we will consider all comments we receive during the comment period as well as any information that may become available after this proposal. Based on the new information we receive, we may conclude that the species is endangered instead of threatened, or we may conclude that the species does not warrant listing as either an endangered or a threatened species. Based on public comment, we may determine there are additional areas that meet the definition of critical habitat and, therefore, we may propose critical habitat in the future. In addition, we may change the parameters of the prohibitions or the exceptions to those prohibitions in the protective regulations issued under section 4(d) of the Act if we conclude it is appropriate in light of comments and new information received. For example, we may expand the prohibitions if we conclude that the protective regulation as a whole, including those additional prohibitions, is necessary and advisable to provide for the conservation of the species. Conversely, we may establish additional or different exceptions to the prohibitions in the final rule if we conclude that the activities would facilitate or are compatible with the conservation and recovery of the species. In our final rule, we will clearly explain our rationale and the basis for our final decision, including why we made changes, if any, that differ from this proposal.
Public Hearing
Section 4(b)(5) of the Act provides for a public hearing on this proposal, if requested. Requests must be received by the date specified in
DATES
. Such requests must be sent to the address shown in
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
. We will schedule a public hearing on this proposal, if requested, and announce the date, time, and place of the hearing, as well as how to obtain reasonable accommodations, in the
Federal Register
and local newspapers at least 15 days before the hearing. We may hold the public hearing in person or virtually via webinar. We will announce any public hearing on our website, in addition to the
Federal Register
. The use of virtual public hearings is consistent with our regulations at
title 50 of the Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) at § 424.16(c)(3).
Previous Federal Actions
We identified the White Sands pupfish as a Category 2 candidate on December 30, 1982 (
47 FR 58454
). Category 2 candidates were defined as species for which we had information that proposed listing was possibly appropriate, but conclusive data on biological vulnerability and threats were not available to support a proposed rule at the time. The species remained so designated in subsequent annual candidate notices of review (CNOR) (
50 FR 37958
, September 18, 1985;
54 FR 554
, January 6, 1989;
56 FR 58804
, November 21, 1991;
59 FR 58982
, November 15, 1994). In the February 28, 1996, CNOR (
61 FR 7596
), we discontinued the designation of Category 2 species as candidates; therefore, the White Sands pupfish was no longer a candidate species.
Subsequently, on June 25, 2007, we received a petition dated June 18, 2007, from Forest Guardians (now WildEarth
(
printed page 75260)
Guardians) to list 475 species, including the White Sands pupfish, in the Southwestern United States as endangered or threatened species and to designate critical habitat under the Act. On December 16, 2009, we published a partial 90-day finding (
74 FR 66866
) on 192 species from that petition; in that document, we announced that the petition presented substantial information that the White Sands pupfish may be warranted for listing.
Peer Review
We conducted an SSA and prepared an SSA report for the White Sands pupfish. The SSA report documents the results of our comprehensive biological review of the best scientific and commercial data available regarding the viability of the species, which is then used to support our decision regarding whether a species warrants listing under the Act. In accordance with our joint policy with the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) on peer review that published in the
Federal Register
on July 1, 1994 (
59 FR 34270
), and our August 22, 2016, memorandum updating and clarifying the role of peer review in listing and recovery actions under the Act (
https://www.fws.gov/​sites/​default/​files/​documents/​peer-review-policy-directors-memo-2016-08-22.pdf
), we solicited independent scientific review of the information contained in the White Sands pupfish SSA report. We sent the SSA report to eight independent peer reviewers and received four responses. The peer reviews can be found at
https://www.regulations.gov
at Docket No. FWS-R2-ES-2026-1651. In preparing this proposed rule, we incorporated the results of these reviews, as appropriate, into the SSA report, which is the foundation for this proposed rule.
Summary of Peer Reviewer Comments
As discussed in Peer Review, above, we received comments from four peer reviewers on the draft SSA report. We reviewed all comments we received from the peer reviewers for substantive issues and new information regarding the contents of the SSA report. The peer reviewers generally concurred with our methods and conclusions and provided additional information, clarification, and suggestions. Reviewers primarily requested that we make revisions to further explain the rationale for the monitoring methods and models used for our analysis. We addressed all substantive comments, including recommended changes to our analysis or conclusions within the SSA report, in version 1.1 of the SSA report (Service 2026, entire). We provide a brief summary of substantive comments below.
One peer reviewer suggested that there was a need for a taxonomic reassessment given the results from a recently published scientific paper by Black et al. 2024, “Rapid vertebrate speciation via isolation, bottlenecks, and drift.” In that paper, the authors concluded that vertebrate speciation can occur rapidly as a result of isolation, genetic bottlenecks, and genetic drift and suggested that there may be two distinct species of pupfish in the Tularosa Basin.
We reviewed the recent paper by Black et al. (2024, entire) that suggests two evolutionary significant units (ESUs) of the White Sands pupfish may actually represent two distinct species, based on their study of genome-wide variation and differentiation among two natural populations and one translocated population. The authors found significant neutral genetic differentiation between the two natural populations; however, they did not detect any signals of natural selection, arguing that the separation of these ESUs occurred due to genetic drift rather than selection. Given the short generation times of pupfish, the potential for genetic drift could lead to rapid differentiation over thousands of generations, allowing for the possibility of speciation in small, isolated populations. Despite these findings, the authors do not provide evidence of adaptive differences or reproductive incompatibilities between the populations—two factors important in confirming speciation. While the study highlights a high genome-wide neutral differentiation, we conclude that there is insufficient evidence to support that speciation has occurred between these populations and will continue to classify them as members of the same taxon. The “Genetics” section of the SSA report was updated to include our assessment of the literature.
Another peer reviewer stated that the SSA report needs to provide more details regarding the climate model projections. They emphasized that climate variability and extreme weather in a warmer climate could lead to severe flooding impacts, posing a significant threat to the White Sands pupfish.
We addressed this comment by providing supplemental information in Chapter 5 of the SSA report to include more detail regarding the climate model projections and interpretation of several climate variables, which include air temperature and precipitation. In addition, we have highlighted in the SSA report that extreme precipitation events could lead to flooding that could potentially displace White Sands pupfish, such as in Salt Creek.
Another peer reviewer suggested that we improve our rationale and assumption of the use of N-mixture models (a model effective for analyzing sparse catch data) for evaluating White Sands pupfish monitoring data by clarifying the justification and assumptions used in our conclusion.
We addressed this comment by providing additional information in both Section 3.8.3 and Section 4.1 of the SSA report. We emphasized that, despite long-term monitoring efforts, we only utilized the most recent sampling data from 2017 to 2022 due to the robust sampling protocol and statistical analysis from this period. This approach accounts for instances where many data points result in zeros. Accordingly, using this approach reflects the best available science available and enables us to better estimate the likelihood of detecting fish.
I. Proposed Listing Determination
Background
A thorough review of the taxonomy, life history, and ecology of the White Sands pupfish is presented in the SSA report (Service 2026, pp. 3-20).
The White Sands pupfish is a small fish (less than 50 millimeters (mm) (1.97 inches (in)) in length) in the Cyprinodontidae family (pupfish and killifish) known only from the Tularosa Basin in southern New Mexico. White Sands pupfish are sexually dimorphic (physical characteristics differ between the sexes) with males exhibiting a black band on the caudal (tail) fin and a metallic/iridescent blue on their backs during breeding periods. Females and nonbreeding males are grayish-blue on the sides and olive green on the upper and back portions of the body, with fins a pale yellow to whitish color. Females also possess a “false eye” in the dorsal fin (Service 2026, p. 4).
White Sands pupfish are omnivorous, and food selection is dependent on resource availability. Food sources may include algae, diatoms, detritus, chironomids (non-biting midges, bloodworms), diptera (flies), copepods (small aquatic crustaceans), and ostracods (seed shrimp) (Terry 1971, p. 5; Hoover et al. 1999, p. 30).
Currently, the White Sands pupfish only occurs in seven localities in southern New Mexico (Pittenger 2023, p. 1). This includes two native populations at Malpais Spring and Salt Creek, and five replicate (introduced) populations at Lost River, North Mound Spring, Main Mound Spring, South Mound Spring, and Bradford Spring
(
printed page 75261)
(Pittenger and Springer 1999, entire; Pittenger 2023, entire). These replicate populations largely occur on White Sands Missile Range (WSMR) and Holloman Air Force Base (HAFB). A small ephemeral portion of one replicate population (approximately 1.8 kilometers (1.12 miles) of Lost River) is located on White Sands National Park; the rest of the population occurs on WSMR and HAFB.
Genetic analyses show that the two native populations, Malpais Spring and Salt Creek, have diverged significantly since the mid-Holocene. Initial estimates of this divergence place it approximately 6,000 years ago, leading to their classification as two evolutionarily significant units (ESUs) in 1998 (Stockwell et al. 1998, pp. 218-220). A more recent study suggests that Malpais Spring and Salt Creek diverged more recently, approximately 4,000-5,000 years ago (Black et al. 2024, p. 2). ESUs reflect populations that are reproductively isolated and constitute an important component of the evolutionary legacy of the species (Waples 1991, p. 11). This supports the practice of maintaining and managing the two native White Sands pupfish populations separately to maintain genetic representation of the species. Of the existing replicate populations, North Mound Spring and South Mound Spring consist of fish from the Malpais Spring ESU while Main Mound Spring, Bradford Spring, and Lost River consist of fish from the Salt Creek ESU.
The White Sands pupfish occurs within a variety of natural and artificial habitats including a laguna (a small brackish lake), wetlands, creeks, and springs (Pittenger 2015, pp. 11-24; WSMR 2015, p. 3-70). White Sands pupfish habitats can contain a diverse variety of substrates, such as detritus, silt, sand, cobble, and gravel (Pittenger 2024, pers. comm.). Vegetation found in White Sands pupfish habitat is similarly diverse, with a variety of algae, aquatic, semi-aquatic and halophytic vegetation. Specifically, vegetation may include saltcedar (
Tamarix ramosissima
), chairmaker's bulrush (
Schoenoplectus americanus
), beaked spike-rush (
Eleocharis rostellata
), saltgrass (
Distichlis spicata var. stricta
), common reed (
Phragmites australis
), spiral ditchgrass (
Ruppia cirrhosa
), alga muskgrass (
Chara
sp.), limewater brookweed (
Samolus ebracteatus
), alkali sacaton (
Sporobolus airoides
), alkali muhly (
Muhlenbergia asperifolia
), mule-fat (
Baccharis salicifolia
), iodinebush (
Allenrolfea occidentalis
), and southern goldenbush (
Isocoma pluriflora
) (Muldavin et al. 2000, p. 64; Allen et al. 2005, entire; Sivinski and Tonne 2011, p. 81; Pittenger 2020, entire).
White Sands pupfish occupy brackish (dissolved salt concentrations between 1,000 and 10,000 milligrams per liter (mg/L)) to saline water (dissolved salt concentrations greater than 10,000 mg/L). White Sands pupfish can occur in waters with a wide range of temperatures, and hourly water temperature readings from -1.9 degrees Celsius (°C) to 38 °C (28.5 degrees Fahrenheit (°F) to 100.4 °F) have been reported in occupied habitats (Pittenger 2015, p. 24). Temperatures above 42.7 °C (108.9 °F) may be lethal to White Sands pupfish (Schoenherr and Feldmeth 1992, p. 50).
Regulatory and Analytical Framework
Regulatory Framework
Section 4 of the Act (
16 U.S.C. 1533
) and the implementing regulations in
title 50 of the CFR
set forth the procedures for determining whether a species is an endangered species or a threatened species, issuing protective regulations for threatened species, and designating critical habitat for endangered and threatened species.
The Act defines an “endangered species” as a species that is in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range and a “threatened species” as a species that is likely to become an endangered species within the foreseeable future throughout all or a significant portion of its range. The Act requires that we determine whether any species is an endangered species or a threatened species because of any of the following factors:
(A) The present or threatened destruction, modification, or curtailment of its habitat or range;
(B) Overutilization for commercial, recreational, scientific, or educational purposes;
(C) Disease or predation;
(D) The inadequacy of existing regulatory mechanisms; or
(E) Other natural or manmade factors affecting its continued existence.
These factors represent broad categories of natural or human-caused actions or conditions that could have an effect on a species' continued existence. In evaluating these actions and conditions, we look for those that may have a negative effect on individuals of the species, as well as other actions or conditions that may ameliorate any negative effects or may have positive effects.
We use the term “threat” to refer in general to actions or conditions that are known to or are reasonably likely to negatively affect individuals of a species. The term “threat” includes actions or conditions that have a direct impact on individuals (direct impacts), as well as those that affect individuals through alteration of their habitat or required resources (stressors). The term “threat” may encompass—either together or separately—the source of the action or condition or the action or condition itself.
However, the mere identification of any threat(s) does not necessarily mean that the species meets the statutory definition of an endangered species or a threatened species. In determining whether a species meets either definition, we must evaluate all identified threats by considering the species' expected response and the effects of the threats—in light of those actions and conditions that will ameliorate the threats—on an individual, population, and species level. We evaluate each threat and its expected effects on the species, then analyze the cumulative effect of all of the threats on the species as a whole. We also consider the cumulative effect of the threats in light of those actions and conditions that will have positive effects on the species, such as any existing regulatory mechanisms or conservation efforts. The Secretary determines whether the species meets the definition of an endangered species or a threatened species only after conducting this cumulative analysis and describing the expected effect on the species.
The Act does not define the term “foreseeable future,” which appears in the statutory definition of threatened species. Our regulations at
50 CFR 424.11(d)
set forth a framework for evaluating the foreseeable future on a case-by-case basis which is further described in the 2009 Memorandum Opinion on the foreseeable future from the Department of the Interior, Office of the Solicitor (M-37021, January 16, 2009; “M-Opinion,” available online at
https://www.doi.gov/​sites/​doi.opengov.ibmcloud.com/​files/​uploads/​M-37021.pdf
). The foreseeable future extends as far into the future as we can make reasonably reliable predictions about the threats to the species and the species' responses to those threats. We need not identify the foreseeable future in terms of a specific period of time. We will describe the foreseeable future on a case-by-case basis, using the best scientific and commercial data available and taking into account considerations such as the species' life-history characteristics, threat projection timeframes, and environmental variability. In other words, the foreseeable future is the
(
printed page 75262)
period of time over which we can make reasonably reliable predictions. “Reliable” does not mean “certain”; it means sufficient to provide a reasonable degree of confidence in the prediction, in light of the conservation purposes of the Act.
Analytical Framework
The SSA report documents the results of our comprehensive biological review of the best scientific and commercial data available regarding the viability of the species, including an assessment of the potential threats to the species. The SSA report does not represent our decision on whether the species should be proposed for listing as an endangered or threatened species under the Act. However, it does provide the scientific basis that informs our regulatory decisions, which involve the further application of standards within the Act and our regulations and policies.
To assess White Sands pupfish viability, we used the three conservation biology principles of resiliency, redundancy, and representation (Shaffer and Stein 2000, pp. 306-310). Briefly, resiliency is the ability of the species to withstand environmental and demographic stochasticity (for example, wet or dry, warm or cold years); redundancy is the ability of the species to withstand catastrophic events (for example, droughts, large pollution events); and representation is the ability of the species to adapt to both near-term and long-term changes in its physical and biological environment (for example, climate conditions, pathogens). In general, species viability will increase with increases in resiliency, redundancy, and representation (Smith et al. 2018, p. 306). Using these principles, we identified the species' ecological requirements for survival and reproduction at the individual, population, and species levels, and described the beneficial and risk factors influencing the species' viability.
The SSA process can be categorized into three sequential stages. During the first stage, we evaluated the individual species' life-history needs. The next stage involved an assessment of the historical and current condition of the species' demographics and habitat characteristics, including an explanation of how the species arrived at its current condition. The final stage of the SSA involved making predictions about the species' future condition, including responses to positive and negative environmental and anthropogenic influences. Throughout all of these stages, we used the best scientific and commercial data available to characterize viability as the ability of a species to sustain populations in the wild over time, which we then used to inform our regulatory decision.

Summary of Biological Status and Threats
In this discussion, we review the biological condition of the species and its resources, and the threats that influence the species' current and future condition, in order to assess the species' overall viability and the risks to that viability.
Species Needs
For the White Sands pupfish to have sufficient resiliency, redundancy, and representation, individuals need suitable habitat that supports essential life functions at all life stages (see table 1, below). Based upon the best available scientific and commercial information, and acknowledging existing ecological uncertainties, White Sands pupfish individual needs include: (1) suitable water quality, (2) sufficient water quantity, and (3) habitat diversity. These needs are summarized below. For additional information, please see the SSA report (Service 2026, pp. 3-12).
