Suitable Water Quality
Like other pupfish in the
Cyprinodon
genus, the White Sands pupfish is able to tolerate a wide range of water quality conditions (Hoagstrom and Brooks 1999, p. 5). However, temperature extremes, extremely low dissolved oxygen, and salinity extremes can all result in fish mortality.
For instance, high salinities (>35,000 mg/L) have been found to affect larval and egg development in desert pupfish and Pecos pupfish (Kinne and Kinne 1962, p. 250; Hoagstrom and Brooks 1999, p. 21), suggesting a possible upper limit to salinity tolerance. Maximum salinity levels affecting White Sands pupfish development or survival are unknown. However, given that salinities higher than 35,000 mg/L were found to retard egg and larval development in closely related species, we assume salinities in excess of 35,000 mg/L would also affect White Sands pupfish.
Studies examining thermal tolerance of other pupfish have found thermal tolerance to range from below 0 °C to 45 °C (32 °F to 113 °F), although data collected in studies of desert pupfish (
Cyprinodon macularius
) found that temperatures above 42.7 °C (108.9 °F) may be lethal (Schoenherr and Feldmeth 1992, p. 50). Temperature may also influence egg development and reproduction (Shrode and Gerking 1977, p. 8), which is the most vulnerable stage in the
Cyprinodon
genus (Kodric-Brown 1983, p. 135). Another closely related species, the Amargosa pupfish (
Cyprinodon nevadensis
), was found to produce lower quality eggs (small, fragile eggs lacking a yolk) at temperatures in excess of 32 °C (89.6 °F) and increased mortality of adult pupfish at temperatures greater than 38 °C (100.4 °F) (Shrode and Gerking 1977, p. 8). Therefore, although specific data for White Sands pupfish are unavailable, the available evidence from related species suggests that temperatures in
(
printed page 75263)
excess of 42.7 °C (108.9 °F) would also negatively affect White Sands pupfish.
Based on studies of White Sands pupfish and other related species, habitats with optimal water quality conditions (temperatures between 8 °C (46.4 °F) and 30 °C (86 °F) and no known water quality impairments) are expected to support pupfish with higher body conditions, higher fecundity rates, and higher population densities (Kinne and Kinne 1962, entire; McMahon and Tash 1988, p. 1879; Hoover et al. 1999, pp. 28-29).
Pupfish, including the White Sands pupfish, exhibit a wide tolerance for varied dissolved oxygen levels. White Sands pupfish have been observed in environments with dissolved oxygen levels as low as 1.4-1.5 mg/L; however, their population sizes in these conditions are considered low (Carman 2004, pp. 44-48; Carman 2005, pp. 1-3, 34-38). Although a specific minimum tolerance level for the White Sands pupfish is not established, the desert pupfish, a close relative, has a minimum tolerance of 0.88 mg/L, suggesting that the White Sands pupfish may also survive in low dissolved oxygen conditions (Ostrand and Wilde 2001, p. 745). Based on habitats occupied by White Sands pupfish, the ideal dissolved oxygen level for White Sands pupfish is greater than 4 mg/L (Pittenger 2010, p. 27).
Sufficient Water Quantity
White Sands pupfish depend on water to complete all stages of their lifecycle. While White Sands pupfish can survive in very shallow water, they need deeper water to provide thermal refugia during the winter and summer, and sufficient water quantity throughout the year for breeding and adult survival. Reaches or areas that have water year-round, with no recorded events of drying or observed significant reductions in water volume or discharge, have a higher probability of persistence than reaches or areas that experience periodic drying or low-flow events (Service 2026, p. 35). Mortality of White Sands pupfish from stream drying has been documented in portions of Salt Creek (Pittenger et al. 2019, pp. 26-27, 36).
Habitat Diversity
White Sands pupfish need access to heterogeneous depths of water for breeding, sheltering, and feeding. Both reproductive-age and juvenile White Sands pupfish use habitats less than 50 cm (19.7 in) deep (Barlow 1961, p. 349; Hoover et al. 1999, pp. 24, 28; Pittenger 2015, p. iii). White Sands pupfish also seek refuge from avian predators, high summer temperatures, and cold winter temperatures in deeper water (Barlow 1961, p. 353; Pittenger 2015, p. 35). Therefore, we find that the presence of heterogeneous depths result in more resilient White Sands pupfish populations by supplying breeding habitat, protection from predators, and thermal refuge.
Reproductive success of male pupfish is driven by available breeding substrate for breeding territories, topographic diversity, and minimal vegetation established on sites (Barlow 1961, p. 358; Echelle 1973, p. 70; Kodric-Brown 1977, p. 751; Leiser and Itzkowitz 2003, p. 119). White Sands pupfish spawning occurs on males' territories that have suitable substrate and in shallow water habitats that are less than 50 cm (19.7 in) in depth (Hoover et al. 1999, p. 28). Based on monitoring observations, White Sands pupfish will use substrate types that are available for spawning, including submerged aquatic vegetation (
e.g.,
the macroalgae
Chara vulgaris
), firm substrates, and relatively soft or loosely clumped substrates (Pittenger 2024, pers. comm.).
Population-Level Needs
In addition to these individual-level needs, White Sands pupfish require sufficiently large pupfish abundances such that the population can withstand environmental and demographic fluctuations. Therefore, sufficient reproduction and recruitment is needed to maintain White Sands pupfish within each population. Lastly, an adequate extent of suitable habitat should be present to support a stable population of pupfish, allow for a variety of habitat features, and provide refuge during stochastic events within a population.
Species-Level Needs
At the species level, the White Sands pupfish requires demographically, physically, and genetically healthy populations across a diversity of environmental conditions to ensure resiliency across the range. These would consist of self-sustaining populations that are demographically, genetically, and physiologically robust and have sufficient suitable habitat. To ensure sufficient redundancy for the species, the White Sands pupfish needs multiple self-sustaining populations, distributed across the range of the species, to guard against population losses and losses in species' adaptive capacity. Adequate species representation requires the maintenance of both adaptive capacity and evolutionary processes. This involves maintaining populations across the breadth of behavioral, physiological, ecological, and environmental diversity, including the maintenance of both ESUs.
Threats (Stressors, Risk Factors, Etc.)
In this discussion, we review the primary threats that influence the species' current and future condition, in order to assess the species' overall viability and the risks to that viability.
We analyzed several potential threats in the SSA report and determined the primary stressors affecting the White Sands pupfish's viability were extreme flooding events, increased drying, increased temperatures, and saltcedar and aquatic emergent vegetation. Other threats we analyzed included water use and management, non-native aquatic organisms, military operations, disease, and water quality; however, these stressors were not found to be the primary drivers of White Sands pupfish viability and are not discussed further here. For a full description of all threats we considered, see the SSA report (Service 2026, pp. 21-25).
Extreme Flooding Events, Increased Drying, and Increased Temperatures
The Southwestern United States is extremely likely to experience increased drought and higher average temperatures (Sheffield and Wood 2008, p. 101). Air temperatures across New Mexico, including in the Tularosa Basin, have increased by more than 1-2 °C (2 °F) between 1970 and 2020, and temperatures are expected to continue to rise, at the same rate or higher, into the future (Dunbar et al. 2022, pp. 4-5, 11). This is likely to result in higher high temperatures, higher overnight low temperatures, and higher average temperatures (Brown et al. 2008, pp. 1, 10; Hayhoe et al. 2018, pp. 86-88).
In terms of precipitation, broadly speaking, wet areas are expected to get wetter and experience more intense precipitation events, while dry areas are expected to get drier and experience more intense drought events (Garfin et al. 2014, p. 466; Garfin et al. 2018, pp. 1109-1110). In addition, as temperatures rise, the magnitude of future storms may lead to extreme precipitation events and increased flooding. However, extreme precipitation events are difficult to simulate (Dunbar et al. 2022, p. 15). Nevertheless, intense precipitation and storm events are projected to overall increase in New Mexico, leading to an increased risk of flooding (Dunbar et al. 2022, pp. 119-120).
Potential environmental changes that are likely to affect water resources include increased air and water temperatures, evaporation, evapotranspiration, drought, earlier
(
printed page 75264)
snowmelt runoff, and reduced or increased precipitation (Llewellyn et al. 2021, p. 98). Recent models show significant changes in temperature and rainfall patterns in this region, especially under scenarios where greenhouse gas emissions remain at medium to high levels (Marvel et al. 2021, pp. 4-19). These models suggest that there will be significant changes in the timing and intensity of rainfall throughout the year.
A main uncertainty is the resulting changes to surface and ground water flow, both of which support habitat for the White Sands pupfish. We examined the potential consequences to White Sands pupfish and their habitats that arise from changes in environmental conditions, such as changes to habitats or conditions that exceed the species' physiological tolerances (
e.g.,
salinity and temperature tolerances). Increasing temperature results in decreased streamflow and increased evapotranspiration, which, in turn, result in concentrated levels of salinity. Increased temperatures and salinity levels can influence White Sands pupfish distribution and habitat use. A decrease in precipitation with an increase in evapotranspiration can lead to stream drying, resulting in a reduction in available habitat for spawning or nursery habitat, leading to reduced reproduction and survival. The lowest reach of Salt Creek is mostly intermittent, has experienced drying in the majority of the reach, and has high salinity levels. Because of this, this reach has poor habitat condition. Additionally, some of the replicate populations at Salt Creek (Bradford Spring and the upper and lower reaches of Lost River) are also experiencing drying and thus have poor habitat condition. In addition, the recent monitoring report for White Sands pupfish provided evidence that abundance is potentially influenced by the frequency of flood flow and that floods displace White Sands pupfish into lower reaches (Pittenger 2024, p. 22).
Saltcedar and Aquatic Emergent Vegetation
Dense emergent aquatic vegetation can reduce the quality and extent of White Sands pupfish habitat by altering habitat use, reducing diurnal warming, reducing food availability, and restricting visual cues needed for breeding (Pittenger et al. 2018, pp. 242-243).
Occupancy and abundance of White Sands pupfish are influenced by saltcedar presence. Dense saltcedar stands contribute to lowered water temperatures from increased shading of water and increased water loss as a result of increased uptake via roots and increased evapotranspiration (Solis et al. 2024, pp. 1-2). Saltcedar can not only indirectly increase salt concentrations within nearby water bodies by reducing water levels, but also directly increase them by extruding salt from leaves (Service 2011, p. 9). At Ash Meadows National Wildlife Refuge, Amargosa pupfish density increased following saltcedar removal, as dense saltcedar heavily shaded riparian habitat and reduced the availability of algae, an important pupfish food resource (Kennedy et al. 2005, p. 2080). Given these mechanisms and the ecological similarities between the species, the presence of saltcedar is expected to similarly reduce habitat quality for White Sands pupfish, leading to lower population densities and less favorable environmental conditions. Saltcedar is currently present at both Lost River and Bradford Spring replicate populations, although it is being managed at White Sands pupfish sites.
Conservation Efforts and Regulatory Mechanisms
The White Sands pupfish has been listed as a threatened species by the State of New Mexico since 1975. In 1990, the New Mexico Department of Game and Fish (now the New Mexico Department of Wildlife) developed a conservation plan (The White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan) as a cooperative effort with the Department of the Army and the Service to identify actions that could be implemented on WSMR and HAFB to improve the security of the species (Propst 1990, entire). The recommendations from this conservation plan included forming a White Sands Pupfish Conservation Team and the establishment of replicate populations (Propst 1990, pp. 11-15). The White Sands Conservation Plan was revised in 1994 and again in 2015 (Propst and Pittenger 1994, entire; Pittenger 2015, entire).
There are two established replicate populations for Malpais Spring (North Mound Spring and South Mound Spring) and three established replicate populations for Salt Creek (Main Mound Spring, Lost River, and Bradford Spring). Because these replicate populations have been established in areas that have natural habitat that supports the White Sands pupfish, they are only being managed by periodic vegetation control and additional translocations of White Sands pupfish from the native populations to ensure genetic diversity is maintained. Because natural habitat is present at these sites, the replicate populations are intended to be self-sustaining (Pittenger 2015, p. 38) and thus are effective in-situ conservation efforts. Similar to populations that are maintained in hatcheries, the main purpose of the replicate populations is to add redundancy to the native populations by serving as a source of fish for stocking into native populations in the event of stochastic or catastrophic events that may reduce or eliminate native populations.
In 1994, the New Mexico Department of Wildlife, the Service, WSMR, HAFB, and White Sands National Park (formerly White Sands National Monument) signed a cooperative agreement to protect and maintain viable populations of White Sands pupfish within its entire range (White Sands Pupfish Conservation Team (WSPT) 1994, entire). This agreement was updated most recently in 2020 and remains in effect until 2029, at which point it can be updated and re-signed (WSPT 2020, entire). This agreement has been continuously in effect for the 32 years since its original signing. The signatories agreed to participate on the White Sands Pupfish Conservation Team, to implement and maintain the White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan, and to fulfill their respective roles and responsibilities. This includes protecting and managing White Sands pupfish habitats on the WSMR, HAFB, and White Sands National Park, reviewing any activities that might affect the White Sands pupfish or its habitat, providing logistical and financial resources to carry out the outlined responsibilities, and ensuring that monitoring continues.
In addition, the cooperative agreement delineated areas where certain installation activities are prohibited; identified and defined specific area types covered under the agreement (essential habitat, limited-use habitat, and areas of concern); and provided specific ongoing protections as follows (WSPT 2020, pp. 2-3):
(1) Essential habitat is aquatic habitat that is occupied by White Sands pupfish on a perennial or intermittent basis. It is protected from adverse anthropogenic disturbances to ensure survival of the species. All non-emergency vehicular traffic is restricted within this habitat, with the exception of existing improved and unimproved roads. Likewise, all non-emergency activities are restricted within this habitat, unless the responsible and relevant official is consulted. In the case of emergency activities (such as chemical spills, debris recovery from military activities, or carrion removal), New Mexico
(
printed page 75265)
Department of Wildlife and the Service will be notified and conferred with, as appropriate. For detailed descriptions of the White Sands pupfish essential habitat refer to the cooperative agreement (WSPT 2020, pp. 2-3).
(2) Limited-use areas are lands adjacent to essential habitat where activities are managed to ensure that degradation of essential habitat does not occur through direct or indirect effects such as contaminant runoff and excessive soil erosion. The Service and New Mexico Department of Wildlife coordinate, as appropriate, to avoid or minimize degradation of essential habitat due to activities on limited-use areas.
(3) Areas of concern are watersheds within the topographic drainage basin of Salt Creek, Malpais Spring, Malone Draw-Lost River, Bradford Spring, and Mound Springs complex. Activities within these areas are reviewed based on their cumulative impacts on White Sands pupfish habitats.
The most recent White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan also outlines conservation goals, objectives, and actions, and describes an implementation schedule of these conservation actions (Pittenger 2015, entire). These actions included the establishment of additional replicate populations (including North, South, and Main Mound Springs) and implementing improved monitoring, which have successfully been accomplished in the subsequent years (Pittenger 2015, p. 74). The White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan is ongoing and is revised as needed.
The White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan aims to enhance the conservation status of the White Sands pupfish through several key initiatives. It includes ongoing reviews of installation activities to protect essential habitats from military operations, the development of restoration alternatives for spring-supported wetlands, and measures to reduce the risk of land-based chemical spills that could adversely affect pupfish habitats. The plan emphasizes conservation-focused research to improve understanding of the pupfish's life history and habitat dynamics, enabling informed decision-making for its management. Overall, the White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan seeks to significantly contribute to the protection and recovery of the White Sands pupfish. The White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan has been successful in meeting these goals, particularly through the establishment of replicate populations which provide redundancy for the species. Despite the success of the White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan and the cooperative agreement, the White Sands pupfish faces large-scale threats that cannot be fully or directly addressed by such a plan. Extreme flooding, increasing drying, and increased temperatures are anticipated to affect all populations of White Sands pupfish, including replicate populations. Overall, the Southwestern United States is thought to be extremely sensitive to increased drought and higher average temperatures, and there is an expectation that intense precipitation and storm events will increase in New Mexico.
A White Sands pupfish monitoring program was established in 1995 to identify factors affecting population persistence, abundance, and distribution, characterize population dynamics, and identify refugia habitats (Pittenger 1995, p. 1; Pittenger and Springer 1996, p. 3). The primary metric used between 1995 and 2014 was raw catch per unit effort, where catch is the total number of pupfish in a minnow trap and effort is the number of hours the trap was in the water. A population estimate model was then developed that considered capture probabilities of individuals. Although there is no current range-wide population estimate, abundance estimates are available for the native populations of Malpais Spring and Salt Creek and two replicate populations (North Mound Spring and Main Mound Spring) for three different years ranging from 2017 to 2023 (Service 2026, pp. 76, 79).
Cumulative Effects
By using the SSA framework to guide our analysis of the scientific information documented in the SSA report, we have analyzed the cumulative effects of identified threats and conservation actions on the species. To assess the current and future condition of the species, we evaluate the effects of all the relevant factors that may be influencing the species, including threats and conservation efforts. Because the SSA framework considers not just the presence of the factors, but to what degree they collectively influence risk to the entire species, our assessment integrates the cumulative effects of the factors and replaces a standalone cumulative-effects analysis.
Current Condition
For a full description of our analysis of current condition, please see the SSA report (Service 2026, pp. 29-47). For our analysis of the current condition of the White Sands pupfish, we delineated each native population into either four areas (for Malpais Spring) or four reaches (for Salt Creek) that we refer to as analysis units. The analysis units are defined using sections that have been identified in previous monitoring efforts and tend to have similar hydrologic conditions, which allowed us to incorporate the fine-scale data available from ongoing monitoring, as well as address spatial heterogeneity in habitat quality within each population (Pittenger 2022, p. 5; Pittenger 2023, p. 4). The four area analysis units for Malpais Spring are Area I, Area, J, Area K, and Area L. The four reach analysis units for Salt Creek are Reach A-B, Reach C-D, Reach E-F, and Reach G-H. Additionally, we analyzed replicate populations independently and used that information to inform the redundancy of the native populations (Service 2026, appendix C).
We used an expert panel of members from the White Sands Pupfish Conservation Team, including members from the Service, the New Mexico Department of Wildlife, the National Park Service (NPS), and DoW, to develop condition categories and associated probabilities of persistence (Service 2026, pp. 32-33). We then used three habitat metrics (water quality, water depth diversity, and water permanence) and three population metrics (abundance, extent of occurrence, and secure replicate populations) to describe the current resiliency of the White Sands pupfish at the area/reach level. An area/reach that is assessed to be in high condition generally has a low risk of extirpation, with adequate water quality, high water depth diversity, stable water levels over time, abundances generally greater than 2,500 fish, occupies multiple sites in the area/reach, and contains secure replicates. An area/reach that is assessed to be in low condition generally has a high risk of extirpation, with known water quality issues, a lack of water depth diversity, prevalent low flows or drying events, abundances generally less than 500 fish, a low extent of occurrence, and no secure replicate populations. Moderate areas/reaches fall between these two.
White Sands pupfish experience habitat contraction during periods of drying, relying on areas with deeper and cooler water, or moving closer to the spring source where water is more reliable. However, movement upstream from the lower reaches of Salt Creek is not possible due to the presence of a headcut (vertical drop in a stream bed) waterfall below the upper two reaches.

In Salt Creek, similar to Malpais Spring, the upper reach (Reach A-B) has high resiliency due to optimal water quality and water permanence, moderately heterogeneous depths, and a relatively high abundance and extent of occurrence of White Sands pupfish. The next reach downstream (Reach C-D) supports moderate resiliency due to moderate water quality and depth diversity, moderate extent of occurrence, and low estimated abundance. The lower reaches (Reaches E-F and G-H) have low resiliency due to low water quality, occasional drying, and a more restricted extent of occurrence. Salt Creek has two replicate populations with variable water sources (perennial or some drying has occurred), heterogeneous habitat, and moderate abundance of fish, and one replicate population with low poor habitat conditions and low abundance of fish. Although the habitat condition of Salt Creek's replicate population is lower quality, these replicate populations do still provide redundancy to support the native population and help mitigate the risk of population loss due to stochastic and catastrophic events. Overall, the Salt Creek population is currently moderately resilient to stochastics events.
Currently, the White Sands pupfish has limited redundancy because it is a narrow endemic with only two native populations, and current redundancy has not been reduced from known historical levels. Additional redundancy over a large geographic area is not possible due to limited connectivity and lack of other water bodies. However, in the event of a catastrophic event affecting one or both native populations such as drought, fish from a replicate population could be reintroduced to re-establish the population. Fish from a replicate population have not been used to re-establish a native population to date, but they have been used to supplement the Main Mound Spring replicate population in 2022 (Pittenger 2023, p. 1).
The White Sands pupfish maintains sufficient representation in the form of two ESUs (genetic lineages) and the ability to withstand a wide variety of ecological conditions. Each ESU consists of one native population and two to three replicate populations. This genetic diversity between the two ESUs allows for increased adaptive capacity in the face of future change. Ensuring persistence of each native population is therefore important to ensure no loss of representation. White Sands pupfish, similar to other species of
Cyprinodon,
have some of the widest temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen tolerances, making them well-suited to arid climates and providing some adaptive capacity. Overall, White Sands pupfish have been shown to have some ability to adapt to different environmental settings, as demonstrated in the morphological differences they exhibit when exposed to varying salinity levels (Collyer et al. 2011, p. 1).
Despite being restricted to two native populations, the White Sands pupfish is currently maintaining moderate to high resiliency to stochastic events, some redundancy from replicate populations, and some representation in the form of two ESUs (genetic lineages) and the ability to adapt to a wide range of water and habitat conditions. Additionally, the conservation efforts in place for this species ensure the protection and management of the species.
Future Conditions
For a full description of our analysis of future conditions, see the SSA report (Service 2026, pp. 48-61). Using the same analysis units described above, we then assessed future conditions of the White Sands pupfish. We developed two future scenarios at three time steps (2025-2049, 2050-2074, and 2075-2099) to project how the viability of the White Sands pupfish may change in the future. These timeframes were chosen based upon available projections (U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) 2024, unpaginated) and our ability to determine the species' response to those changes. We used two SSP greenhouse gas emission scenarios (SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5) to assess the effects on species' resiliency, redundancy, and representation, and how those changes affect the overall viability of White Sands pupfish.
Scenario 1 uses the SSP2-4.5 greenhouse gas emission scenario in which carbon dioxide (CO
2
) emissions continue to increase during the first half of the 21st century and then stabilize and decline from 2050 to 2100. Under SSP2-4.5, warming is expected to increase, along with the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, such as flooding and drought. Within the Tularosa Basin, surface temperatures are likely to be 5.4 °C (9.8 °F) warmer by 2099 compared to the 1981-2010 mean of 14.6 °C (58.2 °F) (Service 2026, p. 81). Additionally, total winter and spring precipitation is anticipated to decrease by 12.4 percent by 2099, compared to the 1981-2010 mean of 7.6 cm (3.01 in) (Service 2026, p. 81). In this scenario, future annual air temperature increases, and annual precipitation decreases throughout the Tularosa Basin (USGS 2024, unpaginated; Service 2026, p. 81).
Scenario 2 uses the SSP5-8.5 emissions scenario, where CO
2
emissions continue at a higher rate than the SSP2-4.5 scenario (Service 2026, p. 51). The SSP5-8.5 scenario projects significant increases in the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, such as drought and floods. Within the Tularosa Basin, surface temperatures are likely to be 5.7 °C (10.2 °F) warmer by 2099 compared to the 1981-2010 mean of 14.6 °C (58.2 °F) (Service 2026, p. 81). Additionally, total winter and spring precipitation is anticipated to decrease
(
printed page 75267)
by 24.5 percent by 2099, compared to the 1981-2010 mean of 7.6 cm (3.01 in) (Service 2026, p. 81).
Using projections for stream temperature, precipitation, and evaporative deficit (a measure of aridity that uses the difference between potential evapotranspiration and actual evapotranspiration) under these two scenarios, we then projected the potential range of outcomes to White Sands pupfish. Under both future scenarios, mean annual air temperature is projected to increase through 2099 with a decrease in winter and spring precipitation (including snow) of 12.4 to 24.5 percent through 2099. Decreases in soil moisture, earlier snowmelt runoff timing, and shorter snowmelt runoff duration are virtually certain to occur, as well as increases in seasonal evaporation patterns (Dunbar et al. 2022 pp. 17-18, 120). We find that intermittent reaches will experience earlier and longer drying periods (
i.e.,
lower reaches of Salt Creek) and the extent of habitat may become contracted during drier periods (
i.e.,
Malpais Spring). The extent of increased soil drying is projected to be higher under scenario 2 than scenario 1. Future conditions of White Sands pupfish populations are projected to be similar across all time steps and under both scenarios, with overall population resiliency anticipated to decline within both populations (see tables 3 and 4, below).

Overall, Malpais Spring is projected to decline from high to moderate resiliency under both future scenarios due to increased drying of the lower areas and reduced water depths, leading to habitat contractions, decreased hiding cover, and increased water temperatures. Under scenario 1, Area I, the uppermost reach, is anticipated to remain in high condition because it is directly downstream from a spring, which provides a stable source of water in terms of water quantity and water quality (
i.e.,
temperature). The most severe impacts are anticipated to the lower reaches of Malpais Springs and to areas that have more homogenous depths in later time steps because habitat contraction will reduce water depths, further increase the proportion of shallow depths and likely decrease the difference between the maximum depth and minimum depth. An increase in shallower depths could lead to increased temperatures as well as increased avian predation since White Sands pupfish use deeper water to hide. Additionally, we expect that the frequency of hot water temperatures will increase in areas where water temperatures already exceed 35 °C (95 °F), such as Area L. In the second and third timesteps (2050-2099), we anticipate that we would see more homogenous depths in Area J and Area K and water temperatures are anticipated to remain between 30 °C (86 °F) and 35 °C (95 °F).
Under scenario 2, negative effects are expected to affect the lower reaches of Malpais Spring; the most severe impacts are anticipated in areas that have somewhat heterogeneous depths. This is because habitat contraction will reduce water depths, further increasing the proportion of shallow depths and decreasing depth heterogeneity. An increase in shallower depths could lead to increased temperatures. Additionally, we expect that the frequency of hot water temperatures will increase in the lower reaches where water temperatures already exceed 30 °C (86 °F). Resiliency is expected to remain at elevated risk from 2074 to 2099, but not further degrade after 2074, as the upper portions have a reliable groundwater source and vegetation that minimizes the evaporation rate and mitigates increased temperatures. However, these upper portions are small, comprising only 9.5 percent (37.3 acres; scenario 2) to 28 percent (77.3 acres; scenario 1) of the current wetted area at Malpais Spring. Because these areas are so small, any impacts to the upper portions by stochastic or catastrophic events such as extreme storm events or extreme drying
(
printed page 75268)
could eliminate the species from Malpais Spring entirely.
Salt Creek is projected to decline from moderate to low resiliency at every time step and under both scenarios due to severe impacts to the lower reaches from long-term drought; however, the most severe impacts are anticipated in the lower reaches. At each time step in scenario 1, one analysis unit (Reach A-B) is projected to be in moderate condition and analysis units (Reaches C-D, E-F, G-H) are projected to be in low condition, where one analysis unit (Reach C-D) declines in overall condition from moderate to low condition from current condition. At each time step in scenario 2, Reach A-B is projected to decline from high to moderate condition, and Reach C-D is projected to decline from moderate to low condition. Reach G-H remains in low condition. The reduction in precipitation and increased evapotranspiration is projected to result in increased drying and shallower water depths, leading to habitat contractions, increased temperatures, and a reduction in hiding cover and thermal refugia. Additionally, Salt Creek is connected to an active channel and, therefore, subject to catastrophic flooding. Fish pushed downstream in floods are unable to move upstream towards more stable water during times of drying due to the presence of a headcut waterfall below the upper two reaches and, therefore, remain trapped in reaches more subject to drying.
Replicate populations were assessed independently and are considered to add redundancy to the native populations in the event of a stochastic or catastrophic event impacting a native population, rather than as independent populations. These populations are needed to mitigate catastrophic events, such as drought, that may occur within the native population of Malpais Spring, which becomes increasingly at risk of extirpation into the future. Both of the replicate populations for Malpais Spring are expected to continue to have a stable water source, heterogeneous habitat, and high abundance of fish. Therefore, these replicate populations currently support the native population at Malpais Spring and will help mitigate the future risk of population loss due to stochastic and catastrophic events.
For Salt Creek, all three replicate populations will experience increased drying and decreased heterogeneous water depths. These declines in habitat suitability of Salt Creek's replicate population will limit their ability to serve as refugia populations and result in an overall decline in species redundancy and representation.
Under both scenarios, the White Sands pupfish will experience reduced resiliency, redundancy, and representation across its range. Many of the analysis units within the two native populations are projected to have reduced water quantity, water quality, and depth heterogeneity conditions that would significantly impact these populations. These declines in habitat condition are likely to reduce the survival and fecundity of individuals due to reductions in available habitat and increases in salinity and water temperature. As a result of these changes, the two native populations are more vulnerable to stochastic and catastrophic events. Although the two replicate populations for Malpais Spring will provide continued redundancy for the native population, the native population at Malpais Spring is projected to decline in resiliency to some degree in most areas, with the exception of the one area (Area I) at the spring source. Salt Creek is at risk from catastrophic flooding which would flush fish downstream below a headcut waterfall, preventing movement back upstream into higher quality habitats. These lower reaches occasionally dry and, therefore, isolated White Sands pupfish within these lower reaches of Salt Creek may be exposed to desiccation and lethal stream temperatures. The replicate populations at Salt Creek will experience declines in habitat suitability and thus will have reduced capacity to provide redundancy to mitigate the impacts of catastrophic events at the native population of Salt Creek.
In summary, White Sands pupfish will be impacted by increased air temperature, decreased winter and spring precipitation, and increased evapotranspiration. These changes will likely increase water temperatures and the seasonal drying of reaches that are further from groundwater or spring discharge. In Salt Creek, this is particularly concerning because the two reaches farthest from the spring, along with part of a third reach that is likely to seasonally dry up, are disconnected from the stable perennial reaches by a headcut waterfall, which prevents fish from moving upstream into habitats with a more stable water supply.
The native populations of White Sands pupfish have very limited redundancy. The replicate populations provide some level of mitigation of risk; however, the decline in condition of replicate populations in Salt Creek may limit their ability to serve as refugia populations and would result in an overall decline in species redundancy because the native populations may not be able to be reestablished after catastrophic events, such as flooding. Because the species is projected to maintain populations in both Malpais Spring and Salt Creek into the future, genetic diversity will continue to exist among the two ESUs. Given the current cooperative agreement, the White Sands Pupfish Conservation Team will continue to implement measures that help maintain resiliency of each of the native populations, to the extent possible. This, in addition to the White Sands Conservation Team managing the replicate populations, increases the likelihood some level of genetic diversity will be maintained among the two ESUs. However, the decline in resiliency of the native populations and some of the replicate populations will potentially limit their adaptive capacity into the future. Furthermore, all populations, both native and replicate, are vulnerable to catastrophic events, particularly large-scale drought.
Determination of Status Background
Section 4 of the Act (
16 U.S.C. 1533
) and our regulations at
50 CFR part 424
set forth the procedures for determining whether a species meets the definition of an endangered species or a threatened species. The Act requires that we determine whether a species meets the definition of an endangered species or a threatened species because of any of the following factors: (A) The present or threatened destruction, modification, or curtailment of its habitat or range; (B) overutilization for commercial, recreational, scientific, or educational purposes; (C) disease or predation; (D) the inadequacy of existing regulatory mechanisms; or (E) other natural or manmade factors affecting its continued existence. We consider these five factors and the species' responses to these factors when making these determinations.
Section 3 of the Act defines endangered species and threatened species. An endangered species is any species which is in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range, and a threatened species is any species which is likely to become an endangered species within the foreseeable future throughout all or a significant portion of its range. Both definitions include not only the phrase “throughout all,” but also the phrase “or a significant portion of its range.” Thus, there are ultimately four bases for listing a species under the Act (in danger of extinction throughout all of its range, in danger of extinction throughout a significant portion of its range, likely to become an endangered species within the foreseeable future throughout all of
(
printed page 75269)
its range, or likely to become an endangered species within the foreseeable future throughout a significant portion of its range). These four bases are made up of two classifications (
i.e.,
endangered or threatened) and two components (
i.e.,
throughout all of its range or throughout a significant portion of its range).
Beginning in 2001, a number of judicial opinions addressed our interpretation of the phrase “or a significant portion of its range” (the SPR phrase) in the statutory definitions of endangered species and threatened species. In
Defenders of Wildlife
v.
Norton,
258 F.3d 1136 (9th Cir. 2001) regarding the flat-tailed horned lizard, the court held that the interpretation of the SPR phrase that we had applied in analyzing the status of the flat-tailed horned lizard was unacceptable because it would allow for a species to warrant listing throughout a significant portion of a species' range only when the species “is in danger of extinction everywhere” (id. at 1141). The court held that the SPR phrase must be given independent meaning from the “throughout all” phrase to avoid making the SPR phrase in the statute superfluous.
In an attempt to address the judicial opinions calling into question our approach to evaluating whether a species was endangered or threatened throughout a significant portion of its range, the Services published a Final Policy on Interpretation of the Phrase “Significant Portion of Its Range” in the Endangered Species Act's Definitions of “Endangered Species” and “Threatened Species” (hereafter “2014 SPR Policy;”
79 FR 37578
, July 1, 2014). The notice of the draft 2014 SPR Policy provides more detail about litigation before 2014 regarding the phrase (
76 FR 76987
, December 9, 2011). The 2014 SPR Policy included four elements:
(1) Consequence—that the consequence of determining that a species warrants listing based on its status in a significant portion of its range is to list the species throughout all of its range;
(2) Significance—a definition of the term “significant;”
(3) Range—that the species' “range” is the current range of the species; and
(4) DPS—that, if a [vertebrate] species is endangered or threatened in an SPR and the population in that SPR is a distinct population segment (DPS), the Service will list just the DPS.
Subsequently, two district courts vacated the definition of “significant” contained in the 2014 SPR Policy (
Ctr. for Biological Diversity
v.
Jewell,
248 F. Supp. 3d 946, 959 (D. Ariz. 2017) (“
CBD
v.
Jewell”
) and
Desert Survivors
v.
U.S. Dep't of the Interior,
321 F. Supp. 3d 1011, 1070-74 (N.D. Cal. 2018) (“
Desert Survivors”
)). The courts found that the definition in the 2014 SPR Policy set too high a threshold and rendered the SPR language in the statute superfluous, failing to give it independent meaning from the “throughout all” phrase. In 2020, another court (
Ctr. for Biological Diversity
v.
Everson,
435 F. Supp. 3d 69 (D.D.C. 2020) (“
Everson”
)) also vacated the specific aspect of the 2014 SPR Policy under which, “if the Services determine that a species is threatened throughout all of its range, the Services will not analyze whether the species is endangered in a significant portion of its range” (id. at 98). This was an extension of the definition of “significant,” which required a stepwise process in which we only considered whether a species may be endangered or threatened throughout a significant portion of its range when the species was not endangered or threatened throughout all of its range. In an extension of the earlier rulings from
CBD
v.
Jewell
and
Desert Survivors,
the court found that this aspect of the definition of the 2014 SPR Policy was not only inconsistent with the statute because it “rendered the `endangered in a significant portion of its range' basis for listing superfluous,” but was also “inconsistent with [Endangered Species Act] principles” and “not a logical outgrowth from the draft policy.” Under this ruling, if we find a species is not in danger of extinction throughout all of its range, we must evaluate whether the species is in danger of extinction throughout a significant portion of its range, even in cases where we have determined that the species is likely to become in danger of extinction within the foreseeable future (threatened) throughout all of its range. The remaining three elements of the 2014 SPR Policy remain intact.
In short, the courts have directed that the definition of “significant” must afford the phrase “or a significant portion of its range” an independent meaning from the “throughout all of its range” phrase. Therefore, to determine whether any species warrants listing, we determine for each classification (endangered and threatened) the appropriate component to evaluate (throughout all of its range or throughout a significant portion of its range).
We make this determination based on whether the best scientific and commercial data available indicate that the species has a similar extinction risk in all areas across its range (at a scale that is biologically appropriate for that species). When making a listing determination for a species that has a similar extinction risk
in all areas
across its range, we determine its regulatory status using the component “throughout all of its range.” For example, in some cases there is no way to divide a species' range in a way that is biologically appropriate. This could be because the range is so small that there is only one population or because the species functions as a metapopulation such that effects to one population directly result in effects to another population. On the other hand, when making a listing determination for a species whose extinction risk varies across its range, we determine its regulatory status using the component “throughout a significant portion of its range.”
For either classification (endangered or threatened), we consider the five factors and the species' responses to those factors regardless of which component (throughout all of its range or throughout a significant portion of its range) we are evaluating. When assessing whether a species is endangered or threatened throughout a significant portion of its range, we address two questions because we must determine whether there is any portion of the species' range for which both (1) the portion is “significant” and (2) the species is in danger of extinction or likely to become in danger of extinction within the foreseeable future throughout that portion. We may address either question first. Regardless of which question we address first, if we reach a negative answer with respect to the first question that we address, we do not need to evaluate the other question for that portion of the species' range.
Determination of White Sands Pupfish's Status
We propose listing the White Sands pupfish as a threatened species because it is not in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant portion of its range, but it is likely to become in danger of extinction within the foreseeable future
throughout all of its range.
As stated above, when the species has similar extinction risk
in all areas
across its range (at a scale that is biologically appropriate for that species), we determine its classification based upon its regulatory status throughout all of its range. Conversely, if the extinction risk varies across its range such that the species' regulatory status may be different in a portion of its range, we determine a species' classification based upon its regulatory status throughout a significant portion of its range. Either way, we need to begin by determining the scale that is
(
printed page 75270)
biologically appropriate for a classification determination for that species.
For many species, we can divide its range in an infinite number of ways. As described in
Current Condition,
for the White Sands pupfish, we divided the range into four analysis units within each of the two native populations to incorporate the fine-scale data available from ongoing monitoring and address spatial heterogeneity in habitat quality within each population. The two native populations were called “population analysis units” to show the distinction between the two populations that have diverged over time. The smaller scale analysis units within the larger population analysis units were called “area analysis units” in Malpais Spring and “reach analysis units” in Salt Creek. We used the larger units, population analysis units (Malpais Spring and Salt Creek), for our analysis of the regulatory status of White Sands pupfish because, as discussed above, those populations are separate based on genetic representation of the species. In summary, population analysis units (Malpais Spring and Salt Creek) are the units that provide the appropriate scale to assess extinction risk for the White Sands pupfish.
We then evaluated whether the White Sands pupfish has a similar risk of extinction within the foreseeable future
in all areas
across its range by assessing its extinction risk within each population analysis unit. Our review indicated that while the White Sands pupfish's populations have different future resiliency, their extinction risks are not significantly different across the species' range. Each area is a single population with limited redundancy, and so even Malpais Spring, with moderate resiliency, faces elevated threats from stochastic and catastrophic events in the foreseeable future. Since all areas may be in danger of extinction in the foreseeable future, we evaluated whether the White Sands pupfish may be threatened based upon the “throughout all of its range” component. In undertaking this analysis, we reviewed the best scientific and commercial data available regarding threats to the species, its responses to those threats, and any associated conservation measures. We then assessed the cumulative effects of those threats and conservation measures within the foreseeable future under the Act's section 4(a)(1) factors. We examined the following threats: extreme flooding events, increased drying, and increased temperatures (Factors A and E) and saltcedar and dense aquatic emergent vegetation (Factor A), including cumulative effects.
The statutory difference between an endangered species and a threatened species is the timeframe in which the species becomes in danger of extinction; an endangered species is in danger of extinction while a threatened species is not in danger of extinction but is likely to become so within the foreseeable future.
Under both future scenarios, and at all three time steps, resiliency of both native populations, as well as all three replicate populations for Salt Creek, decline into the future. Future scenarios project changes out until 2099, which we are considering the foreseeable future because that is the time period for which there are available projections for air temperature and precipitation (USGS 2024, unpaginated) and we can make reasonably reliable predictions about the species' response to those changes. By the first time step (2025-2049), Malpais Spring is projected to decline from high to moderate resiliency due to increased drying of the lower areas and reduced water depths, leading to habitat contractions, decreased hiding cover, and increased water temperatures, which will elevate the overall extirpation risk during this period. Similarly, Salt Creek is projected to decline from moderate to low during the same time period due to increased drying and shallower water depths, leading to habitat contractions, increased temperatures, and a reduction in hiding cover and thermal refugia for an overall high extirpation risk.
Resiliency within Malpais Spring declines until the 2050-2074 time step, where the most significant impacts are likely to occur in the lower portion due to evaporation and increased temperatures. The upper portions near the spring source that are expected to maintain most of the White Sands pupfish population comprise only 9.5 percent (37.3 acres; scenario 2) to 28 percent (77.3 acres; scenario 1) of the current wetted area at Malpais Spring. Because these areas are relatively small, any impacts to the upper portions by stochastic or catastrophic events such as extreme storm events or extreme drying would likely impact the entire Malpais Spring system. This reduction of quality habitat for the White Sands pupfish is projected to result in a contraction in the area occupied by the species, making it more vulnerable to both catastrophic and stochastic events. Salt Creek continues to decline in condition until 2075-2099 under both scenarios due to a reduction in year-round precipitation such that the overall extirpation risk for this population analysis unit is high. Most areas of Salt Creek are far from a groundwater source and will likely experience increased evaporation and water temperatures. Additionally, Salt Creek is at the highest risk from catastrophic flooding, which would flush fish from the higher-quality habitat near the springhead into the lower-quality habitat downstream. The presence of a headcut below the first two reaches prevents upstream movement, thereby trapping fish in reaches that are subject to increased drying.
The replicate populations at Salt Creek will experience declines in habitat suitability and thus will have reduced capacity to provide redundancy to mitigate the impacts of catastrophic events at the native population of Salt Creek. Therefore, the ability of fish from replicate populations to provide rescue support to Salt Creek will be limited, reducing overall species redundancy. Additionally, representation will further decline with the degradation and potential loss of replicate populations for Salt Creek.
Despite the numerous successes of the White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan, such as the establishment of replicate populations and the implementation of monitoring efforts and habitat management, the species faces large-scale threats that cannot be directly or fully addressed by the White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan. Changes in hydrological conditions, increasing temperature, and extreme precipitation events are anticipated to affect all populations of White Sands pupfish, including replicate populations of Salt Creek. Overall, the Southwestern United States is thought to be extremely sensitive to increased drought and higher average temperatures, and intense precipitation and storm events are projected to increase in New Mexico. Recent models project significant changes in temperature and rainfall patterns in this region, especially under scenarios where greenhouse gas emissions remain at medium to high levels (Marvel et al. 2021, pp. 4-19).
We find that both White Sands pupfish native populations are projected to decline in resiliency into the future due to increased drying, water temperatures, and evaporation, resulting in shallower water depths, habitat contraction, and a reduction in hiding cover and thermal refugia. Species redundancy is expected to decline in the future due to the potential extirpation of one replicate population, and additional declines in the resiliency of the remaining replicate populations for Salt Creek due to decreased water
(
printed page 75271)
levels, resulting in more homogeneous depths. Given that the Salt Creek native population is most at risk of extirpation from catastrophic flooding, the loss of replicate populations further diminishes the likelihood that the population could successfully be repopulated following a catastrophic event. Representation is projected to decline due to the degradation and potential loss of replicate populations for Salt Creek.
In summary, the White Sands pupfish is likely to become in danger of extinction within the foreseeable future in all areas across its range (
i.e.,
in every population analysis unit); thus, for the threatened classification, there is no portion of the range where the White Sands pupfish may have a regulatory status that is different from its status in the rest of its range. Based on the best scientific and commercial data available, we conclude that the White Sands pupfish is likely to become in danger of extinction within the foreseeable future throughout all of its range.
In accordance with the court's holding in
Everson,
when we find a species warrants listing as a threatened species, we must also consider whether the species is in danger of extinction throughout a significant portion of its range. We determined that the White Sands pupfish is not in danger of extinction throughout a significant portion of its range. To reach this determination, we first assessed whether we could divide the species' range at a biologically appropriate scale. As discussed above, population analysis units are the units that provide the appropriate scale to assess extinction risk for the White Sands pupfish.
We then evaluated whether the White Sands pupfish has a similar near-term risk of extinction in all areas across its range by assessing its extinction risk within each population analysis unit. Our review indicated that the White Sands pupfish's near-term extinction risk is similar in all areas across its range; therefore, we evaluated whether it may be endangered based upon the “throughout all of its range” component. In undertaking this analysis, we reviewed the best scientific and commercial data available regarding threats to the species, its responses to those threats, and any associated conservation measures. We then assessed the cumulative effects of those threats and conservation measures under the Act's section 4(a)(1) factors. We examined the following threats: extreme flooding events, increased drying, and increased temperatures (Factors A and E) and saltcedar and dense aquatic emergent vegetation (Factor A), including cumulative effects.
The White Sands pupfish is currently maintaining moderate to high resiliency at both native populations, has five replicate populations which provide redundancy, and has representation that is maintained in the reproductively separate ESUs (Malpais Spring and Salt Creek), each preserving a unique portion of the species' genetic legacy. Additionally, the species is protected by ongoing conservation efforts through the cooperative agreement and White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan. Although there is a risk of catastrophic flooding at Salt Creek, fish from replicate populations can be used to repopulate the area following extirpation.
The White Sands pupfish is currently restricted to two native populations and five replicate populations. Malpais Spring and Salt Creek support fish from different ESUs, which are needed to maintain the genetic diversity and adaptive capacity of the species. Replicate populations add additional redundancy in that they can serve as a source of fish in case of a catastrophic event at one of the native populations. Within both native populations, areas closer to the spring source are more resilient due to the presence of more reliable water, and resiliency declines as you move downstream and away from the water sources. Malpais Spring is currently highly resilient to stochastic events due to optimal water quality, heterogeneity of water depths, and a large extent of occurrence. Salt Creek is currently moderately resilient to stochastic events with declining habitat conditions further downstream. Although the upper reach of Salt Creek maintains high resiliency, resiliency declines moving downstream, with the lower two reaches subject to occasional drying.
Although both population analysis units occur within a very small geographic area and experience similar effects of climate change, we found that, currently, Salt Creek has lower resiliency than Malpais Spring. We also found that the replicate populations for Salt Creek are in poorer condition than those for Malpais Spring. Salt Creek is currently moderately resilient to stochastic events due to the presence of permanent water in the upper two reaches, high water quality, abundance, and extent of occurrence in the uppermost reach, and presence of three replicate populations. The presence of these three replicate populations provides redundancy to the Salt Creek ESU. Although Salt Creek has a moderate probability of persistence overall, the upper reach has a high probability of persistence and pupfish from one of the three replicates could be used to repopulate Salt Creek following a reduction or elimination of pupfish. Therefore, we found no portion of the White Sands pupfish's range where threats are affecting individuals differently from how they are affecting the species elsewhere in its range such that the status of the species in that portion differs from any other portion of the species' range.
Additionally, the White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan and cooperative agreement have, and will continue to, provide guidance for agencies and partners working towards White Sands pupfish conservation through several means. First, there is consistent and rigorous monitoring across the spatial distribution of the species, providing a long-term dataset on the persistence of the White Sands pupfish and population estimates (Pittenger 2017, entire; Pittenger 2019, entire). This monitoring allows for the detection of population declines that may require stocking of fish from replicate populations. The Main Mound Spring replicate population had more pupfish added in 2022 (Pittenger 2023, p. 1). Secondly, the cooperative agreement guarantees an effective and cooperative working relationship between all signatories and provides for the protection, management, and maintenance of White Sands pupfish habitat on the WSMR, HAFB, and White Sands National Park (WSPT 2020, entire). Third, the White Sands Pupfish Conservation Plan identifies several conservation actions, objectives, and goals that will help to improve the security of the species by protecting and managing White Sands pupfish habitats, reviewing any activities that might affect the White Sands pupfish or its habitat, and ensuring that monitoring continues (Pittenger 2015, entire).
In summary, we find that the White Sands pupfish is not in danger of extinction in any areas across its range (
i.e.,
in no population analysis unit). Therefore, no portion of the species' range provides a basis for determining that the species is in danger of extinction throughout a significant portion of its range.
Determination of Status
Based on the best scientific and commercial data available, we determine that the White Sands pupfish meets the Act's definition of a threatened species because it is likely to become in danger of extinction within the foreseeable future throughout all of its range. Therefore, we propose to list the White Sands pupfish as a threatened
(
printed page 75272)
species in accordance with sections 3(20) and 4(a)(1) of the Act.
Available Conservation Measures
Conservation measures provided to species listed as endangered or threatened species under the Act include recognition as a listed species, planning and implementation of recovery actions, requirements for Federal protection, and prohibitions against certain practices. Recognition through listing results in public awareness, and conservation by Federal, State, Tribal, and local agencies, foreign governments, private organizations, and individuals. The Act encourages cooperation with the States and other countries and calls for recovery actions to be carried out for listed species. The protection required by Federal agencies, including the Service, and the prohibitions against certain activities are discussed, in part, below.
The primary purpose of the Act is the conservation of endangered and threatened species and the ecosystems upon which they depend. The ultimate goal of such conservation efforts is the recovery of these listed species, so that they no longer need the protective measures of the Act. Section 4(f) of the Act directs us to develop and implement recovery plans for the conservation and survival of endangered and threatened species unless we determine that such a plan will not promote the conservation of the species. Under section 4(f)(1)(B)(ii), recovery plans must, to the maximum extent practicable, include objective, measurable criteria which, when met, would result in a determination, in accordance with the provisions of section 4 of the Act, that the species be removed from the Lists of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants.
Recovery plans provide a roadmap for us and our partners on methods of enhancing conservation and minimizing threats to listed species, as well as measurable criteria against which to evaluate progress towards recovery and assess the species' likely future condition. However, they are not regulatory documents and do not substitute for the determinations and promulgation of regulations required under section 4(a)(1) of the Act. A decision to revise the status of a species, or to delist a species, is ultimately based on an analysis of the best scientific and commercial data available to determine whether a species is no longer an endangered species or a threatened species, regardless of whether that information differs from the recovery plan.
The recovery planning process begins with development of a recovery outline made available to the public soon after a final listing determination. The recovery outline guides the immediate implementation of urgent recovery actions while a recovery plan is being developed. Recovery teams (composed of species and other experts, including those from Federal and State agencies, Tribes, the academic community, or nongovernmental organizations) may be established to develop and implement recovery plans. The recovery outline, draft recovery plan, final recovery plan, and any revisions will be available on our website as they are completed (
https://www.fws.gov/​program/​endangered-species
) or from our New Mexico Ecological Services Field Office (see
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
).
Implementation of recovery actions generally requires the participation of a broad range of partners, including other Federal agencies, States, Tribes, nongovernmental organizations, businesses, and private landowners. Examples of recovery actions include habitat restoration (
e.g.,
restoration of native vegetation), research, captive propagation and reintroduction, and outreach and education. The recovery of many listed species cannot be accomplished solely on Federal lands because their range may occur primarily or solely on non-Federal lands. Section 7 of the Act is titled, “Interagency Cooperation,” and it mandates all Federal action agencies to use their existing authorities to further the conservation purposes of the Act and to ensure that their actions are not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of listed species or destroy or adversely modify critical habitat. Regulations implementing section 7 are codified at
50 CFR part 402
.
Section 7(a)(2) states that each Federal action agency shall, in consultation with the Secretary, ensure that any action they authorize, fund, or carry out is not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of a listed species or result in the destruction or adverse modification of designated critical habitat. Each Federal agency shall review its action at the earliest possible time to determine whether it may affect listed species or critical habitat. If a determination is made that the action may affect listed species or critical habitat, formal consultation is required (
50 CFR 402.14(a)
), unless the Service concurs in writing that the action is not likely to adversely affect listed species or critical habitat. At the end of a formal consultation, the Service issues a biological opinion, containing its determination of whether the Federal action is likely to result in jeopardy or adverse modification.
In contrast, section 7(a)(4) of the Act requires Federal agencies to confer with the Service on any action which is likely to jeopardize the continued existence of any species proposed to be listed under the Act or result in the destruction or adverse modification of critical habitat proposed to be designated for such species. Although the conference procedures are required only when an action is likely to result in jeopardy or adverse modification, action agencies may voluntarily confer with the Service on actions that may affect species proposed for listing or critical habitat proposed to be designated. In the event that the subject species is listed or the relevant critical habitat is designated, a conference opinion may be adopted as a biological opinion and serve as compliance with section 7(a)(2) of the Act.
Examples of discretionary actions for the White Sands pupfish that may be subject to conference and consultation procedures under section 7 are management of Federal lands administered by the DoW or NPS, as well as actions that require a Federal permit (such as a permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers under section 404 of the Clean Water Act (
33 U.S.C. 1251
et seq.
)) or actions funded by Federal agencies such as the Federal Highway Administration, Federal Aviation Administration, or the Federal
(
printed page 75273)
Emergency Management Agency. Federal actions not affecting listed species or critical habitat—and actions on State, Tribal, local, or private lands that are not federally funded, authorized, or carried out by a Federal agency—do not require section 7 consultation. Federal agencies should coordinate with the New Mexico Ecological Services Field Office (see
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
