39-23520; Docket No. FAA-2026-4656; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-00214-R.
(a) Effective Date
This airworthiness directive (AD) is effective December 28, 2026.
(b) Affected ADs
None.
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to all Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Model EC135P1, EC135P2, EC135P2+, EC135P3, EC135T1, EC135T2, EC135T2+, EC135T3, and EC635T2+ helicopters, certificated in any category.
(d) Subject
Joint Aircraft System Component (JASC) Code 6410, Tail Rotor Blades.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by a report of a separated tail rotor blade (TRB) assembly due to a crack in the TRB assembly caused by intergranular corrosion. The FAA is issuing this AD to detect and address cracks in the TRB assembly. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in separation of the TRB assembly and reduced control of the helicopter.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Requirements
Except as specified in paragraphs (h) and (i) of this AD: Comply with all required actions and compliance times specified in, and in accordance with, European Union Aviation Safety Agency AD 2026-0031, dated February 19, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0031).
(h) Exceptions to EASA AD 2026-0031
(1) Where EASA AD 2026-0031 refers to its effective date, this AD requires using the effective date of this AD.
(2) Where EASA AD 2026-0031 refers to flight hours, this AD requires using hours time-in-service (TIS).
(3) Where paragraph (1) of EASA AD 2026-0031 specifies “Before an affected part exceeds 1432 FH [flight hours] since first installation on a helicopter”, this AD requires replacing that text with “Before an affected part accumulates 1,432 hours TIS since first installation on a helicopter, or within 10 hours TIS after the effective date of this AD, whichever occurs later”.
(4) Where paragraph 4.3 of the material referenced in EASA AD 2026-0031 recommends type II visible dye inspections, this AD requires the inspection methods in paragraphs (h)(4)(i), (ii), or (iii) of this AD, as applicable:
(i) If the affected part has previously been inspected using a type II visible dye method, perform type II visible dye (Method B of the material referenced in EASA AD 2026-0031) or eddy current inspections, instead of fluorescent penetrant inspections.
(ii) If the affected part has not previously been inspected using a type II visible dye inspection, perform eddy current or fluorescent penetrant inspections, instead of type II visible dye inspections.
(iii) If you cannot determine whether the affected part has previously been inspected by a type II visible dye method, clean all surfaces to be inspected and perform an eddy current or a fluorescent penetrant inspection, instead of a type II visible dye inspection.
Note 1 to paragraph (h)(4):
The FAA reminds operators of the airworthiness concern regarding type II visible dye inspections of critical parts discussed in FAA Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB) CE-18-26R1, dated October 30, 2018 (SAIB CE-18-26R1). SAIB CE-18-26R1 explains the risks associated with using type II visible dye inspection methods, including the prohibition in American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) E1417 on the use of type II visible dye penetrant prior to the use of type I fluorescent penetrant on the same surface. SAIB CE-18-26R1 also advises of the importance of pre- and post-inspection cleaning to ensure proper detection of cracks. You can find SAIB CE-18-26R1 at
drs.faa.gov.
Note 2 to paragraph (h)(4):
The material referenced in EASA AD 2026-0031 identifies a type II visible dye inspection as Method A (not allowed), or Method B; eddy current inspection as Method C; and fluorescent penetrant inspection as Method D.
Note 3 to paragraph (h)(4):
When entering compliance with the applicable paragraph of the AD into the helicopter maintenance records, documenting that a type II visible dye inspection was performed improves the accuracy of maintenance records.
(5) This AD does not adopt paragraphs (3) and (7) of EASA AD 2026-0031.
(6) This AD does not adopt the “Remarks” section of EASA AD 2026-0031.
(i) No Reporting or Returning of Parts

On November 17, 2026, the Department of Justice lodged a proposed Consent Decree Amendment with the United States District Court for the District of New Jersey in the lawsuit entitled
United States, et al.
v.
Morton Thiokol, Inc. et al.,
Civil Action No. 2:83-cv-4787.
The proposed Amendment modifies a consent decree with Morton Thiokol, Inc. that was entered in 1988 (Morton Consent Decree). The Morton Consent Decree required Morton Thiokol to perform a cleanup at the Goose Farm Superfund Site in Plumsted Township, New Jersey (Site) in accordance with a 1985 EPA record of decision. During post cleanup sampling, Morton Thiokol discovered further contamination in the Site's soils. In September 2025, EPA issued an amended record of decision addressing the remaining contamination. The proposed Amendment provides for the cleanup of this contamination.
As a result of Morton Thiokol having undergone a series of corporate transitions, Morton Thiokol no longer exists and Morton International LLC takes responsibility for Morton Thiokol's liabilities. Accordingly, the proposed Amendment also adds Morton International to the Morton Consent Decree and requires it to perform the additional soil cleanup.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notification of enforcement of regulation.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard will enforce a safety zone for the City of Richland Lighted Boat Parade Fireworks on December 5, 2026, to provide for the safety of life on navigable waters during a fireworks display. Our regulation for the fireworks display within the Northwest Coast Guard District designates safety zones and identifies approximate dates for these events. Specific date and times are identified in this notice. These regulations prohibit persons and vessels from entering or remaining in the safety zone unless authorized by the Captain of the Port Sector Columbia River or a Designated Representative.
DATES:
The regulations in
33 CFR 165.1315
will be enforced from 7 p.m. to 9:30 p.m. on December 5, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have questions about this notification of enforcement, call or email Lieutenant Commander Jesse Wallace, Waterways Management Division, Sector Columbia River, Coast Guard; 503-572-3524, email
SCRWWM@USCG.MIL
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Coast Guard will enforce a safety zone for the City of Richland Lighted Boat Parade Fireworks event found in line 42 of Table 1 to
Paragraph (a) of 33 CFR 165.1315
, on December 5, 2026 from 7 p.m. to 9:30 p.m. during the designated enforcement period, and within a 450-yard radius of the launch site located at 46°16′29″ N, 119°16′10″ W. This action is being taken to provide for the safety of life on navigable waterways during this event.
During the enforcement periods, as reflected in § 165.1315, persons and vessels are prohibited from entering or remaining in the safety zone unless authorized by the Captain of the Port Sector Columbia River or a Designated Representative. All vessel operators who desire to enter the safety zone must obtain permission from the Captain of the Port or Designated Representative by contacting either the on-scene patrol craft on VHF Ch 13 or Ch 16 or the Coast Guard Sector Columbia River Command Center via telephone at (833) 769-8724. In addition to this notification of enforcement in the
Federal Register
, the Coast Guard will provide notification of these enforcement periods via the Local Notice to Mariners and Broadcast Notice to Mariners.

AGENCY:
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) invites public comment on a proposed rule that would amend the brokered deposit regulations to implement section 901 of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act related to custodial deposits.
DATES:
Comments must be received no later than January 19, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments on the notice of proposed rulemaking, identified by RIN 3064-AG38 using any of the following methods:
FDIC Website:
https://www.fdic.gov/​federal-register-publications
.
Follow the instructions for submitting comments on the agency website.
Email:
Comments@fdic.gov
.
Include RIN 3064-AG38 on the subject line of the message.
Mail:
Jennifer M. Jones, Deputy Executive Secretary, Attention: Comments—RIN 3064-AG38, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, 550 17th Street NW, Washington, DC 20429.
Hand Delivery to FDIC:
Comments may be hand-delivered to the guard station at the rear of the 550 17th Street NW building (located on F Street NW) on business days between 7 a.m. and 5 p.m.
Public Inspection:
Comments received, including any personal information provided, may be posted without change to
https://www.fdic.gov/​federal-register-publications
.
Commenters should submit only information that the commenter wishes to make available publicly. The FDIC may review, redact, or refrain from posting all or any portion of any comment that it may deem to be inappropriate for publication, such as irrelevant or obscene material. The FDIC may post only a single representative example of identical or substantially identical comments, and in such cases will generally identify the number of identical or substantially identical comments represented by the posted example. All comments that have been redacted, as well as those that have not been posted, that contain comments on the merits of the proposed rule will be retained in the public comment file and will be considered as required under all applicable laws. All comments may be accessible under the Freedom of Information Act.
This proposal, all comments received, and a summary of not more than 100 words of the proposed rule pursuant to the Providing Accountability Through Transparency Act of 2023 are available at
https://www.fdic.gov/​federal-register-publications
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Legal Division: Chantal Hernandez, Counsel, (202) 898-7388,
chhernandez@fdic.gov
;
Ryan McCarthy, Counsel, (202) 898-7301,
rymccarthy@fdic.gov
;
Shane Bogusz, Senior Attorney, (571) 366-0212,
sbogusz@fdic.gov
.
Division of Risk Management Supervision: Brian Cox, Deputy Director, Capital Markets, Accounting, and Policy, (703) 254-0763,
brcox@fdic.gov
;
Justin Hagerty, Senior Examination Specialist, (319) 382-2760,
jhagerty@fdic.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background and Policy Objectives
The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act (the Housing Act) became effective on July 11, 2026.
[
1
]
Section 901 of the Housing Act amended section 29 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (FDI Act)
[
2
]
to: (1) provide a limited exception for an eligible institution to except a capped amount of custodial deposits from being considered brokered; and (2) restrict the interest rate that a covered insured depository institution (IDI) may pay on certain custodial deposits. Through this proposal, the FDIC would amend its brokered deposit regulations to conform with these provisions of the Housing Act.
II. Legal Framework
A. Section 29 of the FDI Act—Brokered Deposits and Interest Rate Restrictions
Section 29 of the FDI Act restricts IDIs from accepting deposits by or through a deposit broker if the institution is less than well capitalized for Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) purposes.
[
3
]
The FDIC may waive this restriction if the IDI is adequately capitalized; however, the restriction cannot be waived if the institution is undercapitalized.
[
4
]
A “deposit broker,” as defined by section 29 of the FDI Act, includes “any person engaged in the business of placing deposits, or facilitating the placement of deposits, of third parties with insured depository institutions or the business of placing deposits with insured depository institutions for the purpose of selling interests in those deposits to third parties,” subject to certain exceptions.
[
5
]
Section 29 of the FDI Act also imposes interest rate restrictions on IDIs that are less than well capitalized. In particular, IDIs that are less than well capitalized may not pay a rate of interest on brokered deposits accepted pursuant to a waiver, or on reciprocal deposits excluded by section 29 from being considered brokered deposits, that “significantly exceeds” (1) the rate paid on deposits of similar maturity in such institution's normal market area for deposits accepted in the institution's normal market area; or (2) the national rate paid on deposits of comparable maturity, as established by the FDIC, for deposits accepted outside the institution's normal market area.
[
6
]
The FDIC has implemented regulations governing the acceptance of brokered deposits and interest rate restrictions and related filing procedures in its regulations at
12 CFR 303.243
,
337.6
, and
337.7
.
B. Section 29(j)—Limited Exception for Custodial Deposits
The Housing Act added a limited exception for custodial deposits under section 29(j) of the FDI Act. Section 29(j) provides that custodial deposits of an
(
printed page 75235)
eligible institution shall not be considered to be brokered deposits to the extent that the total amount of such custodial deposits does not exceed 20 percent of the total liabilities of the eligible institution.
[
7
]
The exception is available only to an “eligible institution,” which is defined as an IDI that accepts custodial deposits, if the IDI has less than $10 billion in total assets as reported on its Consolidated Report of Condition and Income (Call Report) and (1) when most recently examined was assigned a composite rating of 1, 2, or 3 under the Uniform Financial Institutions Rating System and is well capitalized; or (2) has obtained a waiver pursuant to
12 U.S.C. 1831f(c)
.
[
8
]
The statute provides that a “custodial deposit” is:
[A] deposit that is not deposited at an insured depository institution in return for fees paid by the insured depository institution pursuant to an agreement with a third party and that would otherwise be considered to be obtained, directly or indirectly, by or through a deposit broker, if the deposit is deposited at 1 or more insured depository institutions, for the purpose of providing or maintaining deposit insurance for the benefit of a third party, by or through any of the following, each acting in a formal custodial or fiduciary capacity for the benefit of a third party:
(i) An insured depository institution serving as agent, trustee, or custodian.
(ii) A trust entity controlled by an insured depository institution serving as agent, trustee, or custodian.
(iii) A State-chartered trust company serving as agent, trustee, or custodian.
(iv) A plan administrator or investment advisor, acting in a formal custodial or fiduciary capacity for the benefit of a plan.
C. Section 29(k)—Restriction on Interest Paid on Certain Custodial Deposits
The Housing Act also added a restriction on the interest paid on certain custodial deposits under section 29(k) of the FDI Act. Specifically, section 29(k) prohibits a covered IDI
[
9
]
from paying a rate of interest on custodial deposits that are accepted while not well capitalized that, at the time the funds or custodial deposits are accepted, significantly exceeds the limit on interest rates.
[
10
]
The statute provides that the limit on the rate of interest shall not be greater than (1) the rate paid on deposits of similar maturity in the normal market area of the covered IDI for deposits accepted in the normal market area of the covered IDI; or (2) the national rate paid on deposits of comparable maturity, as established by the FDIC, for deposits accepted outside the normal market area of the covered IDI.
[
11
]
III. Overview of the Proposal
To implement the custodial deposit exception and interest rate restriction added in sections 29(j) and (k) of the FDI Act, the FDIC proposes to amend
12 CFR 303.243
,
337.6
, and
337.7
, as discussed below.
A. Limited Exception for Qualifying Custodial Deposits
Consistent with section 29(j)(1) of the FDI Act, as amended by the Housing Act, proposed § 337.6(f)(1) would provide that certain custodial deposits, known as “qualifying custodial deposits,” of an eligible institution will not be considered to be funds obtained, directly or indirectly, by or through a deposit broker to the extent that the total amount of such custodial deposits does not exceed 20 percent of the total liabilities of the eligible institution. As further explained below, the FDIC proposes to use the term “qualifying custodial deposit” to distinguish deposits eligible for this exception from deposits held in other custodial arrangements. Further, under the proposal, any amount of qualifying custodial deposits exceeding the 20 percent cap would be considered funds obtained, directly or indirectly, by or through a deposit broker, with respect to the eligible institution.
Question Regarding the Limited Exception for Qualifying Custodial Deposits
Question 1:
What additional clarification, if any, should be made to the proposal with respect to the determination of the amount of the 20 percent cap? What alternative determination should the FDIC consider regarding an amount of qualifying custodial deposits in excess of the 20 percent cap?
B. Definitions
Proposed § 337.6(f)(2) would define relevant terms for purposes of the new exception.
1. Qualifying Custodial Deposit
The FDIC proposes to use the term “qualifying custodial deposit” to describe deposits that meet the statutory and regulatory requirements for the new exception. The term would be defined consistent with the definition of “custodial deposit” in section 29(j)(2)(A). The FDIC believes that using this term would be helpful as a way to distinguish between those deposits that are eligible for the exception versus those that are held in other arrangements that may have “custodial” features but not otherwise satisfy the statutory criteria.
[
12
]
Under the proposed rule, a “qualifying custodial deposit” would mean a deposit that would otherwise be considered to be obtained, directly or indirectly, by or through a deposit broker,
[
13
]
which is placed:
At one or more IDIs for the purpose of providing or maintaining deposit insurance for the benefit of a third party who is the beneficial owner of the deposit;
Not in return for fees paid by the IDI pursuant to an agreement with a third party; and
By or through a qualifying entity acting in a formal custodial or fiduciary capacity for the benefit of a third party who is the beneficial owner of the deposit.
a. Relevant Third Parties Involved in Qualifying Custodial Deposit Arrangements
To clarify the relevant third parties referred to in the statutory definition, the proposed “qualifying custodial deposit” definition would differentiate, based on contextual use in the statute, between a third party involved in the deposit placement arrangement and the third-party beneficial owner of the deposited funds.
The FDIC would interpret the first reference to “third party” in the statutory language—“a deposit that is not deposited at an insured depository institution in return for fees paid by the insured depository institution pursuant to an agreement with a third party”—to mean any person involved in the deposit placement arrangement (other than the IDI receiving the deposits). This would include a deposit broker, third-party intermediary, subcustodian, or any other person or entity involved in placing, assisting in placing, or facilitating the placement of the
(
printed page 75236)
underlying beneficial owners' deposits at the receiving IDI, or maintaining an account at the receiving IDI to hold the deposits.
In contrast, the second and third usages of “third party” in the statutory language—“for the purpose of providing or maintaining deposit insurance for the benefit of a third party” and “by or through any of the following, each acting in a formal custodial or fiduciary capacity for the benefit of a third party”—would be interpreted to mean the beneficial owner of the underlying deposited funds. In particular, the “for the benefit of a third party” and “providing or maintaining deposit insurance” language support the reading that the third party is the underlying depositor whose funds are ultimately being placed at the receiving IDI and the party for which deposit insurance is being sought. Such beneficial owners of the deposited funds may not have a direct relationship with the receiving IDI or each intermediary involved in the deposit arrangement.
b. Deposits Not in Return for Fees Paid by an IDI
The statutory definition of “custodial deposit” explicitly excludes deposits that are deposited at an IDI in return for fees paid by the IDI pursuant to an agreement with a third party. Under the proposal, use of the phrase “deposited . . . in return for fees paid by the IDI” would be interpreted to refer to monetary compensation paid by the IDI to a third party for the placement, or the facilitation of the placement, of deposits.
The statutory provision refers to fees “paid” by the IDI. Based on the use of the term “paid,” the FDIC would interpret the provision as contemplating monetary compensation. Thus, under the proposal, the FDIC would not consider non-monetary compensation, such as non-cash benefits like discounted banking services, to be fees that are “paid” by the IDI.
Additionally, under the proposal, fees that are based, directly or indirectly, on the amount of deposits that the third party is placing or the number of deposit accounts that the third party is opening would be considered to be fees for the placement, or facilitation of the placement, of deposits. For example, an IDI paying a third party placement or referral fees, subscription or membership fees, or any other fee for the facilitation or the placement of deposits (calculated on a fixed or volume basis), would be an impermissible fee for purposes of the qualifying custodial deposits exception.
The proposal would not preclude third parties that place, or facilitate the placement of, deposits that qualify for the exception from receiving fees that are for a purpose other than the placement of deposits—for example, a fee for recordkeeping services. Such fees would be regarded as payments separate and apart from payment “in return for” the placement, or the facilitation of the placement, of deposits.
Additionally, interest paid by an IDI would not be considered to be fees paid in return for the placement, or the facilitation of the placement, of deposits. This includes interest payments in which a third party receives an ongoing portion of interest payments made to beneficial owners of the deposits. In other contexts, the FDIC has generally,
[
14
]
but not always,
[
15
]
distinguished fees and interest. In this case, the FDIC understands that Congress's intent was not to capture interest when using the term “fees.” The proposed interpretation is consistent with the statute and would not impact the FDIC's use of the terms “fees” and “interest” in other circumstances.
The FDIC particularly encourages comment on this provision of the proposal. The FDIC is interested in learning more about different compensation structures that exist in the market and any recommended alternative interpretations. The FDIC seeks to interpret this provision in a manner that is both principled and faithful to the plain meaning of the statute.
c. For the Purpose of Providing or Maintaining Deposit Insurance
Consistent with the statute, the proposed rule would require a qualifying custodial deposit to be “for the purpose of providing or maintaining deposit insurance” for the benefit of a third party who is the beneficial owner of the deposit. Under the proposed rule, the FDIC would consider the purpose to be providing or maintaining deposit insurance if the deposits placed (by or through a qualifying entity) are limited to an amount that does not exceed the Standard Maximum Deposit Insurance Amount (SMDIA) for each beneficial owner at each IDI.
[
16
]
The FDIC is proposing to interpret this provision to apply at a program level; the deposit placement program would qualify if the third party placing deposits keeps the amount at or below the SMDIA for each beneficial owner at each IDI where it places deposits. If a third party places a beneficial owner's funds in an IDI in amounts that exceed the SMDIA, the FDIC interprets such a program as being for a purpose other than providing or maintaining deposit insurance.
d. Notice Process
In order to provide transparency to IDIs regarding entities that qualify for the custodial deposit exception, the FDIC is proposing to establish a notice process through which eligible institutions (the IDIs receiving the custodial deposits), qualifying entities, or other third parties within the deposit placement arrangement would notify the FDIC that deposits being placed pursuant to a particular deposit placement arrangement are eligible for the custodial deposit exception.
The written notice would need to include:
The name of the notice filer;
A brief description of the deposit placement arrangement pursuant to which the deposits are being placed;
The name of the qualifying entity in the deposit placement arrangement and identification of the qualifying entity as an IDI, a trust entity controlled by an IDI, a State-chartered trust company, or a plan administrator or investment advisor;
A statement that the deposits placed as part of the deposit placement arrangement are limited to an amount that does not exceed the SMDIA at any IDI for any beneficial owner of the deposits; and
A description of all agreements associated with the deposit placement arrangement that contain provisions related to fees or other compensation paid by IDIs to third parties.
The description of the deposit placement arrangement would need to be sufficiently detailed so that the FDIC is able to determine whether deposits held by an IDI are part of the deposit placement arrangement described in the notice. The FDIC would generally defer to the notice filer's descriptions regarding the deposit placement arrangement, including the description of any associated fees or other compensation paid by the receiving IDIs. However, the FDIC retains discretion to confirm whether such compensation does not constitute a fee paid by the eligible institution to a third party in return for the placement of deposits.
(
printed page 75237)
The FDIC would publish a list of qualifying custodial deposit notice submissions, no later than 30 days after receiving the notice, similar to what the FDIC does for designated business exception notices,
[
17
]
so that IDIs may more easily determine whether deposits being placed by or through certain qualifying entities satisfy this element of the definition.
The FDIC would establish an electronic process for the submission of notices, similar to that used for designated business exceptions.
[
18
]
A notice would be effective immediately upon submission, and notice filers would receive immediate acknowledgement of receipt. The FDIC could, at its discretion, and at any time, including during the supervision and examination of an IDI, require the notice filer to provide additional information to substantiate the information provided in the notice. If the FDIC learns that the purpose of placing the deposits is not for the purpose of providing or maintaining deposit insurance, that an IDI is paying “fees” as described in the proposal, or that information provided in the notice was inaccurate, the FDIC could revoke the notice filing, resulting in the loss of eligibility for the exception. Before revoking a notice, the FDIC would provide notice to the notice filer with the opportunity to respond or remedy the notice.
The notice would need to be submitted on a one-time basis and certified annually. The notice filer would be required to update the notice to the extent the information previously submitted is no longer accurate.
2. Qualifying Entity
Section 29 of the FDI Act identifies certain entities “by or through” which the deposit must be deposited in order for the deposits to be considered custodial deposits eligible for the exception. In addition, such entities must be acting in a formal custodial or fiduciary capacity for the benefit of a third party. The FDIC proposes to use the term “qualifying entity” to describe these entities. Specifically, a “qualifying entity” would mean:
An IDI serving as agent, trustee, or custodian;
A trust entity controlled by an IDI serving as agent, trustee, or custodian;
A State-chartered trust company serving as agent, trustee, or custodian; or
A plan administrator or investment advisor, acting in a formal custodial or fiduciary capacity for the benefit of a plan.
Deposits placed through an arrangement that does not involve a “qualifying entity” would not meet the “qualifying custodial deposit” definition.
For purposes of the “qualifying custodial deposit” definition, the FDIC proposes to define the term “formal custodial or fiduciary capacity” to mean an arrangement that is evidenced by a contract or another writing, providing expressly that the entity placing, assisting in placing, or facilitating the placement of funds is acting in a custodial or fiduciary capacity for the benefit of a third party. This addition would clarify what it means to act in a “formal” custodial or fiduciary capacity.
3. Eligible Institution
The FDIC is proposing to define the term “eligible institution” consistent with the definition provided in section 29(j)(2)(B) of the FDI Act, with certain clarifications described below.
The proposed rule would provide that an “eligible institution” means an IDI that accepts qualifying custodial deposits, if the IDI reports less than $10 billion in total assets in any of the four preceding quarters, as reported on the Call Report and—
When most recently examined under section 10(d) of the FDI Act was assigned a CAMELS composite rating of 1, 2, or 3 under the Uniform Financial Institutions Rating System (or an equivalent rating under a comparable rating system) and is well capitalized; or
Has obtained a waiver pursuant to § 337.6(c).
Under the proposed rule, the FDIC would interpret the statutory requirement on supervisory ratings to be met by an IDI that has most recently received a CAMELS composite rating of 1, 2, or 3. This approach would be consistent with how the FDIC has interpreted the same language elsewhere in the FDI Act.
[
19
]
With respect to the total asset threshold, the FDIC proposes that an IDI that reports less than $10 billion in total assets for any of the four preceding quarters would qualify as an eligible institution. In other words, an institution that reports $10 billion or more in total assets for four consecutive quarters would no longer qualify as an eligible institution. This timing provision would aid IDIs in determining their eligibility for the exception, particularly those that are approaching the $10 billion limit. In the FDIC's supervisory experience, a four-quarter approach is appropriate as some smaller IDIs may experience short periods of asset growth that could temporarily place them at or above the $10 billion threshold, which could otherwise result in an unintended cliff effect.
[
20
]
For IDIs that no longer meet the “eligible institution” definition due to changes in CAMELS composite ratings or capital levels, the proposed rule would describe how an IDI could requalify as an “eligible institution,” similar to the process for an IDI to requalify as an “agent institution” under the reciprocal deposits exception.
[
21
]
4. Plan and Plan Administrator
Lastly, the FDIC is proposing to define the terms “plan” and “plan administrator” to have the same meanings given those terms in sections 29(j)(2)(C) and (D) of the FDI Act.

C. Interest Rate Restrictions for Qualifying Custodial Deposits
Section 29(k) of the FDI Act, as added by the Housing Act, imposes interest rate restrictions on qualifying custodial deposits that are accepted by covered IDIs that are less than well capitalized. The statutory interest rate restrictions established by the Housing Act are identical to the restrictions currently in place on the acceptance of brokered deposits by less than well capitalized institutions. Accordingly, the FDIC is proposing to extend the interest rate restrictions in
12 CFR 337.7(c)(2)
to qualifying custodial deposits that are accepted by a less than well capitalized institution. The FDIC is also proposing a conforming amendment to
12 CFR 337.7(g)(2)
, the provision addressing the acceptance of nonmaturity deposits by a less than well capitalized institution. Additionally, in order to more precisely align with the statutory text, the FDIC is proposing a technical change to refer explicitly to less than well capitalized institutions in these provisions.
To conform with the requirements of section 29(e) of the FDI Act, the proposed rule would also amend the FDIC's interest rate restrictions to clearly cover reciprocal deposits accepted by less than well capitalized institutions.
[
22
]
The FDIC notes that the 20 percent cap on the custodial deposits exception has no bearing on whether a deposit is subject to the interest rate restrictions in section 29(k) of the FDI Act and
12 CFR 337.7(c)(2)
. Qualifying custodial deposits at or below the 20 percent cap are not considered brokered but are still subject to the interest rate restrictions as qualifying custodial deposits if accepted by a less than well capitalized institution. Qualifying custodial deposits in excess of the 20 percent cap must be reported as brokered and are subject to the interest rate restrictions as brokered deposits if accepted by a less than well capitalized institution.

D. Designated Business Exception for Arrangements Involving Non-Discretionary Custodians
The FDIC has recognized a designated business exception
[
23
]
(DBE) for certain deposit placement arrangements involving an agent or nominee that acts in a non-discretionary custodial capacity.
[
24

Funds that are placed at IDIs in conformance with the DBE for non-discretionary custodians are excepted from treatment as brokered.
[
25
]
The FDIC is not proposing to alter the existing DBE for deposit placement arrangements involving non-discretionary custodians.
The DBE is meaningfully distinct from the exception for qualifying custodial deposits established by section 901 of the Housing Act.
[
26
]
In particular, the DBE is available only if the agent or nominee plays a limited role in the deposit placement arrangement. For example, in order to obtain the DBE, the agent or nominee may not exercise discretion concerning the IDI or institutions at which the funds are placed, nor may the agent or nominee negotiate the terms of the deposit account. By contrast, the statutory exception for custodial deposits does not contain these same express conditions.
The FDIC does not intend for the statutory custodial deposits exception to eliminate, narrow, or otherwise alter the
(
printed page 75239)
existing non-discretionary custodian exception. A deposit placement arrangement that satisfies the requirements of the non-discretionary custodian DBE may continue to qualify for that exception, without regard to the new statutory exception.
Treating the two exceptions as separate and preserving the existing non-discretionary custodian exception would avoid disturbing established deposit placement arrangements while also giving effect to the specific limitations Congress adopted for qualifying custodial deposits.

E. Call Report Updates
The Housing Act became effective in the third quarter of 2026. On September 30, 2026, the FFIEC issued Supplemental Instructions as part of the September 30, 2026, Call Report Instructions.
[
27
]
These instructions explain that institutions wishing to utilize the new exception for custodial deposits should “apply the newly defined terms and other provisions of Section 901 of the Housing Act to determine whether an institution and its custodial deposits are eligible for the statutory exception.”
[
28
]
The Supplemental Instructions clarify that, alternatively, institutions could report consistent with prior instructions and amend their reports, as necessary, following the FDIC's issuance of a final rule implementing the statutory exception.
In connection with this proposed rule, the FDIC recognizes that changes to the Call Report instructions may be necessary to ensure accurate and consistent reporting of brokered deposits in line with the new statutory exception for qualifying custodial deposits. The FDIC plans to work through the FFIEC to ensure the necessary changes are made. Additionally, as part of implementation, the FDIC is evaluating whether to add two reporting lines to Schedule RC-E in order to monitor institutions' use of the custodial deposits exception.
The two potential reporting lines would identify the total amount of qualifying custodial deposits (Total qualifying custodial deposits), as well as any additional qualifying custodial deposits that are nevertheless being reported as brokered because they exceed the 20 percent cap (Brokered qualifying custodial deposits). Additionally, it may be advisable to require reporting on custodial deposits only for institutions using the exception.
Any changes to reporting requirements applicable to the Call Reports, and their instructions, would be effectuated in coordination with the FFIEC in a separate Paperwork Reduction Act notice.

IV. Expected Effects
The proposed rule would amend the FDIC's regulations to implement the qualifying custodial deposit exception and related interest rate restrictions consistent with section 901 of the Housing Act, which became effective on July 11, 2026.
[
29
]
This section summarizes the analysis performed by the FDIC to estimate the economic impact of the proposed rule. For this purpose, the FDIC compares estimated economic outcomes under the proposed rule to outcomes under a baseline in which the proposed rule is not promulgated. Because this proposed rule would implement the statutory requirements of the Housing Act, which are in effect currently, the FDIC's analysis focuses on the associated economic effects of proposed provisions where the FDIC is exercising discretion to clarify and interpret the statute for implementation.
[
30
]
The impact of such provisions is discussed below.
A. Scope of Affected Entities
Under the proposed rule, an eligible institution would be permitted to rely on the qualifying custodial deposit exception.
[
31
]
An eligible institution would be defined as an IDI with $10 billion or less in total assets that has either (1) received a CAMELS composite rating of 1, 2, or 3 and is well capitalized, or (2) received a brokered deposit waiver from the FDIC. The FDIC estimates that there are approximately 4,031 IDIs that could meet the eligible institution definition under the proposed rule. As of the quarter ending June 30, 2026, the FDIC insured 4,247 IDIs, of which 4,085 report total assets of less than $10 billion.
[
32
]
Of those 4,085 IDIs, 4,030 are currently well capitalized with a CAMELS composite rating of 1, 2, or 3, and one additional IDI meets the definition of adequately capitalized, which the FDIC extrapolates to represent an IDI eligible for a brokered deposit waiver.
[
33
]
With respect to the 4,031 IDIs that could meet the eligible institution definition, the FDIC cannot accurately estimate, based on available information, how many of those IDIs
(
printed page 75240)
hold brokered deposits that would be reclassified as non-brokered under the qualifying custodial deposit exception. However, the FDIC estimates that 1,629 IDIs that could potentially meet the eligible institution definition currently report positive amounts of brokered non-reciprocal deposits,
[
34
]
which the FDIC views as indicating that as many as 1,629 IDIs may be immediately affected by the proposal, if the proposal were finalized today. The number of affected IDIs is likely to change in future periods, but the FDIC does not currently have the information necessary to estimate such changes.
In addition to affected IDIs, the FDIC anticipates the proposed rule may impact third parties that are involved in deposit placement arrangements and the third parties who are the beneficial owners of the deposits that would qualify for the qualifying custodial deposits exception. The FDIC does not currently have data to estimate the number of affected third parties.
B. Expected Benefits
If finalized, the proposed rule would make several amendments that clarify and interpret certain provisions within the Housing Act that would benefit affected IDIs and third parties.
The proposed rule would define “qualifying custodial deposit,” “qualifying entity,” “fees,” and “formal custodial or fiduciary capacity,” and clarify the relevant “third party” within eligible deposit arrangements. These definitions generally benefit IDIs that may potentially qualify for the exception because the proposed rule would provide additional clarity regarding the new exception, align the proposed rule with other existing brokered deposit regulatory provisions as appropriate, and reflect relevant business practices. The FDIC does not have information, at this time, to estimate whether, relative to the baseline, these aspects of the proposal will result in changes to the number of affected IDIs.
Under the proposed rule, the FDIC would also clarify the timing of the asset threshold for an eligible institution. Specifically, the proposed rule provides that an IDI that reports less than $10 billion in total assets for any of the four preceding quarters would satisfy the asset threshold applicable to an eligible institution. Relatedly, the proposal would establish that any IDI with reported total assets of $10 billion or above for four consecutive quarters would not meet the criteria to qualify as an eligible institution. This aspect of the proposal would generally benefit IDIs that may potentially qualify for the exception, as some smaller IDIs may experience short periods of asset growth that could temporarily place them at or above the $10 billion threshold, which could result in an unintended cliff effect.
The proposed rule could also affect FDIC deposit insurance assessments for some IDIs that would qualify as eligible institutions. Under the FDIC's assessment regulations, IDIs with a significant concentration of brokered deposits may pay higher quarterly assessments, depending on other factors.
[
35
]
To the extent that deposits currently considered brokered would be considered non-brokered under the proposed rule, an eligible institution's assessment may decrease. The FDIC does not have the information necessary to estimate which IDIs would realize this benefit. However, the FDIC believes such effects on assessment revenue are likely to be small in the aggregate.
Lastly, the proposed rule would require eligible institutions, qualifying entities, or other third parties within the deposit arrangement to submit a written notice to the FDIC in order for the deposits to be considered qualifying custodial deposits. The notice would be effective immediately upon filing. The FDIC would also publish a list of qualifying custodial deposit notice submissions. The notice provision would benefit all parties within the deposit placement arrangement by providing transparency regarding entities that meet the requirements of the qualifying custodial deposit exception.
C. Expected Costs
As noted, the FDIC is proposing to require eligible institutions, qualifying entities, or other third parties to submit a notice to the FDIC regarding the deposit arrangement in order for the deposits to qualify as qualifying custodial deposits. The FDIC anticipates that this aspect of the proposed rule would pose small compliance costs for entities that file the notices.
The FDIC estimates that eligible institutions, qualifying entities, and other third parties that submit a notice for deposits to qualify as qualifying custodial deposits would spend approximately four hours of labor time per initial submission and one hour per year to certify its qualifying custodial deposit arrangements. Using a wage rate of $112.12 per hour,
[
36
]
the FDIC estimates that a qualifying entity would incur approximately $450 in labor costs to submit a notice and $112 per year to certify its qualifying custodial deposit arrangements. These estimates do not capture all costs associated with producing and submitting a notice. The FDIC does not currently have information to estimate additional compliance costs. While such costs may be significant for some entities, the FDIC anticipates such costs to be small in the aggregate.
Nonetheless, some entities may not have all the required information in their possession and could incur costs in obtaining the information from other sources. The FDIC anticipates, however, that marginal compliance costs associated with the notice process would likely decline over time as some notice filers could utilize the published list of qualifying custodial deposit notice submissions to more efficiently prepare their notice submissions.
As previously discussed, the FDIC is evaluating whether to add, in coordination with the FFIEC, two potential line items to the Call Report related to the new exception. The FDIC anticipates that any costs associated with such changes will be de minimis as eligible institutions are likely to maintain and keep records supporting their reliance on the qualifying custodial deposits exception given the 20 percent cap.
D. Conclusion
Given the economic effects discussed in section IV.A through IV.C of this Supplemental Information, the FDIC expects that the benefits of the proposed rule would justify its costs. The FDIC invites comments on all aspects of the supporting information provided in the Expected Effects section. The FDIC is particularly interested in comments on any material economic effects that the agency has not identified.

With respect to the 2,857 small entities that could meet the eligible institution definition, the FDIC cannot accurately estimate, based on available information, how many of those small entities currently hold brokered deposits that would be reclassified as non-brokered under the qualifying custodial deposit exception. However, the FDIC estimates that 960 small entities currently report positive amounts of brokered non-reciprocal deposits,
[
44
]
which the FDIC views as indicating that as many as 960 small entities may be immediately affected by the proposal, if the proposal were finalized today. The number of affected small entities is likely to change in future periods, but the FDIC does not currently have the information necessary to estimate such changes.
Effects on Small Entities
Generally, the proposed rule would implement the statutory requirements of the Housing Act, which are in effect currently. However, there are certain provisions of the proposal where the FDIC is exercising discretion to clarify and interpret the statute for implementation. The impact of such provisions on small entities is discussed below.
The FDIC proposes to make several amendments that clarify and interpret certain provisions within the statute. These definitions generally benefit small entities that may qualify for the exception because they would clarify key aspects of the new exception, align the proposed rule with other existing brokered deposit regulatory provisions as appropriate, and reflect relevant business practices and participants associated with qualifying custodial deposits. Relative to the baseline, these clarifications and interpretations may marginally increase the number of affected small entities that would meet the eligible institution definition and rely on the qualifying custodial deposit exception; however, the FDIC does not have information, at this time, to estimate such changes.
The proposed rule could also affect FDIC deposit insurance assessments for some small entities that would qualify as eligible institutions. Under the FDIC's assessment regulations, IDIs with a significant concentration of brokered deposits may pay higher quarterly assessments, depending on other factors.
[
45
]
To the extent that deposits currently considered brokered would be considered non-brokered under the proposed rule, an eligible small entity's assessment may decrease. The FDIC does not have the information necessary to estimate which small entities would realize this benefit. However, the FDIC believes such effects on assessment revenue are likely to be small in the aggregate.
As noted previously, the proposal may pose some compliance costs for notice filers. The FDIC estimates that small entities that are eligible institutions and qualifying entities that submit a notice for deposits to qualify as qualifying custodial deposits would spend approximately four hours of labor time per initial submission and one hour per year to certify its qualifying custodial deposit arrangements. Using a wage rate of $112.12 per hour,
[
46
]
the FDIC estimates that these small entities would incur approximately $450 in labor costs to submit a notice and $112 per year to certify its qualifying custodial deposit arrangements. These estimates do not capture all costs associated with producing and submitting a notice. The FDIC does not currently have information to estimate additional compliance costs. While such costs may be significant for some small entities, the FDIC anticipates such costs to be small in the aggregate.
The FDIC anticipates any such effects are likely to be small for small entities that are notice filers.
For additional discussion of the expected effects of the proposal, please refer to Section IV of this notice, “Expected Effects.”
Other Rules
The FDIC is not aware of any duplicative, overlapping, or conflicting Federal rules.

Alternatives Considered
The FDIC considered not promulgating the rulemaking to implement the custodial deposit exception and interest rate restriction added in sections 29(j) and (k) of the FDI Act. However, the FDIC has determined that the proposed rule is necessary to fully effectuate the amendments to section 29 of the FDI Act made by section 901 of the Housing Act and provide clarity.
The FDIC welcomes comments on any aspect of the information presented in the Regulatory Flexibility Act section and requests comment on whether the proposed rule has a significant effect on a substantial number of small entities.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
FDA is announcing the availability of a document titled “Transfer of a Premarket Notification (510(k)) Clearance—Questions and Answers.” This guidance provides information on the most frequently asked questions regarding the transfer or sale of a 510(k) clearance from one 510(k) holder to another. An owner or operator of an establishment who is engaged in the manufacture, preparation, propagation, compounding, assembly, or processing of a device intended for human use is generally required to register the establishment and submit listing information for all devices in commercial distribution.
[
1
]
Under section
(
printed page 75335)
510(k) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) and its implementing regulations, any person required to register under section 510 (
21 U.S.C. 360
) and
21 CFR 807.20
must generally submit a premarket notification submission, or “510(k),” if the device is being introduced into commercial distribution for the first time, or the device is one that the person currently has in commercial distribution or is reintroducing into commercial distribution, but that is about to be significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use.
[
2
]
When a 510(k) clearance for a specific device is sold or transferred from one person to another, if the new 510(k) holder is engaged in any of the activities requiring listing,
21 CFR 807.25
requires the new 510(k) holder to list their device in FDA's electronic device registration and listing system.
[
3
]
When listing, if the device is not significantly changed or modified in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use,
[
4
]
the new 510(k) holder must enter the original FDA-assigned premarket submission number unless submitting a new 510(k), in which case the new 510(k) holder would supply the new FDA-assigned premarket submission number, in FDA's electronic device registration and listing system.
[
5
]
If the new 510(k) holder has significantly changed or modified the device in design, components, method of manufacture, or intended use, the new 510(k) holder must generally submit a new 510(k), and, when listing following clearance of the new 510(k), would enter the new FDA-assigned premarket submission number in FDA's electronic device registration and listing system.
[
6
]
The new 510(k) holder must, if not previously entered into an operation described in
21 CFR 807.20(a)
, register within 30 days after entering into such an operation and submit device listing information, including the FDA-assigned cleared 510(k) premarket notification submission number,
[
7
]
at that time.
[
8
]
When a 510(k) clearance for a specific device is sold or transferred from one person to another, the labeler must submit an update to the information required by
21 CFR 830.310
by using the Global Unique Device Identification Database (GUDID) if such information (for example, the name of the labeler) has changed.
[
9
]
If you fail to register, list, update GUDID information, or submit a marketing application when required, your device may be considered adulterated and/or misbranded.
[
10
]
A notice of availability of the draft guidance appeared in the
Federal Register
of June 5, 2025 (
90 FR 23937
). FDA considered comments received and revised the guidance as appropriate in response to the comments, including clarifying terminology and further explaining 510(k) holder requirements.
This guidance is being issued consistent with FDA's good guidance practices regulation (
21 CFR 10.115
). The guidance represents the current thinking of FDA on “Transfer of a Premarket Notification (510(k)) Clearance—Questions and Answers.” It does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on FDA or the public. You can use an alternative approach if it satisfies the requirements of the applicable statutes and regulations.

Environmental Protection Agency
40 CFR Part 180
[EPA-HQ-OPP-2025-1444; FRL-13577-01-OCSPP]
AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This regulation establishes a tolerance action for residues of metamitron (CASRN 41394-05-2) in or on the raw agricultural commodity (RAC) of beet, sugar, roots. Under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA), ADAMA Agan Ltd. c/o Makhteshim Agan of North America, Inc. (d/b/a ADAMA) submitted a petition to EPA requesting that EPA establish a maximum permissible level for residues of this pesticide in or on the identified commodity.
DATES:
This rule is effective on November 20, 2026. Objections and requests for hearings must be received on or before January 19, 2027 and must be filed in accordance with the instructions provided in
40 CFR part 178
(see also Unit I.C. of this document).
ADDRESSES:
The docket for this action, identified by docket identification (ID) number EPA-HQ-OPP-2025-1444, is available online at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Additional information about dockets generally, along with instructions for visiting the docket in person, is available at
https://www.epa.gov/​dockets
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Charles Smith, Pesticide Registration Division (7505T), Office of Pesticide Programs, Environmental Protection Agency, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20460-0001; telephone number: (202) 566-1030; email address:
RDFRNotices@epa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Executive Summary
A. Does this action apply to me?
You may be potentially affected by this action if you are an agricultural producer, food manufacturer, or pesticide manufacturer. The following list of North American Industrial Classification System (NAICS) codes is not intended to be exhaustive, but rather provides a guide to help readers determine whether this document might apply to them:
Crop production (NAICS code 111).
Animal production (NAICS code 112).
Food manufacturing (NAICS code 311).
Pesticide manufacturing (NAICS code 32532).
If you have any questions regarding the applicability of this action to a particular entity, consult the person listed under
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
.
B. What is EPA's authority for taking this action?
EPA is issuing this rulemaking under section 408 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA),
21 U.S.C. 346a
. FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(A)(i) allows EPA to establish a tolerance (the legal limit for a pesticide chemical residue in or on a food) only if EPA determines that the tolerance is “safe.” FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(A)(ii) defines “safe” to mean that “there is a reasonable certainty that no harm will result from aggregate exposure to the pesticide chemical residue, including all anticipated dietary exposures and all other exposures for which there is reliable information.” This includes exposure through drinking water and in residential settings but does not include occupational exposure. FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(C) requires EPA to give special consideration to exposure of infants and children to the pesticide chemical residue in establishing a tolerance and to “ensure that there is a reasonable certainty that no harm will result to infants and children from aggregate exposure to the pesticide chemical residue . . .”
C. How can I file an objection or hearing request?
Under FFDCA section 408(g),
21 U.S.C. 346a(g)
, any person may file an objection to any aspect of this regulation and may also request a hearing on those objections. If you fail to file an objection to the final rule within the time period specified in the final rule, you will have waived the right to raise any issues resolved in the final rule. You must file your objection or request a hearing on this regulation in accordance with the instructions provided in
40 CFR part 178
. To ensure proper receipt by EPA, you must identify the docket ID number EPA-HQ-OPP-2025-1444 in the subject line on the first page of your
(
printed page 75229)
submission. All objections and requests for a hearing must be in writing and must be received by the Hearing Clerk on or before January 19, 2027.
The EPA's Administrative Law Judges Division (ALJD), in which the Hearing Clerk is housed, urges parties to file and serve documents by electronic means only, notwithstanding any other particular requirements set forth in other procedural rules governing those proceedings.
See
“Order Urging Electronic Filing and Service,” dated December 3, 2025, which can be found at
https://www.epa.gov/​system/​files/​documents/​2025-12/​2025-12-03-order-urging-electronic-filing-and-service.pdf
.
Although the EPA's regulations require submission via U.S. Mail or hand delivery, the EPA intends to treat submissions filed via electronic means as properly filed submissions; therefore, the EPA believes the preference for submission via electronic means will not be prejudicial. When submitting documents to the ALJD electronically, a person should utilize the ALJD e-filing system at
https://yosemite.epa.gov/​oa/​eab/​eab-alj_​upload.nsf
.
In addition to filing an objection or hearing request with the Hearing Clerk as described in
40 CFR part 178
, please submit a copy of the filing (excluding any Confidential Business Information (CBI)) for inclusion in the public docket at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the online instructions for submitting comments. Do not submit electronically any information you consider to be CBI or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. If you wish to include CBI in your request, please follow the applicable instructions at
https://www.epa.gov/​dockets/​commenting-epa-dockets#rules
and clearly mark the information that you claim to be CBI. Information not marked confidential pursuant to
40 CFR part 2
may be disclosed publicly by EPA without prior notice.
II. Petitioned-For Tolerance
In the
Federal Register
of December 1, 2025 (
90 FR 55065
) (FRL-12474-09-OCSPP), EPA issued a document pursuant to FFDCA section 408(d)(3),
21 U.S.C. 346a(d)(3)
, announcing the filing of a pesticide petition (PP 5F9188) by ADAMA Agan Ltd. c/o Makhteshim Agan of North America, Inc. (d/b/a ADAMA), 8601 Six Forks Rd., Suite 300 Raleigh, NC 27615. The petition requested that
40 CFR 180.726
be amended by establishing tolerances for residues of the herbicide metamitron, including its metabolites and degradates, in or on the RAC beet, sugar, roots at 0.01 parts per million (ppm). That document referenced a summary of the petition that was prepared by the petitioner and included in the docket. There was one (1) non-substantive comment received on December 9, 2025, in response to the notice of filing.
III. Final Tolerance Action
A. Aggregate Risk Assessment and Determination of Safety
Consistent with FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(D), and the factors specified therein, EPA has reviewed the available scientific data and other relevant information in support of this action. EPA has sufficient data to assess the hazards of and to make a determination on aggregate exposure for metamitron including exposure resulting from the tolerances established by this action. EPA's assessment of exposures and risks associated with metamitron is summarized in this unit.
In an effort to streamline its publications in the
Federal Register
, EPA is not reprinting sections that repeat what has been previously published for tolerance rulemaking of the same pesticide chemical. Where scientific information concerning a particular chemical remains unchanged, the content of those sections would not vary between tolerance rulemaking and republishing the same sections is unnecessary. EPA considers referral back to those sections as sufficient to provide an explanation of the information EPA considered in making its safety determination for the new rulemaking.
EPA has previously published a tolerance rulemaking for metamitron in which EPA concluded, based on the available information, that there is a reasonable certainty that no harm would result from aggregate exposure to metamitron and established tolerances for residues of that chemical. EPA is incorporating previously published sections from this rulemaking as described further in this rulemaking, as they remain unchanged.
B. Toxicological Profile
EPA has evaluated the available toxicity data and considered its validity, completeness, and reliability as well as the relationship of the results of the studies to human risk. EPA has also considered available information concerning the variability of the sensitivities of major identifiable subgroups of consumers, including infants and children.
For a discussion of the toxicological profile of metamitron, see Unit III. A. of the March 11, 2025, final rulemaking (
90 FR 11670
) (FRL-12591-01).
C. Toxicological Points of Departure/Levels of Concern
Once a pesticide's toxicological profile is determined, EPA identifies toxicological points of departure (POD) and levels of concern to use in evaluating the risk posed by human exposure to the pesticide. For hazards that have a threshold below which there is no appreciable risk, the toxicological POD is used as the basis for derivation of reference values for risk assessment. PODs are developed based on a careful analysis of the doses in each toxicological study to determine the dose at which no adverse effects are observed (the NOAEL) and the lowest dose at which adverse effects of concern are identified (the LOAEL). Uncertainty/safety factors are used in conjunction with the POD to calculate a safe exposure level—generally referred to as a population-adjusted dose (PAD) or a reference dose (RfD)—and a safe margin of exposure (MOE). For non-threshold risks, the Agency assumes that any amount of exposure will lead to some degree of risk. Thus, the Agency estimates risk in terms of the probability of an occurrence of the adverse effect expected in a lifetime. For more information on the general principles EPA uses in risk characterization and a complete description of the risk assessment process, see
https://www.epa.gov/​pesticide-science-and-assessing-pesticide-risks/​human-health-risk-pesticides
.
For a discussion of the Toxicological Points of Departure/Levels of Concern for metamitron used for human risk assessment, please reference Unit IV. A. of the July 10, 2024, final rulemaking (
89 FR 56669
) (FRL-12054-01-OCSPP).
D. Exposure Assessment
Some of the exposure assessment remains the same although updates have occurred to incorporate updated EDWCs (232 ppb and 127 ppb for the acute and chronic assessments, respectively). For a description of the rest of the EPA approach to and assumptions for the exposure assessment, please reference Unit IV. B. of the July 10, 2024, final rulemaking (
89 FR 56669
) (FRL-12054-01).
Acute and chronic dietary (food and drinking water) exposure and risk assessment was conducted using the Dietary Exposure Evaluation Model software with the Food Commodity Intake Database (DEEM-FCID) Version 4.02, which incorporates 2005-2010 consumption data from the USDA's NHANES/WWEIA. The assessments used combined level of quantification (LOQ) field trial residues from parent
(
printed page 75230)
compound metamitron and metabolite desamino-metamitron for all crops and assumed that 100% of the crops were treated with metamitron. The unrefined acute dietary risk estimates are below the Agency's level of concern (<100% aPAD) at the 95th exposure percentile for the general U.S. population (4.1% of the aPAD) and for all infants (<1-year-old) (14% of the aPAD), the most highly exposed population subgroup. Chronic dietary risks are below the Agency's level of concern of 100% of the cPAD (2.9% for the general U.S. population); they are 11% of the cPAD for all infants (<1 year old), the population group with the highest estimated exposure.
E. Safety Factor for Infants and Children
1.
In general.
FFDCA section 408(b)(2)(C) provides that EPA shall apply an additional tenfold (10X) margin of safety for infants and children in the case of threshold effects to account for prenatal and postnatal toxicity and the completeness of the database on toxicity and exposure unless EPA determines based on reliable data that a different margin of safety will be safe for infants and children. This additional margin of safety is commonly referred to as the Food Quality Protection Act (FQPA) Safety Factor (SF). In applying this provision, EPA either retains the default value of 10X, or uses a different additional safety factor when reliable data available to EPA support the choice of a different factor.
3.
Conclusion.
EPA continues to conclude that there are reliable data to support the reduction of the Food Quality Protection Act (FQPA) safety factor (SF) from 10X to 1X for all risk scenarios. See Unit IV.C. of the July 10, 2024 final rulemaking (
89 FR 56669
) (FRL-12054-01) for a discussion of the Agency's rationale for that determination.
F. Aggregate Risk and Determination of Safety
EPA continues to conclude that there is a reasonable certainty that no harm will result to the general population, or to infants and children, from aggregate exposure to metamitron residues. See Unit IV.D. of the July 10, 2024, final rulemaking (
89 FR 56669
) (FRL-12054-01) for the Agency's full explanation of this conclusion.
IV. Other Considerations
A. Analytical Enforcement Methodology
For a discussion of the available analytical enforcement method for various crops, see Unit V.A. of the July 10, 2024, final rulemaking (
89 FR 56669
) (FRL-12054-01).
B. International Residue Limits
In making its tolerance decisions, EPA seeks to harmonize U.S. tolerances with international standards whenever possible, consistent with U.S. food safety standards and agricultural practices. EPA considers the international maximum residue limits (MRLs) established by the Codex Alimentarius Commission (Codex), as required by FFDCA section 408(b)(4). The Codex is a joint United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization/World Health Organization food standards program, and it is recognized as an international food safety standards-setting organization in trade agreements to which the United States is a party. EPA may establish a tolerance that is different from a Codex MRL; however, FFDCA section 408(b)(4) requires that EPA explain the reasons for departing from the Codex level.
The Codex has not established an MRL for metamitron on beet, sugar, roots, and therefore, harmonization is not an issue at this time.
V. Conclusion
Therefore, a tolerance is established for residues of metamitron, (4-amino-3-methyl-6-phenyl-1,2,4-triazin-5(4 H)-one), in or on the RAC of beet, sugar, roots at 0.01 ppm.
VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews
Additional information about these statutes and Executive Orders can be found at
https://www.epa.gov/​laws-regulations/​and-executive-orders
.
A.
Executive Order 12866
: Regulatory Planning and Review
This action is exempt from review under
Executive Order 12866
(
58 FR 51735
, October 4, 1993), because it establishes or modifies a pesticide tolerance or a tolerance exemption under FFDCA section 408 in response to a petition submitted to the Agency. The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has exempted these types of actions from review under
Executive Order 12866
.
B.
Executive Order 14192
: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation
Executive Order 14192
(
90 FR 9065
, February 6, 2025) does not apply because actions that establish a tolerance under FFDCA section 408 are exempted from review under
Executive Order 12866
.
C. Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA)
This action does not impose an information collection burden under the PRA
44 U.S.C. 3501

Department of Justice
On November 17, 2026, the Department of Justice lodged a proposed Consent Decree and Judgment (Consent Decree) with the United States District Court for the Eastern District of New York in the lawsuit entitled
United States
v.
County of Nassau, Nassau County Department of Parks, Recreation and Museums, and Nassau County Department of Public Works,
Civil Action No. 2:26-cv-07400.
The United States filed this lawsuit under the Safe Drinking Water Act,
42 U.S.C. 300f
et. seq.
(“SDWA”). The complaint seeks civil penalties and injunctive relief for ongoing and past operation of large capacity cesspools (“LCC”) at 14 Nassau County facilities in violation of the SDWA and regulations promulgated thereunder,
40 CFR 144.80 to 144.89
. The relevant regulations required the closure of all LCCs nationwide as of April 5, 2005. Large-capacity cesspools pose a serious risk to the public because they may contaminate underground sources of drinking water.
Defendants collectively own, maintain, and operate LCCs that service restrooms, visitor centers, and recreational/cultural centers located in Nassau County facilities. The Consent Decree requires the Defendants to close the Prohibited LCCs under an aggressive 2-year schedule. The Consent Decree also requires Defendants to: (1) inspect all County facilities for any remaining LCCs and motor vehicle waste disposal wells (“MVWDWs”); (2) submit an inventory of any such LCCs or MVWDWs identified to EPA by December 1, 2027; and (3) work with EPA to ensure the closure of any such wells. “Closure” for purposes of the Consent Decree means permanent closing of a facility upon submission of a Final Closure Report after following the procedures set forth in the memorandum entitled “EPA Region 2 Underground Injection Control (UIC) Program Instructions for Class V Remediation/Closure Plans.” Septic systems will replace the LCCs.
The Consent Decree also requires Defendants to pay a $100,000 civil penalty.
The publication of this notice opens a period for public comment on the Consent Decree. Comments should be addressed to the Assistant Attorney General, Environment and Natural Resources Division, and should refer to
United States
v.
County of Nassau, et al.,
D.J. Ref. No. 90-5-1-1-13185. All comments must be submitted no later than thirty (30) days after the publication date of this notice. Comments may be submitted either by email or by mail:

Assistant Attorney General, U.S. DOJ-ENRD, P.O. Box 7611, Washington, DC 20044-7611.
Any comments submitted in writing may be filed by the United States in whole or in part on the public court docket without notice to the commenter.
During the public comment period, the Consent Decree may be examined and downloaded at this Justice Department website:
https://www.justice.gov/​enrd/​consent-decrees
