[Release No. 34-106921; File No. SR-ICC-2026-012]
November 17, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934,
15 U.S.C. 78s(b)(1)
and Rule 19b-4, 17 CFR
(
printed page 75410)
240.19b-4, notice is hereby given that on November 5, 2026, ICE Clear Credit LLC (“ICC” or “ICE Clear Credit”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II and III below, which Items have been prepared primarily by ICC. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Clearing Agency's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The principal purpose of the proposed rule change is to make revisions to the ICC Credit Default Swap (“CDS”) Clearing Rules
[
1
]
(the “Rules”), End-of-Day Price Discovery Policies and Procedures (the “EOD Policy”), ICC Default Auction Procedures—Initial Default Auctions (the “Initial Auction Procedures”), and ICC Secondary Auction Procedures (the “Secondary Auction Procedures”) for the CDS Clearing Service to modify the terms applicable to the Associate Clearing Participant (“ACP”) category of Clearing Participant (“CP”) and to make minor clean-up changes.
II. Clearing Agency's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, ICC included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change, security-based swap submission, or advance notice and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change, security-based swap submission, or advance notice. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. ICC has prepared summaries, set forth in sections (A), (B), and (C) below, of the most significant aspects of these statements.
(A) Clearing Agency's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
(a) Purpose
The purpose of the proposed changes is to amend certain provisions of the Rules, EOD Policy, Initial Auction Procedures, and Secondary Auction Procedures to modify the terms applicable to the ACP category of CP and make minor clean-up changes. ICC has two categories of CPs, standard CPs (referred to herein as “Full Participants”) and ACPs which are subject to the terms and conditions contained in Rule 212. The terms and conditions applicable to ACPs are designed to facilitate participation by institutions that may not have the global operational or other resources to support price submissions near the end of North American (“NA”) trading hours. In general, Full Participants and ACPs have the same rights, responsibilities, and obligations, with certain exceptions for ACPs currently set out in Rule 212 and the EOD Policy. In particular, ICC maintains dedicated London end-of-day price submission windows for which ACPs are required to make price submissions for instruments primarily traded in NA trading hours (“NA Instruments”), rather than at the end of the New York trading day.
[
2
]
ICC refers to these dedicated London windows as the “NA Instrument EU Submission Windows”, which are designed to facilitate participation by institutions that may not have the global operational or other resources to submit prices near the end of NA trading hours (as is required for Full Participants).
ICC proposes amendments to facilitate participation in the ACP category. ICC established the ACP category in 2022 to broaden participation in ICC's CDS Clearing Service by firms that may not have the global operational or other resources to meet all of the obligations applicable to Full Participants. Although the ACP category was intended to facilitate participation and expand access to clearing, no firms have joined the ACP category since its establishment. Based on ICC's experience with the existing ACP category, ICC believes that additional modifications may facilitate ACP participation by amending requirements that may continue to present obstacles to participation for certain firms. ICC therefore proposes to amend the ACP category to be more accessible to firms while preserving ICC's risk management objectives. Accordingly, ICC proposes to amend the ACP category to, among other things, revise ACP price submission obligations and default auction bidding requirements, while preserving ICC's ability to manage the risk presented by ACPs as further described below. ACPs would largely have the same rights and obligations as Full Participants, with certain exceptions further discussed below.
The proposed changes are designed to make the ACP category of CP more accessible and encourage participation, consistent with the objectives underlying the establishment of the category.
[
3
]
Such changes expand access to ICC's CDS Clearing Service and promote the broader use of central clearing by expanding access to ICC's clearing services to firms that may not otherwise satisfy all requirements applicable to Full Participants, thereby promoting increased clearing activity and applying ICC's risk management framework to a broader range of market activity. ICC proposes to make such changes effective following Commission approval of the proposed rule change. The proposed rule change is described in detail as follows.
CDS Rules
ICC proposes to amend Rule 212 (Associate Clearing Participants), which sets out the terms and conditions applicable to the ACP category, to revise certain terms and conditions applicable to ACPs. Rule 212(b) continues to permit ICC to establish additional or different price submission requirements for ACPs as compared to Full Participants. Under amended Rule 212(b)(i) and (ii), ACPs shall not be required to make end-of-day price submissions with respect to cleared contracts. ACPs are permitted to make end-of-day price submissions on a voluntary basis, and any such voluntary ACP end-of-day price submissions shall be included in the end-of-day price discovery process and may result in firm trade requirements in connection with such submissions on the same basis as Full Participants. In connection with this change, ICC proposes to delete the existing provisions in Rule 212(b) establishing the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows, under which ACPs were required to make price submissions for NA Instruments at the end of the London trading day (“NA Instrument EU EOD Submissions”) and were relieved of NA end-of-day submissions for NA Instruments. ICC proposes additional changes in Rule 212(b) to remove existing provisions related to firm trade requirements and end-of-day price submissions for ACPs. ICC also proposes to delete Rule 212(c) allowing ICC to establish different daily deadlines for the submission of trades by ACPs as compared to Full Participants.
[
4
]
(
printed page 75411)
In addition, ICC proposes to revise subsection (c) (previously subsection (d)) of Rule 212. Currently, ICC may establish different or supplemental margin requirements or related parameters applicable to ACPs. ICC proposes to eliminate the ability to establish different or supplemental margin requirements. However, ICC's ability to establish different or supplemental parameters applicable to ACPs as compared to Full Participants would remain.
ICC proposes to add new subsection (d) to Rule 212 that allows ICC to establish General Guaranty Fund (“Guaranty Fund”) contribution requirements for ACPs that differ from those applicable to Full Participants, including (i) a Guaranty Fund contribution equal to 125% of the Guaranty Fund contribution that would be required with respect to the same cleared positions if held by a Full Participant, and (ii) a minimum Guaranty Fund contribution of $25 million (“Required Contribution”).
[
5
]
ICC proposes to update Schedule 401 (Eligible Collateral & Thresholds) to remove the “$20 MM” figure from the footnotes to the Non-Client US Dollar Denominated and Non-Client Euro Denominated product requirement tables. As amended, each footnote provides that the requirements are subject to the Guaranty Fund minimum required contribution being 100% in US cash. Such change is intended for clarity as ACPs and Full Participants would be subject to different minimum Required Contributions to the Guaranty Fund under the proposed changes.
EOD Policy
ICC proposes to make related changes to the EOD Policy, which describes ICC's end-of-day price discovery process that provides reliable, market-driven prices. The proposed changes to the EOD Policy are consistent with the amended price submission terms for ACPs in the Rules. Specifically, in Section 1.1 ICC proposes to remove the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows from the five sets of submission windows, and change the number of submission windows from “five” to “four” given the removal of the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows. ICC would also remove the statement that the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows were intended primarily to support ACPs.
Additionally, ICC proposes to update Section 2.2. ICC proposes to provide that, in accordance with the Rules, (i) ICC does not require ACPs to make end-of-day submissions and (ii) any end-of-day submissions voluntarily made by an ACP shall be included in the end-of-day price discovery process and may result in firm trade requirements in connection with such submissions on the same basis as Full Participants. In connection with this change, ICC proposes to delete the provision requiring ACPs to provide submissions for the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows and proposes to delete the provision permitting Full Participants to provide voluntary submissions for the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows. ICC proposes corresponding deletions addressing submissions for Indices, single names, and index options.
ICC similarly proposes changes to Section 2.4. Currently, for the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows, ICC would designate firm trades only between ACPs, and voluntary submissions by Full Participants for the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows would not be subject to firm trades. ICC proposes to remove such provision, which is no longer applicable given the amended price submission requirements set out in amended Rule 212. Furthermore, ICC proposes to delete the statement outlining that firm trades originating from the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows are not eligible for reversing transactions.
In Section 2.5, ICC also proposes to delete reference to the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows. ICC would remove provisions indicating that prices established in the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows are not published externally, as such provisions are no longer applicable due to the removal of the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows.
ICC proposes conforming changes to Table 10 in the appendix in Section 4 to remove the reference to the NA Instrument EU Submission Window, as such reference is no longer applicable due to the removal of the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows.
ICC proposes certain clean-up revisions throughout the EOD Policy. ICC proposes to remove references to ICE Clear Europe Limited (“ICEU”), which previously provided CDS clearing services. Given the cessation of CDS clearing services at ICEU, ICC proposes to remove any references to ICEU's CDS clearing services throughout the document.
[
6
]
ICC further proposes minor revisions to reflect an updated entity name of a third-party pricing service and related references to such third party throughout the document. These are non-substantive changes that update the policy to reflect current practices and keep the policy up to date.
Initial Auction Procedures
ICC further proposes to make related changes to the Initial Auction Procedures. In the event of a default of a CP, the Initial Auction Procedures are designed to facilitate liquidation of the defaulter's portfolio through an auction. Currently, the Initial Auction Procedures do not distinguish between Full Participants and ACPs, such that ACPs have the same obligations and bidding requirements as Full Participants under the Initial Auction Procedures. For example, each CP (that is not a defaulting CP) is required to bid in every auction and for every Lot
[
7
]
in an auction for a minimum notional amount of contracts in such Lot (“Minimum Bid Requirement”).
ICC proposes to amend paragraph 2.2, which addresses the determination of the Minimum Bid Requirement. Currently, the sum total of the CPs' Minimum Bid Requirements may be set to an amount greater than 100% (but no greater than 150%) of the notional amount of the contracts in the relevant Lot.
[
8
]
ICC proposes to amend this provision to specify that it applies to Full Participants and to add “Target Full Participant Aggregate Minimum Bid Requirement” as a new defined term. ICC proposes language to account for ACPs to specify that the sum of CP Minimum Bid Requirements across all CPs (including both Full Participants and ACPs) is computed as the Target Full Participant Aggregate Minimum Bid Requirement multiplied by the reciprocal of the sum of Full Participant pro-rata portions. The proposed changes address the Minimum Bid Requirement in the case of an ACP that voluntarily determines to bid in an auction.
ICC proposes to add paragraph 2.13 to further address the participation of ACPs in auctions under the Initial
(
printed page 75412)
Auction Procedures. Under new paragraph 2.13, participation in an auction by an ACP is voluntary. Under the proposed changes, an ACP that chooses not to bid in an auction for any Lot shall be treated as a Subordinate Bidder
[
9
]
and have its Guaranty Fund contribution and Assessment Contribution
[
10
]
in respect of that Lot subordinated (
i.e.,
“juniorized”) in accordance with the order of priority (“Default Auction Priority”) set out in paragraph 3.3. ICC proposes to clarify that an ACP that elects to submit a bid in an auction shall be treated as an auction participant with respect to such auction, with its Minimum Bid Requirement determined pursuant to amended paragraph 2.2. These changes are intended to incentivize ACPs to bid, as non-bidding ACPs' Guaranty Fund and Assessment Contributions would be subordinated.
ICC proposes corresponding amendments to the Default Auction Priority in paragraph 3.3. In general, Guaranty Fund and Assessment Contributions from CPs are subject to “juniorization” and will be applied using a defined auction priority based on the competitiveness of their bids. The changes reflect that ACPs that choose not to bid in an auction for any Lot will be treated as Subordinate Bidders by amending the definitions of “Subordinate Assessment Contribution” and “Subordinate Guaranty Fund Contribution”. As a result, the ACP's Guaranty Fund contribution and Assessment Contribution for that Lot would be treated as subordinated in the order of priority. Such design continues to provide participants with a strong incentive to bid competitively in the auction, with the goal of reaching an efficient auction clearing price that permits ICC to close out the defaulter's portfolio and return ICC to a matched book.
Secondary Auction Procedures
ICC further proposes to make related changes to the Secondary Auction Procedures. If the auctions under the Initial Auction Procedures are not fully successful in closing out the defaulting CP's portfolio, ICC will proceed to use certain secondary default management actions with respect to the remaining portfolio, including conducting a secondary auction with respect to the defaulter's remaining portfolio. Secondary auctions are conducted by ICC to auction one or more Lots representing the remaining contracts of a defaulting CP. Currently, the Secondary Auction Procedures do not distinguish between Full Participants and ACPs, such that ACPs have the same obligations and bidding requirements as Full Participants under the Secondary Auction Procedures.
ICC proposes to amend paragraph 2.2, which similarly addresses the determination of the Minimum Bid Requirement. Currently, the sum total of the CPs' Minimum Bid Requirements may be set to an amount greater than 100% (but no greater than 150%) of the contracts in the relevant Lot.
[
11
]
ICC proposes to amend this provision to specify that it applies to Full Participants and to add “Target Full Participant Aggregate Minimum Bid Requirement” as a new defined term. ICC proposes language to account for ACPs to specify that the sum of CP Minimum Bid Requirements across all CPs (including both Full Participants and ACPs) is computed as the Target Full Participant Aggregate Minimum Bid Requirement multiplied by the reciprocal of the sum of Full Participant pro-rata portions. The proposed changes address the Minimum Bid Requirement in the case of an ACP that voluntarily determines to bid in a secondary auction.
ICC proposes to add paragraph 2.13 to further address the participation of ACPs in secondary auctions under the Secondary Auction Procedures. Under new paragraph 2.13, participation in a secondary auction by an ACP is voluntary. Under the proposed changes, an ACP that chooses not to bid in a secondary auction for any Lot shall be treated as a Subordinate Bidder
[
12
]
and have its Guaranty Fund contribution and Assessment Contribution
[
13
]
in respect of that Lot subordinated (
i.e.,
“juniorized”) in accordance with the order of priority (“Secondary Auction Priority”) set out in paragraph 3.3. ICC proposes to clarify that an ACP that elects to submit a bid in a secondary auction shall be treated as an auction participant with respect to such secondary auction, with its Minimum Bid Requirement determined pursuant to amended paragraph 2.2. These changes are intended to incentivize ACPs to bid, as non-bidding ACPs' Guaranty Fund and Assessment Contributions would be subordinated.
ICC proposes corresponding amendments to the Secondary Auction Priority in paragraph 3.3. In general, Guaranty Fund and Assessment Contributions from CPs are subject to “juniorization” and will be applied using a defined secondary auction priority based on the competitiveness of their bids. The changes reflect that ACPs that choose not to bid in an auction for any Lot will be treated as Subordinate Bidders by amending the definitions of “Subordinate Assessment Contribution” and “Subordinate Guaranty Fund Contribution”. As described above, the ACP's Guaranty Fund contribution and Assessment Contribution for that Lot would be treated as subordinated in the order of priority. Such design continues to provide participants with a strong incentive to bid competitively in the secondary auction, with the goal of reaching an efficient secondary auction clearing price that permits ICC to close out the defaulter's portfolio and return ICC to a matched book.
(b) Statutory Basis
ICC believes that the proposed rule changes are consistent with the requirements of Section 17A of the Act
[
14
]
and the regulations thereunder applicable to it, including the applicable standards under Rule 17ad-22.
[
15
]
In particular, Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act
[
16
]
requires that the rule change be consistent with the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and derivative agreements, contracts and transactions cleared by ICC, the safeguarding of securities and funds in the custody or control of ICC or for which it is responsible, and the protection of investors and the public interest.
As described above, the amendments revise certain provisions of the Rules, EOD Policy, Initial Auction Procedures, and Secondary Auction Procedures to modify the terms applicable to the ACP category of CP and make additional minor clean-up changes.
As discussed above, although the ACP category was intended to facilitate participation and expand access to clearing, no firms have joined the ACP category since its establishment. Based on ICC's experience with the existing ACP category, ICC believes that additional modifications may facilitate participation by amending requirements that may present obstacles to
(
printed page 75413)
participation for certain firms, while continuing to support ICC's risk management objectives. The proposed changes to the Rules and EOD Policy include removing the NA Instrument EU Submission Windows and making end-of-day price submissions by ACPs voluntary. The changes to the Initial Auction Procedures and Secondary Auction Procedures make auction bidding by ACPs voluntary, while subordinating (or “juniorizing”) the Guaranty Fund and Assessment Contributions of an ACP that elects not to bid in order to incentivize auction participation. Additional changes to the Rules allow ICC to impose heightened financial resource requirements on ACPs, including a Guaranty Fund contribution equal to 125% of the Guaranty Fund contribution that would be required with respect to the same cleared positions if held by a Full Participant, and a minimum Required Contribution to the Guaranty Fund of $25 million. The proposed changes are intended to expand access to clearing by facilitating entities becoming clearing participants through such amended requirements, while preserving ICC's ability to manage the risk presented by ACPs. ICC believes that broadening access to central clearing of CDS, in particular by firms that may not otherwise satisfy all requirements applicable to Full Participants, promotes increased clearing activity and applies ICC's risk management framework to a broader range of market activity, which supports the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of CDS and the protection of investors and the public interest. Moreover, ICC's ability to impose heightened financial requirements provides ICC with an additional tool to manage the risks associated with ACP participation. Additional changes include minor clean-up revisions in the EOD Policy to reflect current practices and keep the policy up to date. As a result, in ICC's view, the amendments are consistent with the prompt and accurate clearance and settlement of securities transactions and derivative agreements, contracts and transactions, the safeguarding of securities and funds in the custody or control of the clearing agency or for which it is responsible, and the protection of the investors and the public interest, within the meaning of Section 17A(b)(3)(F) of the Act.
[
17
]
Moreover, the amendments are consistent with relevant provisions of Rule 17ad-22. In particular, Rule 17ad-22(e)(1)
[
18
]
requires each covered clearing agency to establish, implement, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to provide for a well-founded, clear, transparent, and enforceable legal basis for each aspect of its activities in all relevant jurisdictions. As described above, the amendments clearly and transparently describe the terms and conditions applicable to the ACP category of CP. Additionally, these changes enhance ICC's ability to maintain Rules and policies and procedures that clearly and transparently describe the obligations applicable to ACPs. The clean-up changes to the EOD Policy further support a clear and transparent legal basis by ensuring that ICC's policies and procedures are clear and up-to-date. Therefore, these changes are consistent with the requirements of Rule 17ad-22(e)(1).
[
19
]
Rule 17ad-22(e)(4)(ii)
[
20
]
requires each covered clearing agency to establish, implement, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to effectively identify, measure, monitor, and manage its credit exposures to participants and those arising from its payment, clearing, and settlement processes, including by maintaining additional financial resources at the minimum to enable it to cover a wide range of foreseeable stress scenarios that include, but are not limited to, the default of the two participant families that would potentially cause the largest aggregate credit exposure for ICC in extreme but plausible market conditions. As discussed above, proposed changes to the Rules allow ICC to impose heightened financial resource requirements on ACPs, including a Guaranty Fund contribution equal to 125% of the Guaranty Fund contribution that would be required with respect to the same cleared positions if held by a Full Participant, and a minimum Required Contribution to the Guaranty Fund of $25 million. The ability to impose such heightened financial requirements provides ICC with an additional tool to manage the risks associated with ACP participation, which would support ICC's ability to maintain additional financial resources sufficient to cover a wide range of foreseeable stress scenarios. Additionally, ACPs may be further incentivized to participate in auctions, as any subordination of their Guaranty Fund contributions under the amended provisions may apply to a larger contribution amount. ICC would continue to ensure that it has the ability to manage risks, maintain appropriate financial resources, and withstand the pressures of defaults, consistent with the requirements of Rule 17ad-22(e)(4)(ii).
[
21
]
Rule 17ad-22(e)(13)
[
22
]
requires each covered clearing agency to establish, implement, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure it has the authority and operational capacity to take timely action to contain losses and liquidity demands and continue to meet its obligations. Under the proposed changes, ICC will continue to ensure that it can take timely action to contain losses and liquidity demands and continue meeting its obligations in the event of a default. The amended Initial Auction Procedures and Secondary Auction Procedures would continue to provide participants with a strong incentive to bid competitively in the auction, with the goal of reaching an efficient auction clearing price that permits ICC to close out the defaulter's portfolio and return ICC to a matched book. Further, consistent with the requirement in this Rule, ICC continues to require both Full Participants and ACPs to participate in the testing and review of its default procedures. While bidding would be voluntary under the proposed changes to the Initial Auction Procedure and the Secondary Auction Procedures, CPs, including ACPs, would continue to be required to participate in default management simulations, pursuant to existing ICC Rule 201(b). Therefore, ICC believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the requirements of Rule 17ad-22(e)(13).
[
23
]
Rule 17ad-22(e)(18)
[
24
]
requires a covered clearing agency to establish, implement, maintain and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to establish objective, risk-based and publicly disclosed criteria for participation, and to require participants to have sufficient financial resources to meet obligations arising from participation in the clearing agency. The amendments continue to clearly and transparently set out the rights, obligations and responsibilities of ACPs. ACPs would largely have the same rights and obligations as Full Participants, with certain exceptions discussed above. Further, the amendments allow ICC to establish heightened financial resource requirements on ACPs, including a Guaranty Fund contribution equal to
(
printed page 75414)
125% of the Guaranty Fund contribution that would be required of a Full Participant holding the same cleared positions and a minimum Required Contribution to the Guaranty Fund of $25 million. In ICC's view, the proposed amendments facilitate participation in the ACP category of CP, while maintaining robust risk and default management. The proposed rule change is thus consistent with the requirements of Rule 17ad-22(e)(18).
[
25
]
(B) Clearing Agency's Statement on Burden on Competition
ICC does not believe the proposed rule changes would have any impact, or impose any burden, on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The changes amend the ACP category to revise certain terms applicable to ACPs, including price submission obligations and default auction bidding requirements, while preserving ICC's ability to manage the risk presented by ACPs, as described above. The changes are designed to encourage participation in the ACP category and are intended to broaden access to ICC's CDS Clearing Service for institutions that may not otherwise satisfy all requirements applicable to Full Participants, thereby promoting increased clearing activity and applying ICC's risk management framework to a broader range of market activity. ACPs will otherwise be subject to the same rights, obligations and responsibilities as Full Participants. As a result, ICC does not believe the amendments will adversely impact competition among clearing members or other market participants, adversely affect the ability of market participants to access clearing generally, or adversely affect the cost of clearing. ICC thus does not believe the proposed amendments would have any impact, or impose any burden, on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
(C) Clearing Agency's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change, Security-Based Swap Submission, or Advance Notice Received From Members, Participants or Others
Written comments relating to the proposed rule change have not been received. ICC will notify the Commission of any written comments received by ICC.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change, Security-Based Swap Submission, and Advance Notice and Timing for Commission Action
Within 45 days of the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
or within such longer period up to 90 days (i) as the Commission may designate if it finds such longer period to be appropriate and publishes its reasons for so finding or (ii) as to which the self-regulatory organization consents, the Commission will:
(A) by order approve or disapprove such proposed rule change, or
(B) institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule change should be disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views, and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules-regulations/​self-regulatory-organization-rulemaking
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-ICC-2026-012 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-ICC-2026-012. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method of submission. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules-regulations/​self-regulatory-organization-rulemaking
). Copies of such filings will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of ICE Clear Credit and on ICE Clear Credit's website at
https://www.ice.com/​clear-credit/​regulation
.
Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-ICC-2026-012 and should be submitted on or before December 11, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
26
]
Vanessa A. Countryman,
Secretary.

and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
3
]
notice is hereby given that, on November 4, 2026, the Investors Exchange LLC (“IEX” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Pursuant to the provisions of Section 19(b)(1) of the Act,
[
4
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
5
]
the Exchange proposes to amend Rule 11.270 (“Clearly Erroneous Executions”) in light of the Commission's approval of Overnight Price Bands that will apply when trading by other national securities exchanges expands to 23 hours per day, 5 days per week (“23/5 Trading”).
The text of the proposed rule change is available at the Exchange's website at
https://www.iex.io/​resources/​regulation/​rule-filings
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
(
printed page 75415)
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The self-regulatory organization has prepared summaries, set forth in Sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and the Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
In light of the Commission's approval of Overnight Price Bands under the LULD Plan for 23/5 Trading, the Exchange proposes to amend Rule 11.270 (“Clearly Erroneous Executions”).
Background
In conjunction with the industry's plans for the introduction of 23/5 Trading, the Operating Committee of the Plan to Address Extraordinary Market Volatility (“LULD Plan”) filed proposed Amendment 27 to the LULD Plan, which proposed to establish price band protections during overnight trading hours (“Overnight Price Bands”).
[
6
]
The Operating Committee proposed that the Overnight Price Bands would initially be temporary static bands 20% above and below two reference points, and that after implementation, the Operating Committee would evaluate the performance of such Overnight Price Bands and propose appropriate changes in a new plan amendment.
[
7
]
On August 5, 2026, the Commission approved the proposal.
[
8
]
In light of the Commission's approval of these changes to the LULD Plan, the Exchange now proposes several amendments to Rule 11.270 regarding Clearly Erroneous Executions.
In general, Rule 11.270 describes the process a market participant may use to request cancellation of a transaction that was “clearly erroneous.” The current rule's central premise is that if LULD Price Bands under the LULD Plan were available and correct at the time the transaction was executed, the transaction is not eligible for clearly erroneous review. Specifically, Rule 11.270(c)(1) currently provides that “[i]f the execution time of the transaction(s) under review is during Regular Market Hours, the transaction will not be reviewable as clearly erroneous” except in certain limited circumstances, including when (A) the transaction is in an NMS Stock that is not subject to the LULD Plan (
i.e.,
rights and warrants); (B) the transaction was executed at a time when LULD Price Bands were not available or trading should have been prevented due to a regulatory halt or other halt; or (C) several other limited circumstances.
[
9
]
In approving the existing version of the rule, the Commission noted that restricting clearly erroneous review in this way during times when LULD Price Bands were in effect was “consistent with the Act and will further the goal of providing greater certainty to market participants that trades executed within the Price Bands will stand and not be broken . . . . Thus, the proposal is designed to limit the potential discordance between the LULD mechanism and CEE review process.”
[
10
]
Currently, LULD Price Bands are available only during Regular Market Hours, meaning that the restrictions on clearly erroneous review described above apply only during Regular Market Hours. With the introduction of Overnight Price Bands, the Exchange now proposes to extend the existing restrictions on clearly erroneous review to the period when Overnight Price Bands are in place. This proposed change would be consistent with the Commission's rationale in approving the current version of the rule because it would limit any potential discordance between the LULD mechanism and CEE review in the overnight trading session, providing greater certainty to market participants that trades executed within the Overnight Price Bands will stand and not be broken.
Proposed Changes to Rule 11.270(c)(1)
To implement this change, the Exchange proposes to add several definitions to Rule 11.270(c)(1). First, the Exchange would add that the term “LULD Protected Hours” includes Regular Market Hours and “Overnight Protected Hours” defined in Section VIII of the LULD Plan. Second, the Exchange would define “LULD Price Bands” or “Price Bands” to mean the Price Bands defined in Section V of the LULD Plan (
i.e.,
the Price Bands that apply during Regular Market Hours) and “Overnight Price Bands” as defined in Section VIII of the LULD Plan (
i.e.,
the Price Bands that apply to the Overnight Protected Hours from 9:00 p.m. ET through 4:00 a.m. ET).
The Exchange proposes to amend the current first sentence of Rule 11.270(c)(1) to replace the phrase “Regular Market Hours” with “LULD Protected Hours,” to provide that “[i]f the execution time of the transaction(s) under review is during LULD Protected Hours, the transaction will not be reviewable as clearly erroneous . . . .” This change would extend the LULD-based restrictions on clearly erroneous review currently in place during the Regular Market Hours to the Overnight Protected Hours.
The Exchange also proposes to amend Rule 11.270(c)(1)(B)'s reference to “Percentage Parameter” to incorporate the Percentage Parameter that applies to Overnight Protected Hours. The amended provision would provide for the applicability of clearly erroneous review if the price of the transaction to buy (sell) that is the subject of the clearly erroneous complaint is greater than (less than) the Reference Price by an amount that equals or exceeds the applicable Percentage Parameter defined in Appendix A to the LULD Plan (with respect to the Price Bands that apply during Regular Market Hours) or the “Overnight Percentage Parameter” defined in Section VIII of the LULD Plan (with respect to Overnight Protected Hours).
In addition to these changes, the Exchange also proposes to make a non-substantive change to Rule 11.270(c)(1)(A), substituting the term “LULD Plan” for the current text “the Plan to Address Extraordinary Market Volatility Pursuant to Rule 608 of Regulation NMS under the Act (the `Limit Up-Limit Down Plan' or `LULD Plan')” as the “LULD Plan” would be defined in the proposed revision to Rule 11.270(c)(1).
Proposed Changes to Rule 11.270(c)(2), (d)(3), and (f)
As noted above, current Rule 11.270(c)(1)(A) permits clearly erroneous review even during Regular Market Hours when the transaction in question is in an NMS Stock that is not subject to the LULD Plan,
i.e.,
rights and
(
printed page 75416)
warrants. Such transactions are reviewed for clearly erroneous status using the procedures set out in Rule 11.270(c)(2), including the Numerical Guidelines set out in the table accompanying Rule 11.270(c)(2)(A). The Exchange now proposes to introduce a similar provision regarding transactions in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan that are executed during the Overnight Protected Hours; such transactions would be subject to the same Numerical Guidelines as transactions occurring in the Pre-Market or Post-Market Session.
The heading of Rule 11.270(c)(2) addresses “[r]eview of transactions occurring during the Pre-Market or Post-Market Sessions, or eligible for review pursuant to paragraph (c)(1)(A).” The Exchange proposes to replace the phrase “eligible for review pursuant to paragraph (c)(1)(A)” (which, in the current rule, means transactions executed during Regular Market Hours in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan) with “during LULD Protected Hours in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan.” This proposed language would cover transactions in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan in the Regular Market Hours and expand the same treatment to transactions executed in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan during Overnight Protected Hours. As such, the proposed change is not novel.
The Exchange proposes to make the same change everywhere else such language appears in the rule—namely, in the text of paragraphs (c)(2)(A), (c)(2)(B), (c)(2)(C), (c)(2)(D), (d)(3), and (f).
[
11
]
In each case, the Exchange proposes to replace the phrase “transactions occurring during the Pre-Market or Post-Market Sessions or eligible for review pursuant to paragraph (c)(1)(A)” with “transactions occurring during the Pre-Market or Post-Market Sessions or during LULD Protected Hours in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan.”
The Exchange also proposes to make corresponding changes to the headings of the table accompanying Rule 11.270(c)(2)(A). The Exchange proposes to change the heading of the second column from “Regular Market Hours Numerical Guidelines for transactions eligible for review pursuant to paragraph (c)(1)(A)” to “Numerical Guidelines for Transactions Executed During Regular Market Hours in NMS Stocks Not Subject to the LULD Plan.” This change would simply replace the shorthand “eligible for review pursuant to paragraph (c)(1)(A)” with the fuller description that such transactions are “executed during Regular Market Hours in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan,” and is not a substantive change.
Similarly, the Exchange proposes to change the heading of the third column from “Pre-Market and Post-Market Session Numerical Guidelines” to “Numerical Guidelines for Transactions Executed During the Pre-Market and Post-Market Session or During Overnight Protected Hours in NMS Stocks Not Subject to the LULD Plan.” The proposed change addresses the fact that transactions executed during Overnight Protected Hours in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan are eligible for clearly erroneous review—just as are transactions in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan executed during Regular Market Hours—but at the Numerical Guidelines that apply outside of Regular Market Hours.
Together, these proposed changes would extend the eligibility of clearly erroneous review for transactions in NMS Stocks not subject to the LULD Plan that is currently in place during Regular Market Hours to the Overnight Protected Hours and would apply the Commission's recent approval of Overnight Price Bands to the clearly erroneous executions rule.
Implementation
The Exchange understands that the other national securities exchanges and FINRA have already filed or will file similar proposals concerning the proposed amendment to the Clearly Erroneous Executions rule, the substance of which is identical to this proposal. The Exchange proposes that this rule change would become operative at the commencement of 23/5 Trading, which is scheduled to commence industry-wide on December 6, 2026.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder that are applicable to a national securities exchange, and, in particular, with the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
12
]
Specifically, the proposal is consistent with Section 6(b)(5) of the Act
[
13
]
because it would promote just and equitable principles of trade, remove impediments to, and perfect the mechanism of, a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, protect investors and the public interest.
The Exchange believes that the proposed change is consistent with just and equitable principles of trade because it extends the basic premise of the current rule that clearly erroneous review should be generally unavailable any time a transaction is executed within LULD Price Bands at a time the Price Bands were available and correct. Currently, LULD Price Bands are available only during Regular Market Hours, meaning that the restrictions on clearly erroneous review described above apply only during Regular Market Hours. With the introduction of Overnight Price Bands, the Exchange believes that extending such restrictions on clearly erroneous review to the period when Overnight Price Bands are in place would remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system by enhancing the transparency and consistency of the rule.
The resulting rule would thus extend the LULD-related limits on clearly erroneous review that are applicable in Regular Market Hours to the overnight period. The proposed change would also be consistent with the Commission's rationale in approving the current version of the rule because it would limit any potential discordance between the LULD mechanism and CEE review in the overnight trading session, providing greater certainty to market participants that trades executed within the Overnight Price Bands will stand and not be broken.
[
14
]
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange believes the proposal is consistent with Section 6(b)(8) of the Act
[
15
]
in that it will not impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
Rather than impacting competition, the proposed change would simply extend the basic premise of the current rule that clearly erroneous review should be generally unavailable any time a transaction is executed within LULD Price Bands at a time the Price Bands were available and correct. The Exchange understands that the other
(
printed page 75417)
national securities exchanges and FINRA have filed or will also file similar proposals, the substance of which is identical to this proposal. Thus, the proposed rule change will help to ensure consistency across SROs without implicating any competitive issues.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
Written comments were neither solicited nor received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has designated this rule filing as non-controversial under Section 19(b)(3)(A)
[
16
]
of the Act and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
17
]
thereunder. Because the proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
18
]
A proposed rule change filed under Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
19
]
normally does not become operative prior to 30 days after the date of the filing. However, pursuant to Rule 19b-4(f)(6)(iii),
[
20
]
the Commission may designate a shorter time if such action is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. The Exchange has asked the Commission to waive the 30-day operative delay to the extent necessary, so that the proposed rule change may become operative upon effectiveness to enable the proposed rule change to become operative on December 6, 2026, when other exchanges will commence 23/5 trading. Waiving the 30-day operative delay in this manner will help to ensure consistency across SROs and avoid confusion. For these reasons, and because the proposed rule change raises no new or novel legal or regulatory issues, the Commission finds that waiver of the operative delay is consistent with the protection of investors and the public interest. Accordingly, the Commission waives the 30-day operative delay and designates the proposed rule change to be operative upon filing.
[
21
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B)
[
22
]
of the Act to determine whether the proposed rule change should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-IEX-2026-47 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-IEX-2026-47. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-IEX-2026-47 and should be submitted on or before December 11, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
23
]
Vanessa A. Countryman,
Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106919; File No. SR-MEMX-2026-35]
November 17, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”)
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on November 9, 2026, MEMX LLC (“MEMX” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Exchange filed the proposal as a “non-controversial” proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
3
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.
[
4
]
The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange is filing with the Commission a proposed rule change to adopt new Chapter 30 of the Exchange Rules to permit the listing and trading of binary options overlying key performance indicators (“KPIs”) reported by certain issuers of stock (“binary KPI options”) on the Exchange's options platform (“MEMX Options”), and to make related changes to Exchange Rules 16.1, 16.2, 20.6, and 21.17. The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5 and is available on the Exchange's website at
https://info.memxtrading.com/​regulation/​rules-and-filings/​
.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to adopt rules to permit the listing of binary options overlying key performance indicators (“KPIs”) reported by certain issuers of stock (“binary KPI options”) on MEMX
(
printed page 75387)
Options. The proposed rules are substantially similar to rules of Cboe Exchange, Inc. (“Cboe”) that the Commission recently approved.
[
5
]
By way of background, binary options are based on the same framework as traditional, standardized options traded on the Exchange, except the payout of a binary option is a fixed amount contingent upon the occurrence of the option being in- or at-the-money rather than an amount based on the degree to which the option is in-the-money. As a result, payout at expiration of a binary option is an all-or-nothing occurrence.
The Exchange does not currently list binary options. The Exchange proposes to adopt rules to permit the listing of binary KPI options. Binary KPI options are European-style, cash-settled options contracts listed on an underlying KPI of an issuer. The exercise settlement value of a binary KPI option is determined not by the market price of the issuer's stock, but by whether a specific financial or operating metric that is reported by the issuer in an earnings-related filing submitted to the Commission meets or exceeds a pre-specified strike level.
Summary of Differences From the Cboe Rules
The proposed rules are based on, and are substantially similar to, the Cboe Rules, and the Exchange proposes to list binary KPI options on the same issuers and KPIs, with the same contract terms, as the binary KPI options approved for listing on Cboe. Throughout this filing, the Exchange has generally used the same language as the Cboe Proposal where the Exchange is adopting the same approach as Cboe. In addition to non-substantive differences (such as conforming changes to reflect the Exchange's rule numbering, defined terms, and existing rules) and other minor differences described in this filing, the proposed rules differ from the Cboe Rules in the following material respects, each of which is further described below:
Rule structure.
Cboe adopted its binary KPI option rules in part by amending its existing rules governing binary index options. Because the Exchange does not currently list binary options, the Exchange proposes to adopt the rules applicable to binary KPI options in a single new Chapter 30, to add provisions applicable to binary KPI options to Rules 20.6 (Nullification and Adjustment of Options Transactions including Obvious Errors) and 21.17 (Additional Price Protection Mechanisms and Risk Controls), and to make conforming changes to Rules 16.1 and 16.2 to reflect that the Rules applicable to options trading on the Exchange will include Chapter 30. The proposed rules also make conforming changes to reflect the Exchange's rule numbering, defined terms, and existing rules.
Clearing.
Cboe intends to clear binary KPI options through Cboe Clear US, LLC (“CCUS”), and the Cboe Proposal describes certain provisions of CCUS's proposed rules. The Exchange proposes to define “Clearing Corporation,” for purposes of binary KPI options, as the registered clearing agency designated by the Exchange to clear binary KPI options, and to provide that references in the Rules to The Options Clearing Corporation (“OCC”) mean the Clearing Corporation with respect to binary KPI options. The Exchange will submit a separate proposed rule change to the Commission to designate the registered clearing agency that will serve as the Clearing Corporation for binary KPI options. The Exchange represents that it will not list binary KPI options for trading until the Clearing Corporation is registered with the Commission and operationally ready to clear binary KPI options, all applicable filings and documents of the Clearing Corporation related to binary KPI options are approved by the Commission or effective after review by the Commission, as applicable, the applicable disclosure document required by Rule 9b-1 under the Act is in place, and the other conditions described below are satisfied.
Maximum execution price.
Proposed Rule 21.17(h) is substantially similar to Cboe Rule 5.34(d), which permits Cboe to designate a maximum execution price for a binary option class, except that, pursuant to proposed Rule 21.17(h), the System will prevent executions of binary KPI options at prices above the Exchange-designated maximum execution price, rather than adjusting such execution prices down to the maximum execution price, as provided in Cboe Rule 5.34(d). Consistent with that rule, the Exchange will designate the maximum execution price for each class of binary KPI options and will notify Options Members of the designated maximum execution price.
Opening.
Cboe Rule 5.31(d)(1)(D) provides that the opening rotation for binary KPI options is initiated at 9:30 a.m. Proposed Rule 30.6(f) instead provides that binary KPI options will open for trading in accordance with Rule 21.7 (Market Opening Procedures), with the stock of the issuer treated as the security underlying the option for purposes of that Rule.
Trading functionality.
Binary KPI options will generally be subject to the same trading functionality on MEMX Options as other options listed on the Exchange. The Exchange does not currently offer complex order functionality, auction mechanisms, floor trading, or flexible exchange options (“FLEX”) on MEMX Options, and, accordingly, the discussion in the Cboe Proposal of the application of such functionality to binary KPI options does not apply to the Exchange's proposal.
Proposed Chapter 30 and Conforming Changes to Chapter 16
First, the Exchange proposes to adopt Chapter 30 (Binary KPI Options) to describe binary KPI options. The Rules in proposed Chapter 30 apply only to binary KPI options. All other Rules apply to the trading of binary KPI options, except as otherwise provided or the context otherwise requires.
[
6
]
The Exchange also proposes to make conforming changes to Rules 16.1 and 16.2 to reflect the addition of Chapter 30 to the Rules applicable to options trading on the Exchange. Currently, the introductory paragraph to Rule 16.1 provides that the definitions in Rule 16.1 apply with respect to the Rules contained in Chapters 16 to 29, the definition of “Rules of MEMX Options” in Rule 16.1 refers to the rules contained in Chapters 16 to 29, Rule 16.2(a) provides that the Rules contained in Chapters 16 to 29 are the Exchange Rules applicable to the trading of options contracts on MEMX Options, and Rule 16.2(b) provides that, to the extent the Rules relating to options trading contained in Chapters 16 to 29 are inconsistent with any other
(
printed page 75388)
provisions of the Exchange Rules, the Rules relating to options trading control. The Exchange proposes to amend each of these provisions to refer to Chapters 16 to 30. These proposed changes will ensure that the definitions in Rule 16.1 apply to terms used in proposed Chapter 30 (unless otherwise defined in Chapter 30), and that the Rules in proposed Chapter 30 are treated in the same manner as the Exchange's other options Rules.
Additionally, proposed Chapter 30 provides that, with respect to binary KPI options, unless the context otherwise requires, references in the Rules to The Options Clearing Corporation, OCC, or the Clearing Corporation mean the Clearing Corporation (as defined in proposed Rule 30.1), and references to the rules or by-laws of The Options Clearing Corporation mean the Rules of the Clearing Corporation. As discussed below, proposed Rule 30.1 defines the term “Clearing Corporation” as the registered clearing agency designated by the Exchange to clear binary KPI options. Pursuant to the introductory paragraph to proposed Chapter 30, all Rules (including Rules outside of Chapter 30) apply to the trading of binary KPI options, except as otherwise provided or the context otherwise requires. A number of those Rules outside of Chapter 30 refer to OCC, either expressly (for example, references to The Options Clearing Corporation or to the rules or by-laws of OCC) or through the terms “Clearing Corporation” and “OCC,” which Rule 16.1 currently defines to mean OCC (for example, the definitions of “options contract” and “put” in Rule 16.1 and the applicability provision in Rule 16.2(a)).
[
7
]
The purpose of the proposed provision is to ensure that, when these Rules outside of Chapter 30 are applied to binary KPI options, their references to OCC (and to the rules or by-laws of OCC) will be read to refer to the registered clearing agency designated by the Exchange to clear binary KPI options (and to its rules), rather than to OCC specifically, without the need to amend each such Rule. The “unless the context otherwise requires” qualifier ensures that the provision will not apply to references in the Rules that relate to OCC in a context other than the clearing of binary KPI options (for example, references to OCC's calculation of national cleared volume in Rule 21.5).
Proposed Rule 30.1 (Definitions)
The Exchange proposes to adopt Rule 30.1 (Definitions). Like other standardized options, binary KPI options have standardized terms that are established by the Exchange. Standardized terms for binary KPI options include the exercise criterion that is the condition or criterion of a binary KPI option, the exercise settlement amount (
i.e.,
payout amount), the strike price, the expiration date, the settlement type as A.M.-settlement or P.M.-settlement, the exercise style (as European-style), and the requirements used to determine if the KPI condition or criterion of a binary KPI option has been met (the “payout determination”
[
8
]
). The Exchange proposes to establish these terms in proposed Rule 30.1 and additional provisions related to binary KPI options in proposed Chapter 30, as described below.
The Exchange proposes to define a “binary KPI option” in proposed Rule 30.1 as a cash-settled option contract listed on an underlying KPI of an issuer with an exercise settlement amount that is established at the creation of the option and with a settlement value that is determined by whether a specific KPI disclosed by the issuer in an earnings-related filing submitted to the Commission meets or exceeds its exercise price. Binary KPI options are paid out if the reported value of the applicable KPI (1) equals or is greater than (
i.e.,
the payout determination) the exercise price for a call binary KPI option or (2) is less than (
i.e.,
the payout determination) the exercise price for a put binary KPI option.
[
9
]
The Exchange also proposes to provide that unless the context dictates otherwise, the terms underlying security, equity, or index, or any variations of these terms, in the Rules mean KPI for purposes of binary KPI options.
[
10
]
The Exchange proposes to define a “call binary KPI option” as an option contract that returns an exercise settlement amount if the settlement value of the underlying KPI is at or above the exercise price at expiration (
i.e.,
in- or at-the-money).
[
11
]
The Exchange proposes to define “Clearing Corporation” as the registered clearing agency designated by the Exchange to clear binary KPI options.
[
12
]
The Exchange proposes to define “exercise price” (also referred to as “strike price”) as the value
[
13
]
to which the settlement value of the underlying KPI is compared to determine whether the holder of a binary KPI option is entitled to the exercise settlement amount.
[
14
]
For binary KPI options, the exercise price is the exercise threshold of an option contract that establishes the number that is compared against the settlement value of the underlying KPI to determine if the cash payout amount (
i.e.,
the exercise settlement amount) will be paid out. In other words, binary KPI options will have a threshold number as the exercise price that will be used to determine if the exercise criterion of the binary KPI option has been met, in which case the option will be exercised and holders will receive the cash payout amount (
i.e.,
the exercise settlement amount). For binary KPI options, the exercise threshold will be a number that reflects or is compared to the underlying KPI of the binary option.
The Exchange proposes to define the term KPI (or “key performance
(
printed page 75389)
indicator”) as a key financial or operating metric disclosed by an issuer in its earnings-related filings submitted to the Commission (
i.e.,
Form 8-K, Form 10-Q, or Form 10-K, as applicable).
[
15
]
The Exchange proposes to define “put binary KPI option” as an option contract that returns an exercise settlement amount if the settlement value of the underlying KPI is below the exercise price at expiration (
i.e.,
in-the-money).
[
16
]
The Exchange proposes to define “settlement value” as the value of the underlying KPI that is used to determine whether a binary KPI option is in-, at-, or out-of-the-money.
[
17
]
The proposed definition specifies that the “settlement value” is the value of the applicable KPI as disclosed in the applicable issuer's earnings-related filing submitted to the Commission on the applicable expiration date (for both A.M.-settled and P.M.-settled binary KPI options).
[
18
]
The Exchange designates the applicable KPI and the relevant reporting period (for example, a calendar quarter) at the time of listing a binary KPI option.
Proposed paragraph (b) of the settlement value definition provides if the applicable KPI is not reported or is otherwise unavailable on the expiration date,
[
19
]
settlement (including any payout of the exercise settlement amount) will occur in accordance with the Rules of the Clearing Corporation.
[
20
]
The Exchange will not list binary KPI options for trading unless procedures are established that will apply if the KPI value needed to determine whether a binary KPI option is at- or in-the-money is not available (“alternative settlement procedures”), which procedures will be subject to the applicable regulatory process, including review and approval by the Commission, as applicable.
[
21
]
By way of example, the alternative settlement procedures applicable to binary KPI options listed on Cboe (as described in the Cboe Proposal) provide that if the KPI value needed to determine whether a binary KPI option is at- or in-the-money is not available, expiring contracts will be exercised but may result in delivery of an alternative exercise settlement amount. The alternative exercise settlement amount may be the last closing price of the binary KPI option (
i.e.,
the market valuation of the KPI event), meaning that the alternative exercise settlement amount will be between $0.01 and $1.00, rather than the expected $0.00 or $1.00. If an option closing price is not available or is deemed by the clearing agency to be unreliable, the exercise criterion for binary option contracts on that KPI event will be deemed to have not been met, and the binary options will expire unexercised and worthless.
Additionally, proposed paragraph (c) of the settlement value definition states if an applicable KPI is restated after the expiration date and settlement of a binary KPI option, the settlement value (and the exercise settlement amount) of the binary KPI option does not change.

if the most recently disclosed KPI value is greater than or equal to one trillion, the exercise price equals that value divided by one trillion (

if the most recently disclosed KPI value is greater than or equal to one billion but less than one trillion, the exercise price equals that value divided by one billion (
e.g.,
for such KPIs, an exercise price of 112.00 is equivalent to a KPI value of 112,000,000,000.00);
if the most recently disclosed KPI value is greater than or equal to one million but less than one billion, the exercise price equals that value divided by one million (
e.g.,
for such KPIs, an exercise price of 900.00 is equivalent to a KPI value of 900,000,000.00);
if the most recently disclosed KPI value is greater than or equal to one thousand but less than one million, the exercise price equals that value divided by one thousand (
e.g.,
for such KPIs, an exercise price of 42.00 is equivalent to a KPI value of 42,000.00); and
if the most recently disclosed KPI value is less than one thousand, the exercise price equals that value and is not divided by a scaling factor (
e.g.,
for such KPIs, an exercise price of 774.00 is equivalent to a KPI value of 774.00).

As discussed above, while KPI values above 1,000 are generally scaled, there may be circumstances in which the Exchange lists strikes above 1,000 or even 10,000 given the Exchange's proposal to maintain a lower scale level until a KPI value is consistently above a certain level (
e.g.,
above one billion for four consecutive quarters). This may occur when a KPI value is near the top of a scaling range; for continuity, the Exchange will continue listing strike prices using the lower scaling factor and not change to a higher scaling factor until the KPI value is regularly within that higher range (as noted above). Suppose a KPI value is 995,000,000; in this case, strike prices will be scaled by 1,000,000. Thus, the Exchange may list binary KPI options above and below 995 (995,000,000 divided by 1,000,000). However, it is realistic that the KPI may increase to above 1,000,000,000. As proposed, the Exchange may list strike prices, for example, of 1,000 (representing 1,000,000,000) and above, for expirations until the KPI value is above 1,000,000,000 for four consecutive reporting periods. To reduce confusion, the Exchange would not scale strike prices using different scaling factors within a single expiration (and would not change the scale until the KPI value is consistently at the higher level). Therefore, it is possible the Exchange may list strikes greater than 1,000. Similarly, while strikes above 10,000 may be rare, given the Exchange proposes to maintain a lower scale level until a KPI value is consistently above a certain level (
e.g.,
above one billion for four consecutive quarters, as proposed), depending on market factors and demand, it is possible (although unlikely) the Exchange may determine it is appropriate to list strikes above 10,000 if market factors or expectations signify a significant increase of the KPI value. The proposed strike intervals accommodate the listing of binary KPI options in these circumstances before the Exchange shifts the strike prices for an issuer's KPI to a different scaling level.
The proposed strike intervals are generally consistent with current Rules for other options, which provide for larger strike intervals as the values of strike prices increase. Given the scaling factors for larger KPI values, it may appear the proposed rule change will permit smaller strike intervals for larger KPI values if those intervals are considered solely on a nominal basis. However, that is not the case if the actual values of the strike intervals are considered. The corresponding actual value of the strike interval for a strike price that was subject to a larger scale value is higher than the actual value of the strike interval for a strike price that was subject to a smaller scale value. For example, suppose a strike price of 950 represents $950 million. The proposed rule change would permit strike intervals of $1.00. However, that $1.00 corresponds to $1,000,000. In other words, if the Exchange listed strikes of 950, 951, and 952, the difference in the actual value between those strikes is $1,000,000, not $1 (
i.e.,
the strikes represent values of $950,000,000, $951,000,000, and $952,000,000). Similarly, suppose a strike price of 3 represents $3,000,000,000. The proposed rule change would permit strike intervals of $0.01. However, in this case, that $0.01 corresponds to $10,000,000. If the Exchange listed strikes of 3.00, 3.01, and 3.02, the difference in the actual value between those strikes is $10,000,000, not $0.01 (
i.e.,
the strikes represent values of $3,000,000,000, $3,010,000,000, and $3,020,000,000, respectively). As a result, the permissible strike intervals between strike prices representing values in the billions are actually larger than the permissible strike intervals between strike prices representing values in the millions. This is consistent with the general premise underlying current strike intervals that larger strike intervals apply to larger strike values.

The “at-the-money” KPI value may be the value of the KPI in the issuer's most recent earnings-related filing submitted to the Commission, the issuer's disclosed estimate of the KPI for the next reporting period, or analysts' consensus estimate as reported by major market vendors, as the Exchange deems appropriate based on the most recent market information available to the Exchange. Because KPIs are static values, the Exchange believes it is appropriate to determine strike prices based on all available information that would inform expectations about the KPIs (as investors would do). The Exchange understands that an issuer's previously disclosed KPI, as well as issuer and analyst estimates of the KPI, are primary factors investors may consider when determining in which direction the KPI value may move in the next reporting period (similar to how investors consider the then-current price of an underlying stock when considering their options investment strategies and which direction the stock price may move). Therefore, the Exchange believes using the most recently available of these values is appropriate to use for determining which strikes it should list for a specific issuer KPI. The Exchange believes this flexibility to select the most appropriate at-the-money value is similar to current Rules that permit the Exchange to list additional series to maintain an orderly market, to meet customer demand, or when the market price of the underlying security moves substantially.

As proposed, the Exchange would list strikes above and below the at-the-money strike, which at the time of listing may be the settlement value KPI from the issuer's second quarter earnings results disclosure (the most recently available KPI). After the Exchange lists those series, the issuer discloses its third quarter earnings results, including net sales of $57.241 billion. As proposed, after that disclosure, the Exchange may list additional strikes within 30% of $57.24 to reflect the change in value of the underlying (as well as additional series based on customer demand or market changes).
